Syria's former dictator Bashar Assad was sentenced to death for crimes against his own people. But for many civil war survivors, it's not enough
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
18:56:00 UTC
03:56:00 KST

Why many Syrians feel Assad death sentence isn't enough
September 5, 2026
Huda Khayti often finds herself returning to the place where she lost almost everything. Khayti, a Syrian women's rights activist, survived a 2013 chemical weapons attack on the east Ghouta region by forces of the former Syrian dictator Bashar Assad.
Her brother was killed by the bombs of the Assad regime and its allies. Her women's center was destroyed along with her home and in 2018, she had to leave her hometown of Douma — a major city in Ghouta — and flee to Idlib, a rebel stronghold in northern Syria.
Today, Khayti regularly visits her hometown, which is about 10 kilometers (about 6 miles) northeast of the country's capital, Damascus. Since the Assad regime was overthrown in late 2024, Khayti has traveled regularly between Idlib and Douma, where she's even working on opening a new women's center.
"Ghouta means so much to me emotionally," she told DW. But every time she returns there, she is also confronted with remnants of the civil war. "When I'm traveling through the country I see traces of war everywhere, so many houses and so much infrastructure destroyed. So much suffering. So much trauma."
Almost two years since the overthrow of the Assad regime, Syria has started a process to examine the crimes of the regime in court. In mid-August a Damascus court sentenced Bashar Assad and other high-ranking members of his regime to death in absentia. Assad is currently living in Russia, where he fled after his government was overthrown. Many senior officials are also there or hiding elsewhere.
Among other things, Assad was found guilty of premeditated murder, torture and depriving individuals of their liberty. The court said these were war crimes and crimes against humanity.
"Of course, this conviction of Assad is a good thing," Khayti said. "Even if it's only on paper. Bashar Assad may have been convicted but he just continues to live his life in Russia — like so many other Syrian criminals who fled to Russia."
Justice served in Syria?
The court's conviction had a big impact in Syria anyway. "The verdict had a lot of echoes by people, they were so happy," said Lina Chawaf, a Syrian journalist, media expert and researcher at Harvard University's Center for Middle Eastern Studies. "Many media celebrated the verdict on the statement day as a victory and consider it as part of transitional justice."
Still, it remains unclear whether there will be any actual punishment following the conviction. Although Russia and Syria agreed on an extradition treaty in 2023, observers say it's unlikely Russia would send Assad, a long-time ally, back to Syria. Additionally, according to the treaty, if the death penalty is likely, that could prevent extradition too.
In August, Syria's Deputy Justice Minister Mustafa al-Qassem said the country had established a commission to cooperate with Interpol and that cooperation with other countries in extraditing fugitive suspects would speed up legal proceedings.
Rana Sheikh-Ali, founder of Daret Salam (Peace Circuit in English), which uses technology to build peace and empower women, believes the Assad trial in August should be seen as largely symbolic. From a human rights perspective, she opposes the death penalty, but at the same time she says many locals saw the death sentences as just.
But the prosecution of high-ranking regime members is only one aspect of the transitional justice process.
Transitional justice isn't just about criminal trials. Other aspects include searching for missing people, investigating crimes, deciding on reparations and formulating institutional reforms. With all that, the focus should be on victims and survivors.
Numbers supplied by the Syrian Network for Human Rights indicate just how big the task is. In an article, the advocacy network reports that over 234,805 civilians were killed during the civil war, at least 202,000 of them by the Assad regime and its allies.
In addition, there are also at least 181,312 cases of arbitrary arrest and enforced disappearance to investigate as well as 45,339 deaths resulting from torture. It's thought that the actual numbers are likely far higher. The network has also documented 217 chemical weapons attacks by the Assad regime.
Victim-centered process needed
Women's rights activist Khayti was just a few kilometers from the epicenter of one of those attacks in eastern Ghouta in 2013. "I remember it like it was yesterday," she recounted. "I can't forget the screams of the victims. I kept thinking we were next. I felt that scratchiness in my throat, that burning in my eyes."
For a system of transitional justice that is truly victim-centered, it's not enough to just have survivors act as witnesses in court. "Victims must also participate in every detail related to the transitional justice process," she explained.
Additionally, those who were impacted by the crimes must be able to participate voluntarily and be protected as they do, Sheikh-Ali added. They should be able to talk about their experiences and should also be heard on topics like compensation, financial support and public recognition.
For survivors like Khayti, this means not just making Assad and a few top regime officials the primary targets of justice.
"I also want to see convictions for individuals who wrote reports that led to people ending up in the Saydnaya torture prison," Khayti said. "These individuals are just as guilty as the torturers themselves."
At the moment, though, it's unclear exactly how thoroughly Syria will confront its past.
"Convictions in absentia against Assad and other officials send an important signal after decades of impunity," said Sophie Bischoff, managing director of Adopt a Revolution, a German-Syrian human rights organization that supports civil society initiatives. "But for survivors like Huda Khayti, these sentences remain symbolic as long as those convicted are not actually held accountable — and it's also still not transparent exactly who is to be held accountable and on what legal basis, and who would be granted immunity."
Bischoff also noted that the new Syrian state has yet to fully and comprehensively investigate crimes against humanity and war crimes committed in Syria.
"So far it's primarily been Syrian civil society organizations and human rights activists who have been researching and documenting these cases for years," she told DW. "Systematic state documentation of violent crimes committed during the Assad regime era is only just beginning."
The new Syrian government has created two commissions to work on issues of transitional justice. In late August, one of these — the National Commission for Missing Persons — launched a platform called Athar, where families of the missing can submit information.
The other organization, the National Commission for Transitional Justice, was established in May 2025 but has so far dealt only with crimes committed by the Assad regime. It has not dealt with crimes committed by militias fighting the war or the extremist group known as the "Islamic State".
Investigating all war crimes
"This falls far short," said Bischoff. "For a comprehensive reckoning and a new beginning in a Syria for all, the war crimes of all warring parties must be included."
For Khayti, the requirement to place victims at the center of the process of transitional justice also has another difficult aspect. Her testimony is being heard, but at the same time she is forced to return to the original trauma.
"It's difficult for me to talk about it and I often feel like I'm reliving it," Khayti explained.
Sheikh-Ali said centering the victims means those impacted play a meaningful role in the process. But as they do so, she added, they should also be protected.
It's also important to remember these events, Khayti added. In Douma, she is working on ways to preserve recollections of the war. "We need to inform younger people about it so that the memory doesn't fade," she said.
In Syria, she said now it's about finding the missing, holding all perpetrators to account, fully investigating all crimes and giving survivors a voice.
"We will continue to be loud," Khayti said. "And we will continue to demand justice."
This article was originally written in German.

Thousands protest in Croatia to demand government clean up toxic waste
Demonstrators in Zagreb accuse Croatia’s government of dragging its feet on a hazardous waste scandal.
Tens of thousands of protesters have marched through the Croatian capital demanding the government urgently clear a vast illegal dump of hazardous waste that residents say is poisoning a once-pristine mountain region.
Saturday’s demonstration in Zagreb was one of the largest protests Croatia has seen in years, driven by growing frustration that authorities have spent months failing to remove more than 30,000 tonnes of waste, including medical and industrial material, buried near the town of Gospic in the mountainous Lika region.

The anger has widened into a broader challenge to Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic’s conservative government, which opponents accuse of corruption and of covering up the pollution’s true scale.
Police and Europol, the European Union’s law enforcement agency, arrested 13 people in February over the illegal importing and dumping of the waste, brought in from elsewhere in the bloc since 2023.
Investigators said the scheme earned suspects more than $4m before it was uncovered at an abandoned industrial site outside Gospic.
Plenkovic visited the site last week and said his government had chosen a contractor to begin removing the waste, the first phase of a promised cleanup.
Croatian officials have also said soil and water tests around Gospic have not shown contamination, a claim that clashes with an assessment published last month by Croatia’s anticorruption agency, which found elevated metal levels in the soil and detected PFAS chemicals, known as “forever chemicals” for how long they persist, in nearby groundwater.
‘Not a tragedy, a crime’
That gap between the government’s assurances and the pollution findings is what brought crowds into Zagreb’s main square on Saturday, where organisers demanded a complete cleanup plan with binding deadlines within 20 days and the removal of all buried waste within three months.
Many protesters said they no longer trusted official explanations for how so much waste had gone unnoticed for so long.
“This is not a tragedy, this is a crime,” demonstrator Ivan Rittinger told The Associated Press news agency, arguing that someone had profited while officials looked away.
Vjekoslav Busic, who leads the Gospic Is Our Home community group that organised the march, told the crowd the failure went beyond any single official, asking who had built the institutions and appointed the people that let the pollution continue for years.
The rally drew lawmakers from across the political spectrum, including the centre-left Social Democratic Party and Most, a smaller anticorruption party whose name means “bridge”, alongside the well-known Croatian actor Rade Serbedzija, a sign of how far the anger has spread beyond any one faction.
Environmental experts say the damage has stayed local so far, but warn the region’s porous terrain and rivers could eventually carry pollutants towards the Adriatic Sea, a coastline the region’s tourism depends on.
Plenkovic has dismissed the criticism as an attempt by rivals to exploit the scandal, even as prosecutors continue investigating a Croatian company accused of burying toxic waste at several sites beyond Gospic.

Why this El Niño is different from all the others
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
18:41:28 UTC
03:41:28 KST

A record El Niño brews in the Pacific. The world is feeling the first impacts
Climate scientists have been closely monitoring what is happening off Australia's east coast over recent months and are increasingly concerned by what they are seeing. Pacific Ocean temperatures, a key driver of El Niño, are rising at an extraordinary pace and starting to enter uncharted territory.
The dark, red tongue spreading in the Pacific is growing at a rate not seen in living memory. The El Niño brewing there is already breaking records, and it is months away from its peak. The sheer magnitude of the event and the uncertainty over what is driving it have alarmed experts.
Among them is senior climatologist at the Bureau of Meteorology Felicity Gamble, who said the rate of warming over the past six months was the fastest ever recorded.
“In terms of daily observations in the central equatorial Pacific, we’re actually seeing record values and record values by quite a significant margin,” she said.
"So very warm ocean temperatures across much of the equatorial tropical Pacific.
"That does raise a lot of concern by meteorologists, oceanographers and marine scientists."
Across the globe, anxiety over its backlash is growing, triggering a stark warning by the World Meteorological Organization (WMO).
"El Niño in Spanish means boy child, but it has the potential to deliver a massive blow to communities and economies across the world. We are already seeing disruption and devastation," WMO secretary-general Celeste Saulo said.
So far, the impacts of El Niño have been relatively mild in Australia. But in other parts of the world, the first ripples are being felt.
"From droughts and floods, we expect these impacts to increase as El Niño intensifies," Professor Saulo said.
"This exceptional El Niño demands exceptional preparation and response. Never before in the 50-year history of the World Meteorological Organization have we launched such a major mobilisation."
Decades of research have deepened our understanding of how Pacific Ocean temperatures shape global weather, leaving countries better prepared than ever for potential impacts.
But questions remain over how El Niño, and its cooler counterpart La Niña, will behave in a warming world.
Fires linked to El Niño have blanketed Indonesia and Malaysia.
1983 El Niño record looms large
In autumn 1982, weather conditions across eastern Australia shifted dramatically and rainfall effectively ceased. The intense dry spell persisted for almost 12 months, with most of Victoria, southern New South Wales and parts of South Australia and Queensland experiencing record low rainfall.
John McBride was a research scientist at the Bureau of Meteorology at the time and said the event, which triggered severe drought, the 1983 Melbourne dust storm and the Ash Wednesday bushfires, "came from nowhere".
"In the lifetime of the active scientists working on atmosphere and ocean, we'd never seen anything like this," he said.
"The map of Australian rainfall over the 12 months was almost the lowest on record everywhere.
"Globally, there were these huge fires setting up across Borneo and Indonesia, and there were major droughts and major flooding events in the Americas."
Scientists did not know at the time that these conditions coincided with one of the strongest El Niño events in the modern era. El Niño and La Niña are the warm and cool phases of a natural climate pattern known as the El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO), which fluctuates every two to seven years.
In the early 80s, ENSO was not well understood, and there was a widespread belief that it was not possible to forecast weather and climate conditions beyond one to two weeks, a consensus challenged by Dr McBride and his colleague Neville Nicholls. The pair published a scientific paper in February 1983 describing the relationship between ENSO and seasonal rainfall in Australia.
It caused a stir among scientists around the world, given the climate conditions unfolding globally at the time, and the findings were pivotal in shaping the modern understanding of seasonal forecasting.
"No-one believed us when we were doing this work … they were saying, 'Maybe it's just statistics, it's just correlations, but there's no physical mechanism by which you can have forecasts on that time scale,'" Dr McBride said.
"The timing of our paper was fortuitous, I guess; we sort of went from people working on things that were wrong to heroes almost overnight."
The Melbourne dust storm and the Ash Wednesday fires fell into the El Niño event of 1982/83.
This year's El Niño behaving differently
In the more than 40 years since Dr McBride and Professor Nicholls's paper, extensive research has built on their findings, leading to detailed seasonal forecasts that help inform decision-making for farmers and emergency services.
Scientists have now identified regions within the Pacific Ocean where they measure water temperatures to help determine which phase ENSO is in. If temperatures are significantly warmer than usual, an El Niño is likely, but colder than usual means it's likely a La Niña could develop.
The key region is known as Niño3.4, and its associated relative index removes the warming trend due to climate change. That's important because otherwise it might seem like El Niño is happening more often.
Models suggest the index will surpass 2.6 degrees Celsius this month, the January 1983 threshold.
While it reached 2.65C in 1902, the reliability of the data improves as time goes on, so '83 can be considered the strongest in living memory. The forecast for this event is a staggering 3.6C, which would obliterate all previous records if it materialises.
El Niño and climate change 'load the dice'
As the world continues to emit record amounts of greenhouse gases, and temperatures rise, research has suggested the natural swings between La Niña and El Niño are becoming more frequent and intense due to climate change.
While it is not entirely clear what is driving the intensity of this year's event, Monash University adjunct professor and climate councillor Andrew Watkins said warming global temperatures could be contributing.
"Climate change basically means that we're heating up the atmosphere, but about 90 per cent of that heat actually gets driven into the oceans," he said.
"The oceans are really what drives El Niño and its opposite, La Niña, and causes a lot of those changes to Australian climate.
"So we get that double impact of climate change warming our atmosphere, but also changing the strength of our El Niño and La Niña events."
While our understanding of El Niño has grown substantially over the past four decades, predicting the exact behaviour of any single effect remains extremely difficult, given the interaction between oceans and the atmosphere is so complex.
Importantly, a record event does not necessarily mean impacts on Australia will be severe or the same as they were during a previously intense El Niño. Several factors influence Australia's climate and weather, including other drivers like the Southern Annular Mode (SAM) and Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD). Local sea surface temperatures and natural weather variability also play a role, while climate change is increasingly having an impact.
"We have had some big El Niños in the past that haven't actually given us widespread drought," Dr Watkins said.
"But very strong El Niños events do load the dice for a drier spring and start of summer, but also a hotter spring and summer, which can have large influences upon our fire weather.
"Unfortunately, we do see more coral bleaching at the end of summer during these big El Niño events."
This year's event is already proving unique in its own right. The signal is very strong and, as expected, temperatures have been warmer than usual. But so far, there has been much more rainfall than what is typically seen during an El Niño year.
The weather bureau's forecast for rainfall in spring shows below average across parts of southern and eastern Australia and above average across much of the country's west, while temperatures are expected to be warmer than usual across the board.
Off the back of successive record-breaking heatwaves across the Northern Hemisphere, climate scientists are warning that next year could be another scorcher, as global temperatures continue to climb well after water temperatures in the Pacific Ocean peak.
And it is not just the Pacific Ocean that is heating up, with the European climate service Copernicus declaring all the world's oceans reached their highest temperatures on record at the end of last month.
"Globally, the hottest years on record typically follow an El Niño event, as a lot of the heat in the ocean gets released into the atmosphere," Dr Watkins said.
"So lots of scientists are talking about 2027 almost being a dead cert for the globe's hottest year."
World braces for impact
Nathaniel Johnson, a meteorologist at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), said the world should leverage El Niño forecasts to prepare for its impacts.
"El Niño is one of our biggest sources of seasonal predictability," he said.
"We need to capitalise on this opportunity to understand the risks that are associated with El Niño and begin our preparations as early as possible."
Dr Johnson said El Niño was starting to play out as expected around the world.
"We've seen drought conditions throughout Central America, and that also tends to occur over parts of South America, parts of the Amazon Basin," he said.
"Also we've seen some enhanced rainfall in the southern parts of South America, particularly in southern Chile.
"They've been recording some atmospheric rivers and flooding rains, and that may be connected to the ongoing El Niño."
UN secretary-general Antonio Guterres said the unprecedented nature of events was an urgent warning for stronger action to reduce emissions and protect people from the impacts of climate change.
"El Niño is being supersized before our eyes. The science leaves no room for doubt: the planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up," he said.
"The race now is between rising risks and our commitment to take climate action and protect people. We must win that race."
Notes on the data
Sea surface temperature (SST) maps source data from the Copernicus Climate Change Service via the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts. SST anomalies are calculated as the difference from 1993-2016 climatology.
El Niño indices use the BOM's Relative Niño3.4 index.

Milei finds unity in pushback against Falkland Islands oil project
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05

03:36:40 KST

Milei finds unity in pushback against Falkland Islands oil project
BUENOS AIRES, Sept 5 - Argentines have broadly backed President Javier Milei’s forceful push against oil drilling near the Falkland Islands, underscoring the enduring resonance of Argentina's sovereignty claim over the British-controlled archipelago.
In a televised address on Thursday, Milei said he would submit a bill to Congress to toughen sanctions against companies drilling and participating in "other activities on the islands that impact our natural resources."
Milei previously favored diplomacy over confrontation on the Falklands. Argentina has claimed sovereignty over the Falkland Islands for nearly two centuries and lost a war with Britain over them in 1982. Britain said on Friday its position was "unwavering."
Because Argentina does not administer the islands, it cannot directly block drilling there.
In Buenos Aires, Mariana Hamicha, a 49-year-old accountant, said Milei's tougher stance signaled Argentina was standing up for its interests.
"I think taking a firm stand, especially regarding the exploitation by foreign companies and the extraction of oil, can be a way of drawing a line in the sand," Hamicha said.
Milei also proposed creating a national security council to coordinate across aerospace and maritime security policy, and pledged more funding for a naval base in the southernmost province of Tierra del Fuego, a strategic gateway to the Falkland Islands and Antarctica. The government has not provided further details on the bill.
“What Milei understood is, this is the moment to act,” said Juan Battaleme, a former secretary of international affairs for defense under Milei.
U.S. MAY REVIEW STANCE: TRUMP
Milei's speech came days after President Donald Trump suggested the U.S. could reconsider its neutral stance, citing frustration with Britain's limited support for U.S.-led military operations in the Middle East.
The Sea Lion oilfield north of the Falkland Islands is operated by majority owner Navitas Petroleum, with Rockhopper Exploration owning 35%. The two owners have strong ties to Israeli investors.
The companies said on Friday they had valid petroleum licenses and did not think Milei's comments would affect the project. Shares of both companies fell sharply on Friday.
Candela Mascetti, a researcher at the Escuela Superior de Guerra in Buenos Aires, said Milei's remarks marked a notable shift for a president often criticized for not giving enough attention to the Falklands issue.
“I don’t think having a naval base implies a call to arms, but it’s a posture that we hadn’t seen from Milei’s government in such a strong way,” Mascetti said.
LOW APPROVAL RATING
Falklands War veterans and the left-wing opposition have criticized Milei for praising former British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher, whose government defeated Argentina in the war over the islands, as one of the world's "greatest leaders." He also said Argentina hoped islanders would "one day decide to vote for us," a comment critics said echoed Britain's emphasis on the residents' right to self-determination.
Milei, expected to run for reelection in 2027, has a low approval rating of 36.8%, according to an August poll by Zuban Cordoba and Associates.
"Given Milei’s poll numbers — and Trump’s hints that he is reconsidering the U.S. position on the dispute — it makes sense that Milei is adopting a harder line," said Benjamin Gedan, director of the U.S.-based Stimson Center's Latin America program.
Even some of his political opponents welcomed Thursday's announcement, while criticizing Milei for not taking aggressive action earlier.
Juan Grabois, a prominent leftist leader, said on X: “Milei’s 180-degree turn is welcome; he went from being a colonized fool to reclaiming Argentina’s historical stance.”
Guillermo Carmona, who oversaw Argentina's policy regarding its claim to the Falklands under the previous center-left government, said Milei's measures were a positive step but insufficient given Argentina's close diplomatic ties to Israel.
"Milei has to pressure the Israeli government," he said.
Israeli officials did not respond to a request for comment on Milei's proposed sanctions. REUTERS

Guyana latest "third country" to accept migrants deported from U.S.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

18:35:46 UTC
03:35:46 KST

Guyana becomes latest "third country" to accept migrants deported from U.S.
Guyana on Friday became the latest "third country" to accept migrants deported from the United States, a U.S. official told CBS News.
The South American country received a handful of Afghan and Cuban deportees expelled by the Trump administration, the official said.
Guyana is one of more than 30 nations that have now signed deals with the Trump administration to accept deportees from the U.S. who are not their own citizens.
The Guyanese government said in a statement that those relocated to the country under what it called the "Assisted Voluntary Return Program" will await the outcome of their immigration cases in Guyana. They could ultimately return to their country of origin or be relocated somewhere else.
The U.N. International Organization for Migration is responsible for implementing the program, authorities in Guyana said, adding that the government will not bear any housing or support costs.
Guyana's Foreign Secretary Robert Persaud told the Associated Press on Saturday that six nationals from Cuba and Afghanistan arrived on Friday after being vetted by his administration and found to have no criminal backgrounds.
Persaud said his administration reached an agreement to host the deportees after months of negotiations. He also told the AP that "the U.S. has not made any further requests." The arrangement will run for a year and does not constitute permanent resettlement, he said.
Guyana, a founding member of the 15-nation Caribbean Community, is the latest of several member states to have received small groups of U.S. deportees. Others include St. Kitts and Nevis, Belize and St. Lucia, which was due to accept its first group this week, officials said.
Human rights activists have denounced the third-country deportations as inhumane and illegal under international law, saying some countries are returning deportees to places they fled because of persecution.
But the Trump administration has defended the legality and merits of the deportations, portraying them as an effective way to deter illegal immigration.

Cairo’s Egyptian Museum completes restoration, relocation of Ramesses II basalt stele
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
18:32:02 UTC
03:32:02 KST

The Egyptian Museum in Cairo completed restoration work on a stele of Ramesses II, Egypt’s Tourism and Antiquities Ministry announced in a statement last month.
Ramesses II, known also as Ramesses the Great, is believed by many to have been the pharaoh in the biblical story of the Exodus.
Made of black basalt and measuring approximately 240 cm in length and 110 cm in width, the stele dates back to ancient Egypt’s New Kingdom (circa 1570 to circa 1069 BCE). It has been on display at the museum for over a century.
The basalt stele had originally been found in two separate pieces, explained Supreme Council of Antiquities Secretary-General Dr. Hisham El-Leithy, and had previously undergone restoration work to join the two fragments together.
Dr. Ali Abdel Halim, the museum’s director-general, noted that the stele was relocated and restored as part of the museum’s new display plan. It now stands between two other stelae depicting Ramses II.
Museum rejects claims of cement being used in stele’s restoration
He added that as part of the current restoration and relocation, the materials used during the stele’s previous restoration, as well as the wooden panel supporting the artifact, were removed.
The museum’s restoration team treated the joints holding the two together, and it was placed into a free-standing display with new panoramic lighting to highlight the stele’s details.
Further, Halim rejected claims of cement being used during the stele’s restoration that have been circulating on social media and clarified that cement had not been used at any point during the conservation work.
The photos online, he said, were taken while the restoration work was ongoing, and therefore “do not reflect its final condition” now that the work has been completed.
Ramesses II inscription in Sinai points to Egypt’s lost city of Mesn
More recently, excavations to uncover the historic Way of Horus military route, which leads from Egypt into ancient Canaan, archaeologists discovered a large, inscribed sandstone lintel broken into two pieces.
The lintel was found at the Tell Abu Saifi archaeological site, located in the city of Qantara East, in Egypt’s Ismailia Governorate along its eastern border with the Sinai.
Inscribed on three sides of the lintel are the titles of Ramesses II (“Ramesses the Great”), who is believed by many to have been the pharaoh in the biblical story of the Exodus.
But it is the second inscription that caught archaeologists’ eye: a reference to restoration work being carried out on a statue belonging to the deity “Horus, Lord of the City of Mesn.”
Dr. Hisham Hussein, head of the Central Administration for Lower Egypt and Sinai and director of the archaeological mission, said that the inscription represents “highly significant evidence” in studying the identity of the site.
However, Leithy noted that while the newfound is significant, further excavations and research are underway in attempt to uncover additional evidence to conclusively determine the matter.

Egypt discovers remains of tomb, false door of ancient royal chamberlain at Saqqara necropolis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
18:31:22 UTC
03:31:22 KST

The tomb of an ancient Egyptian royal chamberlain was discovered in Sector A of the Bubasteum necropolis in Saqqara during its first excavation season, Egypt’s Tourism and Antiquities Ministry announced on Sunday.
The necropolis, located on the desert boundary of Saqqara, is part of a Ptolemaic and Roman temple complex dedicated to the ancient Egyptian deity Bastet (Bast), the goddess of cats.
Excavations of the site revealed the remains of an Old Kingdom tomb’s funerary chapel, as well as the tomb’s false door still in its original position.
False doors served in ancient Egyptian belief as a threshold between life and death, where deity or spirit of the dead could cross back and forth. They are usually carved or painted along the west wall of a tomb’s funerary chapel, in line with the ancient association of the west with the land of the dead.
In front of the false door, archaeologists uncovered a complete set of alabaster funerary tools, including an offering table and disc, a purification basin, a jug, and a basin.
Tomb belongs to ancient Egyptian royal scribe
Both the false door and several of the tools bear hieroglyphic inscriptions of the tomb owner’s name, Sekhentiu-Ptah, and their titles as one who served in a prominent administrative position.
The titles include Royal Chamberlain, Overseer of All the King's Works, Overseer of Royal Documents, Keeper of the Secrets of Royal Commands, Priest of the goddess Maat (ancient Egyptian deity of truth and balance), and Overseer of Scribes.
Finding the complete set of funerary tools in its original position inside the chapel represents “an important discovery, offering valuable information about funerary rituals and practices during the Old Kingdom,” said Mohamed Abdel-Badie, head of the Egyptian Antiquities Sector.
Several burial shafts looting since antiquity
Kotb Fawzi, head of the Central Administration of Cairo and Giza, added the archaeological mission also uncovered an interconnected system of burial shafts containing several human burials, large quantities of colored funerary cartonnage (a material used in ancient funerary masks), and three sealed stone sarcophagi in their original conditions.
In addition, over 100 faience ushabti figurines, a wooden falcon-shaped statue, and a variety of pottery vessels were found within the burial shafts.
A number of the burial shafts found have been subject to looting since antiquity noted Dr. Amr El-Tayebi, Saqqara Antiquities Area’s director-general and head of the archaeological mission.
Tayebi pointed to openings left behind by tomb robbers between the different funerary chambers, but added that even so, the remaining artifacts still provide “great archaeological and scientific value, contributing to understanding the site's internal layout and the development of its architecture through its successive historical phases.”
The discovery highlights the importance of the Bubasteum necropolis and its continued use across several historical periods, stated Egypt’s Tourism and Antiquities Minister Sherif Fathy.
Dr. Hisham El-Leithy, secretary-general of the Supreme Council of Antiquities, explained that the excavation work followed careful excavation and stratigraphic recording, extensive documentation, as well as archaeological and linguistic studies.
All of this, Leithy noted, “helped situate the discoveries within their cultural context and retrace the necropolis's historical and architectural development.”

The super-producer who made an album while undergoing cancer treatment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

How Arctic Monkeys producer James Ford overcame cancer to make uplifting solo album
Best known for producing records for blockbuster British artists Arctic Monkeys, Florence + The Machine, Blur, Pulp and Jessie Ware, James Ford has stepped out from behind the console for a solo album made under extreme circumstances.
"I'd been ill since Christmas [2024] and under the weather so much that I could barely think or do anything," Ford tells Double J's Tom Ravenscroft.
By the following April, he was admitted to hospital and undergoing chemotherapy for acute myeloid leukaemia (AML), an aggressive form of cancer with an average survival rate of 30 per cent.
Recovering between rounds of chemotherapy, waiting as his "immune system comes back online", Ford's energy slowly returned.
"I needed something to take me out of my situation … to cheer myself up and reconnect back with the version that I recognise," he says.
"Because I make music every day and it makes me feel good. I just wanted to bring that back into my life.
"It seems a little mad from the outside, like I'm some kind of workaholic. But in the moment, it was utterly necessary for me."
Using a spartan set-up brought in by his wife, Ford wrote and recorded music from his hospital bed, "imprisoned" in order to protect his immune system during treatment.
The result? Lost In Another World, an album made in two weeks and released under the 57-year-old's full name, James Ellis Ford.
Music on the ward
Hospital staff were "bemused" that a patient battling cancer was intently beavering away on music between punishing chemotherapy.
"I don't think [the nurses] have ever really seen anyone try to make music in that situation before. But they were very interested and supportive," Ford says.
"Now and again, I'd have my headphones on, and they'd come in and quietly take blood."
Ford would also send "little sketches" out to his father and friends, including Arctic Monkeys frontman Alex Turner and singer-songwriter Bill Ryder-Jones, for feedback.
"It was almost like me waving a flag. It was a nice thing to talk about that wasn't doom and gloom, you know?" he says.
Lost In Another World is coloured by some dark atmospherics and lyrics that are "uncomfortable for me to listen back", Ford says. But they are the exception.
The majority of its 12 tracks are brighter, built upon playful analogue synths, programmed beats and experimental pop with the warm atmosphere of Brian Eno's solo ambience — tying it to Ford's 2023 solo debut The Hum.
"I was trying to make dance music … [to] lift my mood and focus on the positive things in my life," Ford says.
Against the bubbling synths and metallic groove of The Ever After, Ford thinks of his eight-year-old son, Frank.
"It's in the joy you bring," he sings.
"Illuminate everything, even in my darkest hour."
The meditative Overtones embraces a cosmic philosophy and the tuned percussion presets of a Suiko, a rare synthesiser that reproduces traditional Japanese instruments.
Getting into 'The Tunnel'
Like most musicians, Ford reasons, "I have the ability to get into what I call 'The Tunnel'. You're focusing on something and heading towards it and the rest of the world sort of dissolves."
"It's a wonderful feeling. It's something I search for every day," he says.
That single-minded drive and optimism tint the album, and helped Ford persevere through an ordeal most would struggle to contemplate, let alone endure.
"That was the main thing I was looking for, basically. To get in the tunnel and make everything disappear," he says.
For a sought-after producer whose prestige has allowed almost unfettered access — keys to studios, quality equipment, crack musicians and orchestras — Ford says it was "liberating" to work within restrictions.
"I am always a great proponent of limitations. As a producer, you're often just trying to impose a set of rules on someone: 'Let's do this with an acoustic guitar, or drum machines.'
"Suddenly, the universe gave me limitations beyond my control. But then in that moment to not have access and all the choices … was kind of amazing.
"It makes you just focus on the melody and the lyrics and different things."
Once out of hospital, Ford revisited his material but soon feared that tinkering with it would sully the purity of what he'd captured.
"I got someone else to mix it because I like the idea of it being a real snapshot of that moment in time," he says.
Lost In Another World lives up to its title, drawing the listener into a deeply personal, intimate sonic universe crafted under surreal conditions.
"That's kind of the best compliment, honestly. When I left it alone, that's what I was hoping it would achieve. Because that's what it was: there's no filter.
"Part of the feeling I was trying to encapsulate on the record was just how detached and lonely you feel. You've been catapulted into an alternate reality, and it was a very weird thing to go through."
A little help from his friends
Earlier this year, Ford oversaw the release of HELP(2), a charity album compiled with War Child and one of the year's best releases so far.
The all-star release saw Ford "calling in some favours", securing big-name clients (Depeche Mode, Pulp, Fontaines D.C. and Foals) and buzz-worthy younger acts (Wet Leg, Cameron Winter, Beabadoobee, Black Country and New Road).
In July last year, having undergone chemotherapy and a stem cell transplant, Ford was "feeling good".
"We set the whole thing up and I reached out to everyone I could," he says.
However, the week before a "big session" at London's famed Abbey Road studios, Ford says he "got a mouth ulcer, had my blood checked and I didn't have an immune system again."
While Damon Albarn and Arctic Monkeys were in the studio, Ford was "in the ICU with a tube sticking out of my neck and nearly died".
He ended up right back in recovery at the same St Bartholomew's Hospital ward, "where I made my record with the same f***ing laptop".
"I mixed the Arctic Monkeys tune [Opening Night] in there. Then, I was doing remote sessions over video meetings with Last Dinner Party and Olivia Rodrigo," Ford says.
"All of that while having a blood transfusion. And I was just like, what is my life!?"
Inspired by the cadre of A-list talent rallying together for the great good of completing Help (2), Ford dove into the tunnel once again with a death-defying sense of purpose.
"It was an amazing, life-affirming, heartwarming experience," he reflects.
"Everyone pulled together and made something that we're all really proud of."
The entire "mad rollercoaster of ups and downs" has given the super-producer a renewed lease on life.
"It's so hard to actually internalise the things you read about on the internet all the time about gratitude and being present, living in the moment," Ford says.
"You never expect it's going to happen to you … But when you go through something like this, you learn it for real: how valuable those things are and it really refocuses you, gives you a clarity on what's important in life in a way that I'm very grateful for."
Doing press around his new album and rehearsing with a band of "good friends" to bring it to the stage has not been "the most comfortable experience, quite honestly," he adds.
However, "on both counts", each time he revisits the trauma, "it recedes a little bit more in a way. It starts to become more of a story about someone else."
"Maybe it will actually be a good way of putting it to bed," Ford says.
Lost In Another World is out now.

Robin Morgan, child star who became feminist, poet and editor, dies aged 85
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
18:16:41 UTC
03:16:41 KST

Robin Morgan, a child star of the 1940s and 50s who grew up to become an all-American radical as a poet, essayist, editor and second-wave feminist, has died. She was 85.
Morgan’s death was confirmed Saturday by the Women’s Media Center, an organization she co-founded with Jane Fonda and the celebrated author and activist Gloria Steinem, who died Wednesday.
During the 1960s and 70s, Morgan embodied and inspired historic changes in how women lived and thought. As she was happy to point out, the one-time “ideal American girl” and adored “little Robin Morgan” was a rule breaker and justice seeker with a notable list of achievements, along with a prison record and an FBI file.
Julie Burton, president of the Women’s Media Center, called Morgan “one of the architects of the contemporary women’s movement”, hailing her writing and “global leadership for justice and equality”. The statement didn’t specify the location, date or cause of Morgan’s death.
Morgan was at the center of some of the defining moments of what came to be called second-wave feminism, expanding upon the achievements of the suffragists a half-century earlier. In 1968, she was among the organizers of the first protest against the Miss America pageant, joining fellow activists in tossing their bras (soon mythologized as burning) into a “freedom trash can”. The 1970 essay anthology she edited, Sisterhood Is Powerful, is considered one of the essential texts of the modern women’s movement.
Her legacy was one of deeds, words and images. Morgan is widely credited with coining the term “herstory”, the feminist reworking of “history”, and popularizing the clenched fist/female symbol icon of the liberation movement. Her poem Monster, with such lines as “I want a women’s revolution like a lover/I lust for it” was quoted at feminist rallies and beyond. Her poem Arraignment helped capture the movement’s embrace of the late Sylvia Plath and condemnation of her husband, poet Ted Hughes, whom Morgan and others blamed for Plath’s suicide in 1963. Morgan’s rhyming couplet “I accuse/Ted Hughes” inspired the title for Sonic Youth’s song J’Accuse Ted Hughes.
Labeled an “anarchist housewife” in one government report, Morgan confronted the establishment, left and right. In 1970, she and fellow protesters were arrested and jailed after occupying the offices of the avant garde Grove Press, whose owner, Barney Rosset, was fighting employees’ efforts to unionize. In the widely reprinted 1970 essay Goodbye to All That, she called out activists and libertines from Abbie Hoffman and Hugh Hefner to Dave Dellinger and the music group the Fugs.
In her personal life, Morgan had male and female lovers and was married for more than 20 years to the gay poet Kenneth Pitchford, with whom she had a son, the musician, activist and record company executive Blake Morgan. She once described her marriage as a “two-member commune” and was so resistant to labels that she remembered being “straight-baited” by feminists who thought she should be a lesbian and chastised by conservatives who assumed she was a lesbian.
In her 2001 memoir Saturday’s Child, she expressed joy and amazement at how her life had turned out and how she was able to retain “a threadbare, somewhat surreal sense of humor”.
“Put that in your apple pie and smoke it,” she wrote.
Besides Saturday’s Child, she completed more than 20 books, including The Word of a Woman: Feminists Dispatches and the poetry collections Monster and Dark Matter. She followed Sisterhood Is Powerful with Sisterhood Is Global (1984) and Sisterhood Is Forever (2002), featuring such contributors as Steinem, Simone de Beauvoir and Eve Ensler. For several years, she was editor-in-chief of Ms magazine.
In 1984, she was a founder of an early feminist thinktank, the Sisterhood Is Global Institute. In 2005, she, Steinem and Fonda launched the Women’s Media Center, which has a mission to support “the visibility, viability and decision-making power of women and girls in media”.
More recently, she hosted a syndicated radio show and remained active despite being diagnosed with Parkinson’s, which inspired several poems and a TEDWomen talk in 2015.
In a different era, she might have been just another forgotten child star. Born in 1941 in Lake Worth, Florida, and raised in New York, she never saw her father while growing up and was told – falsely – by her mother that he was dead. Her mother also shaved a year off her age, claiming she was born in 1942, to make her early public career seem even more impressive.
She would meet some of the era’s biggest stars, from Abbott and Costello to Sal Mineo, and was popular enough to inspire such commercial tie-ins as Robin Morgan dolls. Magazines described her as “unspoiled” and “courteous” and “the ideal girl-next-door”, immune from “violent outbursts of antagonism against established society”.
As she recalled in Saturday’s Child, producer Dan Ehrenreich squeezed her shoulder so hard that Morgan could feel his fingernails. He turned her microphone away and eventually placed his hand over her mouth.
“I realized that I loved and respected that child who fought back in what was the first political act I recall ever daring to make,” Morgan wrote.

Iraq completes investigation into thousands of ISIS detainees formerly held in Syria - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
18:13:36 UTC
03:13:36 KST

Iraq says it has completed an investigation of roughly 5,700 ISIS detainees who were transferred from Syria earlier this year. The ISIS detainees were mostly men who, since 2019, were held in two dozen detention facilities across eastern Syria. The US-backed Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) had been holding onto them until the Syrian government agreed to integrate the SDF into its army. Once that occurred, the US Central Command initiated a mass transfer of prisoners to Iraq.
Currently, Iraq has reported that it has investigated most of these prisoners. It is unclear how many of them will remain in detention, and how many will go to trial.
By 2019, ISIS was mostly defeated in Syria. At that point, around 50-80,000 ISIS members were detained in Syria by the SDF. Most of these detainees were women and children. Several thousand of these prisoners, however, were men.
A report at Al-Arabiya, which is based on an AFP report, notes that “the cases will now proceed to trial, while more than 450 Syrians will be released and handed over to their country. Iraq’s Supreme Judicial Council said it concluded ‘the interrogation phase’ of the 5,704 ISIS suspects who were brought from northeast Syria and referred them to trial.”
Some detainees to return to home countries
This matters because some of the ISIS members will return to their home countries, such as Syria, Turkey, etc. Notably, many of the ISIS members held in Syria had come from 60 other countries.
The international community, including around 80 countries, backed the anti-ISIS coalition. However, they did not create a means for ISIS members to be formally charged; there was never an international court of any kind for indicting ISIS members. Instead, they were left in limbo for seven years.
Al-Arabia reported that “the investigations led to identifying several ISIS commanders, including top-ranking figures, who were involved in ‘crimes at the international level,’ according to the council.”
Al-Arabia added that at least six suspects were documented to have been involved in the genocide against the Yazidi minority in Iraq. In 2014, ISIS overran the Yazidi areas of Iraq and began massacring the Yazidis. ISIS also kidnapped thousands of women and children and sold them into slavery. These acts galvanized the international community against ISIS.
Yazidis have yet to receive justice
Unfortunately, the Yazidis have yet to receive justice. Most ISIS members have evaded trial. Even now, many thousands of Yazidis remain missing. Over the last decade, Yazidi women and children have continued to be found in Syria and other places.
The New Region reported that “over 20,000 Iraqis [were] rehabilitated from the Al-Hol camp.” This report comes from Iraq’s own government.
The New Region added: “Iraq’s Migration Ministry on Saturday said that over 20,000 Iraqi nationals have been rehabilitated after returning from Syria’s notorious al-Hol camp. The report also noted that “the Iraqi detainees were transferred to al-Jadaa camp, a major government-run rehabilitation and integration center south of Mosul.”
Over the past year, Iraq has worked hard to return ISIS members to their home countries. Many countries, however, refuse to accept their ISIS members. Australia, for instance, was reluctant to take back women and children who had been in Syria’s Al-Hol camp.

Russia’s Putin and US envoys discuss Trump proposal to end Ukraine war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
18:12:52 UTC
03:12:52 KST

Russia’s Putin and US envoys discuss Trump proposal to end Ukraine war
Kremlin aide calls the Moscow talks ‘very frank and constructive’, as US envoys head to Kyiv next.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has met envoys from the United States for talks to end more than four years of Moscow’s war in Ukraine.
Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrived at the Kremlin on Saturday after landing in Moscow earlier in the day. The envoys are expected in the Ukrainian capital on Sunday.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Witkoff and Kushner will travel to ‘end’ Russia’s war in Ukraine: Trump
- list 2 of 3Will Europe pay the US to provide military aid to Ukraine?
- list 3 of 3Trump sends envoys to Russia, Ukraine with new peace plan
Putin welcomed the two in a ceremony aired on Russian television, telling them: “The situation is, of course, not simple.”
US President Donald Trump had said that Kushner, his son-in-law, and Witkoff, his special envoy and business ally, were bringing “a proposal to end the war”.
Following three hours of talks, senior Russian official Kirill Dmitriev, who was also part of the meetings, said the envoys’ trip to Moscow was an “important peacemaking visit”.
Russia and Ukraine both pledged not to strike each other’s capitals for three days during the negotiations, as Washington tries to revive talks to end Europe’s worst conflict since World War II.
Kremlin foreign policy aide Yury Ushakov said that “a whole series of ideas for a peace settlement” had been formulated during the talks, which he described to reporters as “substantive, very frank and constructive”.
He said Putin told the envoys that Russia would achieve its objectives and that the “root causes” of the conflict needed to be resolved.
Moscow is “confident” it can achieve its military goals of seizing the rest of eastern Ukraine, Ushakov added.
Witkoff and Kushner “promised to take Putin’s assessments” to their talks in Kyiv, Ushakov said, and the two sides agreed that Putin and Trump would stay in touch.
Witkoff told Putin that the US president had sent his best wishes and thanked him for the limited ceasefire during the delegation’s visit. The Russian president also conveyed gratitude to Trump and said Moscow would do its utmost to ensure the safety of the mediators.
During the talks, Al Jazeera’s Yulia Shapovalova, reporting from Moscow, said there were “some more or less optimistic reports” from the Kremlin regarding the progress of the discussions.
On the one hand, Putin says he “remains publicly open to peace talks”, said Shapovalova. But on the other, “following all of Ukraine’s escalating drone operations deep inside Russia and the targeting of major economic and logistics hubs like oil infrastructure and online retailers”, he maintains that he will not make any concessions on any key issues, that major differences remain in place, and that he will not negotiate with “terrorists”.
The envoys left Moscow on Saturday evening en route to Kyiv, Russian news agencies TASS and RIA Novosti reported.
Some analysts say that the “expectation in the Kremlin for this particular visit of the US envoys is actually less pessimistic, because previous trips by Witkoff and Kushner have not led to any progress, and Putin believes that Russia holds a military advantage on the battlefield”, Shapovalova added.
‘Refrain from strikes’
The talks come as the grinding war – which began with Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 – has seen increasing civilian deaths and attacks in the past few months.
After seizing and occupying a majority of eastern Ukraine, Putin has repeatedly said that Moscow intends to take the rest of it.
Russian strikes on Ukraine on Saturday killed at least seven people, including in the Kyiv suburbs, Ukrainian officials said.
Meanwhile, a Ukrainian drone attack on Russia’s Belgorod region killed one person and injured another, according to local authorities.
The Kremlin said it would not strike Kyiv from midnight on Saturday, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he would halt attacks on Moscow “from now” until Monday.
“The Russian president, the commander-in-chief, has given the order from midnight tonight not to strike Kyiv for three days,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said.
Zelenskyy – who had offered a truce during the US visits – later said he had spoken to the US envoys and also promised Kyiv would not strike Moscow.
“From now through the end of Saturday, as well as on Sunday and Monday, Ukraine is ready to refrain from strikes on Moscow,” Zelenskyy said on social media.
The Ukrainian leader said he expected the US officials in Kyiv on Sunday.
It will be Witkoff and Kushner’s first visit to Kyiv since Trump returned to office last year with a pledge to resolve the conflict.

An Egyptian court sentenced a well-known television presenter and 11 others to death for manufacturing and trafficking narcotics in a sprawling drug case, official media reported on Saturday.
The presenter, Sarah Khalifa, 39, is best known for her programme Mission Impossible, which dealt with issues concerning security and crime.
The state-linked Al-Ahram newspaper said a Cairo court sentenced “Khalifa and 11 other defendants to death by hanging on charges of forming an organised criminal gang specialising in procuring materials used in manufacturing narcotics, with the intent to traffic them, and possessing and carrying unlicensed firearms and ammunition”.
The verdict came after the court consulted the Grand Mufti of Egypt for his religious opinion, a procedure required by Egyptian law in capital cases.
The verdict is subject to appeal.
Khalifa also owns a cosmetic surgery clinic and a production company that specialises in organising parties and events.

Al-Ahram reported that authorities seized more than 750kg of narcotics and raw materials, and found two apartments used as laboratories as well as unlicensed firearms and ammunition.
The court also sentenced Khalifa and others to five years in prison over a separate case involving the kidnapping and assault of a young man.
Egypt applies the death penalty for premeditated murder, terrorism, some rape offences and drug trafficking.
According to the Egyptian Commission for Rights and Freedoms, 541 death sentences were issued in Egypt in 2025.

People with unfulfilled romantic needs form stronger attachments to fictional characters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
18:00:01 UTC
03:00:01 KST

People who are single or unhappy in their romantic relationships tend to develop stronger romantic feelings for fictional media characters. These findings suggest that one-sided crushes on movie stars or fictional personas can serve as a substitute for unfulfilled emotional needs in real life. The research was published in the journal Psychology of Popular Media.
Psychologists use the term “parasocial phenomena” to describe the one-sided psychological connections viewers form with media figures. First introduced in the 1950s, the concept captures how media consumers can feel as though they are interacting with a character on a screen. These mediated bonds resemble face-to-face social interactions but completely lack any mutual exchange.
Historically, researchers have debated whether these one-sided connections act as a social surrogate. The social surrogacy hypothesis proposes that individuals might use media figures to substitute for real-world social deficits. Past investigations mostly focused on platonic, friendship-like parasocial bonds. The consensus from those studies was generally that lonely individuals do not engage more intensely with media figures than people with active social lives.
Platonic connections represent only one facet of human social behavior. Nicole Liebers, a researcher at the University of Würzburg, conducted this study to explore the neglected romantic dimensions of parasocial phenomena. While platonic media connections might not cure general loneliness, Liebers proposed that romantic media connections might specifically help individuals cope with unfulfilled romantic needs.
Romantic parasocial phenomena involve intense emotional, physical, and sexual attraction toward a character. Liebers designed two studies to test whether relationship status and relationship satisfaction influence how strongly viewers become infatuated with these fictional figures. The research separated these phenomena into immediate parasocial interactions during viewing and long-term parasocial relationships that endure after the screen goes dark.
In the first study, Liebers recruited 96 moviegoers at a public cinema center in Germany. Participants had just watched one of three movies: Wonder Woman, Baywatch, or Transformers 5. These specific films were selected because they all featured at least one male and one female main character that the audience might find attractive.
Researchers asked the participants to complete a smartphone questionnaire immediately after leaving the theater. The viewers identified the specific character they felt most emotionally and sexually attracted to. They then answered questions designed to measure their real-time romantic parasocial interaction, which captures the immediate mental and physical attraction experienced while watching the film.
The researcher divided the participants into three groups based on their social situations. The groups included single individuals who watched the movie with a non-romantic companion, people in relationships who watched with a non-romantic companion, and people who attended the movie with their romantic partner. Individuals who attended the movie alone were excluded from the analysis, as watching a movie alone can alter a viewer’s general immersion in the story.
Liebers found that single individuals experienced more intense romantic parasocial interactions than people who were in a relationship. Specifically, single viewers reported stronger emotional love and a higher desire to interact with the character. The two groups did not differ in their physical attraction to the characters.
The social setting of the theater also influenced the viewers’ experiences. People who attended the movie with their romantic partner reported lower emotional and physical attraction to the characters compared to coupled people who attended without their partner. Having a romantic partner present in the room appeared to dampen the immediate romantic connection to the media figure.
The second study expanded the focus from real-time reactions to long-term romantic attachments. Liebers surveyed 358 volunteers online, asking them to recall a media character from any recently watched movie to whom they felt romantically and sexually attracted. The open-ended prompt resulted in a wide range of reported characters, from Magic Mike to Princess Jasmine in Aladdin.
Participants reported their current relationship status. Those who were currently in a relationship also completed a questionnaire assessing their overall relationship satisfaction, answering questions about how well their partner met their needs. Finally, all participants answered questions measuring their ongoing romantic parasocial relationship with their chosen character.
Unlike the immediate reactions measured in the first study, a parasocial relationship describes a bond that endures well after the movie ends. This survey allowed participants to select from a wide variety of movies. It provided a broader look at how these one-sided romances function in daily life.
Mirroring the first study, single participants developed stronger long-term romantic parasocial relationships than coupled participants. In this broader context, single individuals reported higher levels of both emotional love and physical attraction toward the characters. The data indicated that lacking a real-world romantic partner heightened the overall intensity of the fictional romance.
For participants who were in a relationship, their satisfaction with their real-life partner played a defining role. Lower relationship satisfaction predicted stronger emotional love for the fictional character. However, relationship satisfaction had no statistically significant effect on the physical attraction viewers felt toward the character.
These results suggest that emotional closeness might be a more important driver of parasocial romances than physical attraction. People with unfulfilled romantic needs appear to seek out emotional bonding with fictional characters to compensate for what they lack in real life. This finding aligns with the idea that the human drive for emotional love is often stronger than the drive for physical gratification.
These observational findings rely on self-reported data, which can introduce certain biases. For example, people watching a movie while sitting next to their romantic partner might simply feel more reluctant to admit they are attracted to a fictional character. The social desirability of reporting a crush could vary greatly depending on who is standing nearby.
The research design also prevents definitive conclusions about cause and effect. It is possible that individuals turn to media characters to compensate for romantic deficits. But it is equally possible that engaging in intense parasocial romances creates unrealistic expectations, which then lowers a person’s satisfaction with their real-world partner.
Future research will need to measure subjective feelings of romantic loneliness directly, rather than relying solely on relationship status as a proxy. Tracking these media habits over time could clarify whether fictional romances truly heal unfulfilled needs or simply complicate existing relationships. Accounting for a viewer’s prior exposure to an actor could also help isolate the exact mechanisms driving these one-sided love affairs.
The study, “Unfulfilled Romantic Needs: Effects of Relationship Status, Presence of Romantic Partners, and Relationship Satisfaction on Romantic Parasocial Phenomena,” was authored by Nicole Liebers.

Iran threatens to expand strikes if US keeps 'harassing' its ships
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
17:58:41 UTC
02:58:41 KST

Iran’s top joint military command warned Saturday that its strikes could expand if the United States continues what Tehran called the “harassment” of Iranian ships, in the latest sign that the confrontation between the two countries may be entering a more dangerous phase.
The warning, carried by Iranian state media, came amid a sharp escalation at sea after U.S. forces struck three Iranian crude oil tankers following ballistic missile fire by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps at two U.S. Navy warships.
U.S. Central Command said a U.S. aircraft carrier and a guided-missile destroyer successfully evaded multiple Iranian attacks and that no American personnel were harmed.
CENTCOM then said American forces permanently disabled the M/T Downy off Kharg Island and the M/T Stark 1 near Jask, while completely destroying the unladen M/T Kylo, also known as the Noxen, in the Gulf of Oman after ordering its crew to abandon ship.
“Let the message to the IRGC be clear: If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost, taking out three of yours,” CENTCOM commander Adm. Brad Cooper said.
“We will not hesitate to defend American forces, and if necessary, destroy Iran’s limited and exposed oil fleet,” he added.
The Iranian warning suggests Tehran is prepared to widen its military response if Washington continues targeting vessels tied to the Islamic Republic.
It also comes amid growing concern in Israel and the United States that Iran may deliberately escalate the confrontation in an effort to raise the economic and political cost of the conflict and pressure President Donald Trump back toward negotiations.
An Israeli official familiar with current assessments said Saturday there was substance to recent U.S. intelligence suggesting Tehran is considering a significant escalation. The official said Iran may believe time is working against it and could seek to create greater regional instability, including pressure on oil prices, as leverage over Washington.
The same assessment raised the possibility that Iran could eventually attack Israel directly or first use one of its regional proxies to wear down Israeli defenses and send a signal without immediately exposing Tehran as the direct force behind an attack.
Recent U.S. intelligence reporting has also suggested that Iran has grown more confident in its ability to strike targets across the Middle East after months of fighting and may be prepared to sustain the confrontation at least through the U.S. midterm elections.
That assessment has increased concern that further clashes at sea could become part of a broader Iranian strategy rather than isolated retaliation.
The latest confrontation around Iranian shipping follows renewed fighting near the Strait of Hormuz, where the United States has been escorting commercial vessels and striking Iranian military assets it says threaten freedom of navigation.
For Tehran, attacks on its oil fleet carry both military and economic significance. CENTCOM said the three tankers struck Saturday were part of a multibillion-dollar shadow network used to finance the IRGC and its regional proxies.
Iran’s threat to expand its strikes now raises the prospect of further attacks on U.S. naval forces or other American-linked targets if Washington continues targeting that network.
With both sides publicly signaling that they are prepared to impose higher costs on the other, the risk is growing that the naval confrontation could spill into a wider regional escalation.

Russia attacks military plants and logistics across Ukraine – MOD (VIDEO)
The Russian military has conducted large-scale drone and missile strikes on Ukraine, targeting assorted dual-use infrastructure sites, industry, and shipping in the Black Sea, the Defense Ministry in Moscow said on Saturday.
The ministry named a broad range of targets hit over the past 24-hour period, including two major metal plants in Dnepropetrovsk Region, which have been supplying cast iron and steel to the Ukrainian defense industry.
Footage circulating online suggests the plants sustained considerable damage, with major fires erupting onsite.
The Russian military hit multiple logistic centers and stockpiles across the country, including warehouses in the Odessa, Nikolayev, and Kiev regions. The strikes also targeted two fuel depots near the Gostomel airfield outside Kiev, as well as an electronic reconnaissance point in Brovary on the outskirts of the Ukrainian capital, the ministry said.
Footage shared by the ministry features drone strikes on Ukrainian shipping. Two dry cargo vessels and a container ship were hit at the port of Chernomorsk. Another dry cargo ship was struck at the port of Odessa, the ministry said.
All the vessels were hit by jet-powered Geran-4 Seeker drones, the ministry noted. The Seeker family of drones are said to be fitted with AI-powered machine vision systems, which enable the UAVs to search for, identify, and lock onto targets without input from their operators.
Over the past month, Moscow has drastically ramped up long-range strikes against Ukraine, with the campaign coming in retaliation for Kiev’s efforts to damage Russia’s energy sector and shipping. The retaliatory campaign has effectively brought Ukrainian shipping in the Black Sea to a halt, as well as heavily disrupted ground logistics within the country.
The latest wave of strikes comes ahead of a three-day hiatus in attacks on Kiev ordered by Russian President Vladimir Putin ahead of talks with senior US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who arrived in Moscow on Saturday. The pause in the strikes on the Ukrainian capital is intended to allow US President Donald Trump’s envoys to attend negotiations with Ukrainian officials in the country’s capital, according to Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov.

U.S. ambassador to Israel says "act of terror" cannot continue after weeks of West Bank unrest
The U.S. ambassador to Israel condemned Israeli settler violence in the occupied West Bank again on Saturday, calling the behavior an "act of terror" as he visited with Palestinian American residents shaken by months of attacks.
"If there are squatters that come in and put up their own flags and take possession of something that does not belong to them, if they burn a car, if they torch a mosque, if they go into someone's home and vandalize it, paint graffiti on the walls, that's a criminal act. But it extends beyond a criminal act. It's an act of terror," Ambassador Mike Huckabee said during his visit to the village of Turmus Ayya, which has reported frequent attacks by settlers over the past year.
Such attacks have surged since the war in Gaza began with the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, according to the United Nations humanitarian office.
During Saturday's visit to Turmus Ayya, the ambassador began his remarks by making clear he was addressing U.S. citizens, who make up a small percentage of the roughly 3 million Palestinians in the West Bank.
"I'm very aware that a lot of the American people who live in Turmus Ayya and other communities across this region are not enjoying the life they deserve to live, not enjoying it in a peaceful way," Huckabee said. "It's a life that is disturbed by people who have created extraordinary challenges that are unfair and illegal."
The U.S. Embassy can't investigate criminal activity, he said, but it can tell its host government "there are needs that need to be addressed, there are issues that cannot go unnoticed, and specific crimes and acts of terror that cannot continue without that country doing the investigation and adjudication that every person has a right to expect."
Huckabee met with about 10 Palestinian American residents who described the impact of the violence on their lives and properties, the municipality told The Associated Press.
A week ago, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu condemned the actions of a "handful of rioters," and the foreign ministry called the settlers' actions "a disgrace."
Netanyahu's government is the most ultranationalist and religious in Israel's history. It has presided over a surge of settlement construction in the West Bank.
Israel captured the West Bank, along with Gaza and East Jerusalem, in the 1967 Mideast war, territories the Palestinians want for a future state. The U.N. and much of the international community consider them to be illegally occupied.
Since then, the Israeli government has built nearly 150 settlements that are home to well over 500,000 Jewish settlers. Many settlements resemble developed suburbs.
Israel's military operates in all parts of the West Bank, but rights groups have said the military frequently turns a blind eye to settler violence. The settlers are Israeli citizens, and Israel's defense minister recently announced plans to fully transfer law enforcement among settlers to the Israeli police.

"Behind every photograph is a specific operation, specific work, a specific group of people and risk. Perhaps years from now, these photographs will remind us of the price paid in the struggle for Ukraine's freedom," HUR representative Yevhenii Yerin said.
The presentation was attended by cadets of the Military Institute at Taras Shevchenko National University of Kyiv, Artan X fighters, their commander, known by the call sign "Favoryt," and HUR representative Andrii Yusov.
"The photographs show the guys I worked with, traveled on missions with and returned with. It is good that this is being documented, because the war will end, but the memory of these soldiers must live forever," the commander of the Artan X special unit said.
As reported, Ukraine's Military Intelligence Day was established by a presidential decree on September 7, 2022. It is celebrated annually on September 7.

According to prosecutors, Abu Yahya left the IDF position where he had been working in the so-called Yellow Zone without authorization or a security escort and drove toward the Philadelphi Corridor in southern Gaza.
He allegedly loaded jerrycans that had been left at the roadside into his vehicle, with the drugs concealed inside them. Soldiers later spotted him traveling from Israeli-controlled territory into Gaza and behaving suspiciously.
During the drive, prosecutors say, Abu Yahya stopped and threw one of the jerrycans to the side of the road. A military force that arrived at the scene then detained him.
Despite the initial suspicion of trafficking, prosecutors charged him only with possession of dangerous drugs not intended for personal use, saying they had not gathered enough evidence to prove drug trafficking inside Gaza.
During questioning, Abu Yahya claimed he had picked up the jerrycans because he thought they contained diesel fuel. He said he later stopped to drink water and panicked when an IDF force arrived and fired into the air, causing him to throw one of the containers aside.
The prosecution has asked the court to keep him in custody until the end of the proceedings.
In its detention request, prosecutor Wasim Abu Amer wrote that the alleged conduct indicated involvement in the criminal world because of Abu Yahya’s access to such large quantities of different drugs.
“The audacity involved in committing drug offenses in a combat zone, while exploiting his status and access to the area, increases the danger he poses,” the prosecution said.
