China disrupting Pacific nations’ discussions: official
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
16:38:41 UTC
01:38:41 KST

China’s continued efforts to inject geopolitical rivalry into the region and disrupt Pacific nations’ discussions of regional issues warrant greater international attention, a foreign affairs official said yesterday.
Minister of Foreign Affairs Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍) last week led a delegation to diplomatic ally Palau to attend events related to the 55th Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) summit. However, the absence of some member-state leaders has been interpreted by some people as a sign of fracturing in Pacific unity.
Thirteen PIF members were represented by their heads of state or government, while Fiji, New Caledonia, Vanuatu and Samoa sent ministerial-level representatives, a diplomatic official said on condition of anonymity.
Photo: CNA
Last year, Nauru was represented by a minister, while Samoa sent a senior government official.
The absence of some leaders was not unprecedented, the official said, adding that judging “cracks” in Pacific unity solely by changes in the level of representation would be an oversimplification and fail to reflect the PIF’s actual situation.
Taiwan has participated in PIF-related mechanisms since 1993 under the name “Taiwan/Republic of China” as a “development partner,” they said.
The nation has long respected the “Pacific Way,” which emphasizes mutual respect, consensus and solidarity, and has continued to make substantive contributions through regional mechanisms, including supporting the Pacific Resilience Facility and the 2050 Strategy for the Blue Pacific Continent, the official said.
By contrast, China’s actions over the past few years have increasingly raised concerns among Pacific nations over their security and political autonomy, they said.
Palauan President Surangel Whipps Jr had called on countries conducting intercontinental ballistic missile tests, such as China in July, to “ensure transparency and provide at least 24 hours’ advance notice,” the official said.
However, Nauru opposed the call, they added.
That highlighted a genuine challenge to “Pacific unity,” as some countries with close ties to Beijing showed that they were unwilling to support efforts by Pacific leaders to forge a common position on security issues, the official said.
Pacific unity should not be judged solely by leaders’ attendance at summits, but by whether countries can continue to independently develop a collective voice on issues of common concern, they added.
Taiwan supports the regional agenda led by the PIF and has never asked Pacific nations to choose between Taipei and Beijing, the official said.
Meanwhile, China has continued to heighten regional security concerns through its military activities and use of political influence to hinder PIF members from reaching common positions, highlighting the stark contrast between the two sides’ roles and approaches in the Pacific, they said.

Gunman opens fire on police in Netanya, shot dead by officers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
16:38:40 UTC
01:38:40 KST

A 20-year-old Border Police officer who opened fire at police in Netanya’s Kiryat Hasharon neighborhood on Saturday evening was shot and killed, police said. No one else was injured.
Police identified him as Sgt. 2nd Class David Hoyer Amrani, a Netanya resident serving in compulsory service with the Border Police. The circumstances of the incident are under investigation.
Before the shooting, Amrani was filmed carrying a long gun. Initial assessments suggested he may have been suffering from combat-related trauma. However, the Defense Ministry’s Rehabilitation Department said he had not been treated by the department for post-traumatic stress disorder and was not known to it as suffering from PTSD.
Amrani enlisted in the Border Police in August 2024. After completing his training, he was assigned to serve in Hebron with the Border Police’s West Bank district. About eight months ago, he transferred to the 39th Company in the same district.
He is survived by his parents and two siblings. His family has been notified, police said.
Residents described panic as bursts of gunfire echoed through the neighborhood. One woman said: “We heard shots, everyone was obviously scared and ran inside. I saw people running toward the houses.”
Another resident, Amir, said: “It was very frightening. In the middle of the afternoon, while we were sitting on the balcony, we suddenly started hearing bursts of gunfire. We all immediately ran inside so no one would get hurt. I understood that they had neutralized him.”
Avigal Cohen, who also lives in the neighborhood, said there were “lots of shots” and that residents rushed into nearby buildings for shelter. “We were in the park with my little sister. Everything had been calm, and then we saw people panicking and started hearing bursts of gunfire,” she said. “We started shouting to people to hide. It lasted around 20 minutes.”
Her brother, Harel Cohen, said he heard bursts of gunfire from the direction of the stadium and saw the man moving between buildings. “I saw the man come toward my building and barricade himself there. I reported everything to police and immediately went inside and got my weapon so I would be ready,” he said. “He looked lucid. He was simply moving between the buildings and firing into the air.”
Police said large forces from the Central District were deployed to the scene and surrounding area. Central District commander Amir Cohen was sent to the location.
Magen David Adom said the report of the shooting was received at its 101 emergency hotline at 7:07 p.m. Medics initially reported that the shooter had been neutralized by police and that there were no additional casualties.
Idan Kleiman, chairman of the IDF Disabled Veterans Organization, said the incident required a full investigation and should serve as another warning about the treatment of veterans struggling after combat.
“This difficult incident in Netanya requires a full and thorough investigation,” Kleiman said. “Beyond the circumstances of the incident itself, this is another wake-up call for the State of Israel. It must not abandon the tens of thousands of female and male fighters who continue to face the battle long after returning from the battlefield.”
He called on National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir to order a joint IDF and Defense Ministry review of the circumstances of the case, the support provided and the lessons that could help prevent a similar incident.

Top US military officials face lie-detectors in hunt over classified stockpiles leak: Reports
- The Pentagon is conducting widespread polygraph tests on about 50 high-ranking military officials to find the source of leaked information on US munitions stockpiles.
- Reports of US rationing missile interceptors amid conflict with Iran were denied by officials, including President Trump, who confirmed some shortages of advanced weapons.
- The large-scale lie-detector use in this leak probe is unusual.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – The Pentagon has launched a lie-detector dragnet to comb through high-ranking military officials and identify who leaked information about US munitions stockpiles, according to US press reports.
In July, reports emerged that the United States was rationing munitions – its missile interceptors, in particular – over supply concerns after several months of fighting Iran.
Administration officials vehemently denied those reports, with President Donald Trump saying “we have a lot of ammunition, different types”, while acknowledging that “for some of the more sophisticated stuff, we’d certainly like to have more”.
Late on Sept 4, The New York Times reported that some 50 members of the military’s Joint Staff – the Pentagon’s planning and advisory staff – were being required to take polygraph tests as part of an investigation into how classified stockpile information made its way into journalists’ hands.
CBS News later also reported the wide-scale use of lie detectors, while adding that the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, General Dan Caine, had not been tested.
Both outlets cited unnamed officials.
Asked by AFP about the reports, the Pentagon’s chief spokesman, Sean Parnell, refused to comment on “internal personnel or investigative matters”, but said that it “takes all leaks of classified national security information extremely seriously and investigates accordingly”.
“Securing classified information is critical to ensuring the security of the United States and of our troops deployed around the world,” Parnell added.
Both the Times and CBS noted the scale of the polygraph testing.
Lie-detection testing is routine during background screenings and security clearance renewals for government staff with access to the most sensitive state secrets.
But the wide-scale deployment of the detectors as part of a leak investigation was rare, if not unprecedented, the outlets reported, citing analysts and unnamed officials. AFP

Israel sees rising risk of Iranian attack as Tehran weighs escalation before US midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
16:29:51 UTC
01:29:51 KST

An Israeli official familiar with current security assessments said Saturday there is substance to a U.S. intelligence report that Iran is considering escalating the regional conflict in an effort to pressure President Donald Trump, adding that Tehran’s worsening domestic situation may be providing another incentive for action.
According to the assessment, Iran may seek to force the United States back to negotiations because Tehran increasingly believes time is working against it. After the U.S. midterm elections in November, the official said, Iran may have little meaningful economic or political leverage left over Trump.
The official said the likelihood is increasing that Iran, which so far has refrained from directly attacking Israel in the current phase of the confrontation, could do so. Another possibility is that Tehran would initially use one of its proxies as the “first tool” to wear down Israeli defenses and send a signal without immediately exposing Iran itself as the direct force behind the attack.
Creating broader regional instability, including pressure on oil and fuel prices, is also viewed in Israel as a possible way for Tehran to raise the cost of the confrontation for Washington.
The official pointed to timing as another concern, saying Jewish holiday periods have historically been viewed by Israel’s enemies as a favorable window for attacks. Recent Iranian strikes on Jordan, including Aqaba, were also seen as a signal that Israel could eventually be targeted.
At the same time, the renewed escalation in Lebanon following the IDF’s takeover of the strategic Ali Taher Ridge has increased concern that Hezbollah could intensify attacks on Israeli forces.
The Israeli assessment comes against the backdrop of a New York Times report that recent U.S. intelligence assessments indicate Iran has grown more confident in its ability to strike targets across the Middle East and now appears determined to sustain the confrontation for months, at least through the U.S. midterm elections in November.
People who reviewed the intelligence reports and spoke with the Times said the Iranian regime, which they described as increasingly dominated by hard-line figures, is considering the possibility of a significant escalation.
The reports also suggest that after roughly six months of fighting, Iran has developed a “better understanding” of its military capabilities. That, according to the assessment, could make it more difficult to reach an agreement that fully ends the conflict.
Katz: Iranian attack would ‘free Israel from all constraints’
Against that backdrop, Defense Minister Israel Katz warned Thursday that any Iranian attack on Israel would “free Israel from every existing constraint” in its operations against Iran.
Speaking at a Rosh Hashanah event at the Defense Ministry, Katz said the IDF would strike “all national military and civilian infrastructure” in Iran, including energy facilities, if Tehran attacked Israel.
Katz said there were “signs” of severe economic pressure on the Iranian regime, along with fears of internal unrest and regime collapse, factors he said “could push them toward desperate steps.”
He said the Iranian leadership “knows very well” why it has avoided attacking Israel, after two Israeli operations in which, according to Katz, Iran was hit hard, its nuclear program was destroyed, Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei was killed and key strategic capabilities were damaged.
Katz added that Israel is “well prepared, defensively and offensively, for every possibility” and that the IDF is ready to carry out its mission.
An Israeli official said Israel does not want to be caught by surprise and that Katz’s warning was intended to “minimize the thoughts in the minds of our enemies.”
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu delivered a similarly stark message at a Rosh Hashanah event at the IDF headquarters in Tel Aviv two days earlier.
“The Iranian regime is faltering. It is weaker than ever,” Netanyahu said. “It is fighting for its life, and I am convinced of our ability to remove this threat once and for all. That means bringing down this regime.”
“This is the main mission still ahead of us, but it is close,” he said. “It is not impossible. It is within reach.”
Netanyahu added: “They are not avoiding attacking us for no reason. They attack everyone, just not us. They know our strength, the force of our response and our determination.”
He concluded with a warning: “I say to our enemies: Don’t mess with us.”

ATHENS, Sept. 5 (Xinhua)-- A Greek Air Force F-4 Phantom fighter jet crashed on Saturday afternoon during the Athens Flying Week air show at Tanagra Air Base, Greek national broadcaster ERT reported.
The aircraft suddenly lost altitude and crashed just minutes after the Hellenic Air Force flight demonstration began. The aircraft broke into two pieces, causing fires at separate locations, according to the report.
Two pilots of the fighter jet were found unconscious some distance from the crash site, according to military sources who spoke to ERT.
A total of 95 firefighters, supported by 9 firefighting aircraft and 5 helicopters were deployed to contain the blaze, according to authorities.
The incident occurred during the two-day Athens Flying Week international air show, which featured aerial teams from countries across Europe and Asia. ■

An Se Young hits a return during the women's singles semifinal match between An Se Young of South Korea and Yamaguchi Akane of Japan at China Masters 2026 badminton tournament in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province, Sept. 5, 2026. (Photo by Chu Yan/Xinhua)
SHENZHEN, Sept. 5 (Xinhua) -- World No. 1 An Se-young reached the women's singles final at the China Masters badminton tournament on Saturday with her 31st straight win, while Japan's Tomoka Miyazaki upset China's Wang Zhiyi to join her.
Top-seeded An, who recently won her second world title, defeated third seed Akane Yamaguchi of Japan 21-13, 21-15.
The victory extended An's record this season to 49 wins and just one defeat. Her only loss came in the All England final in March, when Wang beat her in straight games.
An will face Miyazaki in Sunday's final after the Japanese youngster upset second seed Wang 21-19, 23-21.
In women's doubles, China's Bao Lijing and Cao Zihan continued their surprise run by beating fourth seeds Jia Yifan and Zhang Shuxian 21-14, 21-13 to reach their first final at a BWF World Tour Super 750 event.
The result marked another breakthrough for the young pair, who only became a fixed partnership in May. Their combined ranking was initially only 55th in the world, and they entered the main draw in Shenzhen through virtual ranking points.
After starting their first Super 750 tournament with a straight-game win, Bao and Cao continued to knock out higher-ranked opponents and reached the final at their first attempt.
They will face Japan's Sumire Nakade and Miyu Takahashi, who defeated compatriots Hirota Sayaka and Ayako Sakuramoto 21-16, 24-26, 21-16 in the other semifinal.
In men's singles, Hong Kong, China's Lee Cheuk Yiu defeated second seed Christo Popov of France 21-15, 21-19, while Jason Gunawan came from a game down to beat fifth seed Anders Antonsen of Denmark 15-21, 22-20, 21-16, setting up an all-Hong Kong final.
In mixed doubles, top seeds Feng Yanzhe and Huang Dongping of China beat Malaysia's eighth seeds Goh Soon Huat and Shevon Lai Jemie 21-11, 24-22. Malaysia's Hoo Pang Ron and Lai Pei Jing defeated China's Zhu Yijun and Li Qian 21-12, 21-10.
In men's doubles, India's fourth seeds Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty defeated Malaysia's Nur Mohd Azriyn Ayub and Tan Wee Kiong, while China's He Jiting and Ren Xiangyu also advanced to the final.
The China Masters, a BWF World Tour Super 750 event, runs in Shenzhen from September 1 to 6. ■

01:26:30 KST

NANCHANG, Sept. 5 (Xinhua) -- One person has been confirmed dead and 11 others are missing after a mudslide struck a village in Suichuan County, Ji'an City, east China's Jiangxi Province at around 4 a.m. on Saturday, local authorities said.
The disaster was triggered by days of torrential rains brought by Typhoon Saudel, according to the county's flood control and drought relief headquarters.
Two other people have been rescued, and they are in stable conditions. All-out search and rescue operations are underway, while efforts continued to relocate affected residents and prevent secondary disasters.
As of 10 p.m., more than 640 rescuers have arrived at the site for rescue and search, according to the county flood control and drought relief headquarters. The first batch of firefighters with life detectors, drones and sniffer dogs arrived at the site at 11 a.m. by detouring over the mountains, as the road leading to the village was damaged.
So far, 39 villagers have been evacuated to safety. In neighboring areas, more than 5,300 people have been relocated to guard against potential disasters.
Workers are still repairing the road leading to the village and power lines. Telecommunications services have been restored.
Following the disaster, the Jiangxi provincial committee for disaster prevention, mitigation and relief issued a Level-III provincial emergency response for disaster relief at noon on Saturday, as Typhoon Saudel had left around 161,500 residents affected in the province.
China's Ministry of Natural Resources raised its geological disaster response for Jiangxi from Level IV to III at 11 a.m. Saturday and dispatched a work team to the site to guide rescue efforts.
The China National Commission for Disaster Reduction and the Ministry of Emergency Management activated a Level-IV national emergency response for natural disaster relief, and sent a work team and an emergency survey team with equipment including slope radar to assist with rescue operations.
The National Development and Reform Commission on Saturday allocated 20 million yuan (2.95 million U.S. dollars) from the central natural disaster relief funds to support emergency rescue and disaster relief work in Jiangxi.
The fund will be used for the reconstruction of damaged infrastructure, including roads and water conservancy facilities, as well as public service facilities such as schools and hospitals, in a bid to restore normal production and daily life in the affected areas as soon as possible.
China has a four-tier emergency response system, with Level I being the most severe. ■

‘I wasn’t even listening,’ Farage says of donations scandal meeting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
16:26:13 UTC
01:26:13 KST

Nigel Farage has claimed that he “wasn’t even listening” during a meeting at the centre of a controversy about whether his party considered evading the law on accepting donations from overseas.
The Reform UK leader also claimed he knew donation law “better than anybody” during interviews as he sought to salvage the final day of his party conference from the fallout that has already cost him two of his closest aides.
Farage was forced to suspend his close aide Dan Jukes and Reform’s head of policy, James Orr, on Friday after they were filmed in an undercover investigation appearing to plot to get around electoral laws on foreign donations.
The undercover reporters from a group called Verbatim posed as a potential Reform supporter and his wealthy American father, an impermissible donor, who paid for £30,000 of polling commissioned by Reform and which benefited the party when it was published in national newspapers.
The Reform leader himself remains under pressure over a separate clip in which he was heard saying “it’s all above board” after one of the reporters who was posing as the UK-based son of a wealthy US backer told Farage he had been in discussions with Jukes and Orr for some time.
“I’ll be the registered donor,” the son says. “But then dad will send the money to me, and then as soon as that’s done and all those conversations are had the money is available.”
In an interview on Saturday, Farage told the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg that “of course” he knew it was illegal for foreign firms to donate to UK parties, adding he was told the money was being given via a UK family office.
When challenged by Kuenssberg that while in Farage’s presence, one of the undercover reporters had said they “run an American family office”, the Reform leader said: “I am not a compliance officer. I was in the middle of canvassing in the Clacton byelection. I turn up. I frankly wasn’t even listening.”
He added: “I was told there was a global family office based in London, so the money could have come from Singapore. The money could come from all over the world, you know. Income could have come from all over the world into a family office based in London. I know electoral law. I know donation law better than anybody.”
Farage’s party had been hoping to move the focus to policy announcements, including on tax cuts, as Reform’s conference closed in Birmingham on Saturday.
Its Treasury spokesperson, Robert Jenrick, gave a keynote speech in which he pledged to increase the tax-free personal allowance to £15,000 within the first 100 days if the party were to take office. The threshold has been set at £12,570 since 2021 and is due to remain there until 2031.
But in interviews given earlier in the day to trail the policy, he also found himself forced to deflect from the donations controversy. “That’s been dealt with,” he told GB News. “The two individuals concerned have gone, and we’re here today moving forward. The language that they used was clearly inappropriate, that was very disappointing.”
In an interview with Times Radio he said Orr and Jukes had been “permanently suspended”, appearing to differ from the latest party line that they had “stepped down pending outcome of an investigation”, indicating a possible way back.
Farage meanwhile accused “the establishment” of trying to derail Reform UK, when challenged by ITV’s Robert Peston on the string of allegations related to his and the party’s finances.
“And it will go on. You come back and see me in six months, there’ll be five more investigations. It won’t end. This won’t end,” he said.
Farage said he had some “thoughtful” moments over the summer, claiming his family had been asking him to “walk away” from politics amid pressure on them and him.
Despite Reform’s efforts to insulate Farage, the Met police are now assessing evidence after a complaint that the Reform leader, as well as Orr and Jukes, may have broken political funding laws. They all deny wrongdoing.
The final day of the conference also coincided with an appeal by West Midlands police for a woman, who was among climate activists who were removed from the hall on Friday as they heckled Farage’s speech, to come forward after footage emerged over her allegedly being assaulted.
The police initially responded on X to a clip that appeared to show audience members pulling her hair and grabbing her head as she was carried out of the conference hall. West Midlands police later said in a statement that they were aware of a video circulating from the Reform UK conference showing an incident with a protester, and had asked the woman to come forward.
The activist group Climate Resistance, which claimed responsibility for the protest during Farage’s speech , said the protester was considering whether to speak to police.
Nadine Dorries, a former Conservative MP who has joined Reform, said sensitivities were “heightened” in the aftermath of the killing of the Reform spokesperson Ann Widdecombe in July.
“They tried to completely derail the speech. It was an organised sting again,” she said in an interview with LBC when asked about the incident.
Also speaking on Saturday was Suella Braverman, the party’s education spokesperson who, like Jenrick, is another defector from the Conservatives.
Her speech announced a planned cut of 20% to the number of student loans given, with funds only granted to university courses that can demonstrate good economic returns, with exceptions for some courses “of strategic or cultural importance”.
Farage ended the conference with closing comments to the main hall, where sections of seating were unoccupied and the mood was more subdued than earlier in the event, by telling the Reform faithful that “there would be good days and bad days”.
“Sometimes we will get things wrong and get a bit of a kicking, but what this conference has shown is that whatever you throw at the leadership, whatever you throw at you, the people’s army, we immediately stop, pick ourselves up and start all over again,” he said.

Gaza teams recover remains of 55 people nearly 3 years after Israeli strike

Gaza teams recover remains of 55 people nearly 3 years after Israeli strike
The victims, all members of the Malka family, had been sheltering in the family home when it was hit by Israel in November 2023.
The remains of 55 Palestinians have been recovered from the rubble of a residential building in Gaza City destroyed in an Israeli air strike nearly three years ago, according to Gaza’s civil defence.
The recovery operation, which concluded on Saturday, marks the latest in a slow, largely manual campaign to retrieve the dead from beneath Gaza’s ruins. Such efforts are hampered by a chronic shortage of the heavy machinery needed to clear broken concrete.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3No end to torture of Gaza doctor Abu Safia in Israeli prison: What to know
- list 2 of 3Israel’s siege on Gaza is forcing dentists to operate in the streets
- list 3 of 3Israel kills 3 in Gaza as far-right minister plans for Palestinian removals
Rescue teams said the remains were found beneath the rubble of the Malka family home, the Palestinian Wafa news agency reported.
Colonel Muhammad Abu Dan, who has been supervising the rescue teams, said they had been searching for more than 60 bodies of victims from the Malka family over the past 72 hours.
Situated in the Zeitoun neighbourhood, Israeli forces struck the building on November 19, 2023, as the family members sought shelter inside after being displaced from their own homes over the course of Israel’s genocidal war, said Wafa.
According to the United Nations Satellite Centre, 82 percent of all buildings in Gaza have been destroyed or damaged during the war.
Gaza’s Ministry of Health, along with UN agencies and aid organisations, estimate that between 10,000 and 14,000 people remain missing under rubble across the territory.
Abu Dan has called on international humanitarian organisations to provide as much equipment as possible so that his teams can recover the largest number of people possible from the rubble, as reported by Gaza’s Government Media Office.
As most of the bodies have been recovered, a joint funeral procession is expected to take place next weekend.
‘No plan’ to displace people from Gaza
The recovery operation took place after United States ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, said there was no plan to force Palestinians to leave Gaza after two Israeli ministers earlier in the week floated proposals for the mass removal of people from the besieged territory.
“I can tell you categorically there is no plan of the Israelis to displace people out of Gaza against their will,” Huckabee told reporters in Turmus Ayya, a town in the Israeli-occupied West Bank.
“Nobody is suggesting that there will be forced displacement. The Israelis are not. The Americans are certainly not. I know of no one who supports that.”
Earlier this week, Defence Minister Israel Katz said there was “no real solution for Gaza in the end without this migration”, while National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir outlined a seven-year plan for expelling Gaza’s population through what he described as “voluntary emigration”.
Meanwhile, Gaza’s Ministry of Health said hospitals in the strip received 17 bodies over the past 48 hours as well as 27 injured people, according to figures compiled from admissions.
The latest casualties included five new fatalities, one person who died from previous wounds and 11 bodies recovered from beneath debris. Additional victims remain trapped under rubble or lying in the streets, with ambulance and civil defence teams still unable to reach them, it added.
At least three Palestinians were injured in Israeli attacks on Saturday, two in an Israeli attack on a beach in the al-Khalidi area, north of Gaza City, and one in a targeted attack on the al-Sudaniyya area, northwest of Gaza City.
Since the “ceasefire” took hold last October, at least 1,344 people have been killed and 4,464 injured while at least 815 bodies have been recovered from the rubble, according to the Health Ministry.
The overall death toll since October 2023 has risen to 73,470, with at least 174,540 injured, according to the latest available figures.

Colombia drone attack by suspected guerrillas kills 3 soldiers, army says

Colombia drone attack by suspected guerrillas kills at least 3 soldiers, army says
An attack involving explosives dropped from drones followed by a clash inside a military compound in northeastern Colombia has killed at least three soldiers and wounded four, Colombia's army said Saturday.
Local authorities blamed the attack late Friday on the rebel National Liberation Army (ELN). It targeted a military unit in the municipality of Ocaña, in the Norte de Santander department, which borders Venezuela. Two soldiers died at the site and a third after receiving medical attention, Colombia's military said on X.
"In the context of the operations deployed following these events, Captain Marco David Pirajón Montezuma, Professional Soldier Joel Alberto Jiménez Jaramillo, and Professional Soldier Jhon Carlos Marrugo Manjarrez were killed during an engagement in combat, while honorably and committedly carrying out their duty in service to the Nation," the military said.
President Abelardo de la Espriella condemned the attack.
"For every police officer or soldier murdered, we will bring the full weight and legitimate force of the State down upon the criminals," the president said.
De la Espriella, a millionaire who earned President Trump's endorsement, won a close runoff election in June. He started his four-year term on Aug. 7. Since taking office, De la Espriella has joined the Shield of the Americas, an anti-cartel alliance headed by the U.S.
He has said he plans to forge a military alliance with Israel and the U.S. to help strengthen his war against Colombia's guerrillas.
Much of ELN, an armed group active since 1964, is based in the Catatumbo region, which includes parts of the Norte de Santander and Cesar departments. ELN also harbors dissident factions of the now-defunct Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) that did not join the peace agreement a decade ago.
Both groups are vying for control of the strategic region, which connects to the porous border with Venezuela and is one of Colombia's primary coca-producing areas.
In August, an explosion outside a police station in Cucuta injured 11 police officers and killed a police dog. Officials also blamed that attack on the ELN. Earlier this week, at least one civilian was killed and 11 other people were injured after a car bomb exploded outside a police station in northeastern Colombia.

====================================================================================================

AfD is not the heroic opposition it claims to be
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
16:11:16 UTC
01:11:16 KST

AfD is not the heroic opposition it claims to be
Recently, a middle-aged man on an e-bike was passing me on the sidewalk. Out of nowhere, he swerved, kicked me in the shin, shouted “Leftist pig!” and sped off. An elderly woman with a walker asked me, visibly shaken, if I knew him. I said no, just as alarmed as she was.
A little later, a woman was handing out SPD balloons between market stalls and a stage in the town center. I listed the cruelties her party in Berlin is currently shoving down the throats of workers. She squeezed out the word “constraints,” pointed to the CDU, and brushed me off. The DGB trade union federation has also apparently awakened from its coma. A Verdi trade union member was recruiting members and babbling about “solidarity.” I asked him whether he meant that “social partnership between capital and labor” that has never actually existed. He looked at me in confusion and said this was all about the AfD. When I replied that the AfD also just wants to enforce capital’s interests through law, just as the SPD does in government, he quickly cut the conversation short. He had no interest in leaving his parallel world.
The closer the state election gets, the more madness spreads in Saxony-Anhalt. The SPD presents itself as a “workers’ party” while throwing workers’ rights in the trash. The Greens pose as protectors of homosexuals while beating the war drum loudest for war against Russia. The CDU waxes lyrical about tried and tested traditions while implementing one AfD demand after another. The still-governing FDP markets the leftovers of its neoliberal fairy tale about the “trickle-down effect.” Helplessly, The Left wobbles back and forth because it does not want to miss out on bourgeois respectability – a sorry spectacle.
Panicked democrats
That means the AfD doesn’t have to do much more than counter this madness with a parallel world of its own. Its lead candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, smiles into many cameras. Before his supporters, he even rhapsodizes about the GDR, which he never experienced himself, while his party constantly accuses The Left of socialism and being the Stasi the moment it so much as utters the word “social.” Siegmund moves from talk show to talk show, complaining about exclusion, even though right now nothing is more omnipresent than his party.
One could laugh at how the ‘bourgeois center’ and its media keep boosting the AfD with all their fuss. The panic does seem genuine; more than a few public employees probably quite rightly fear that they will soon be “cleaned out” politically, to borrow the words of one AfD campaigner I met. Better not to mention that under CDU rule this has long been happening quietly already. Only now the circle of those purged could grow, and posts and mandates are at risk of collapsing. Once again, it is mainly about money and status.
In their own reality, the bourgeois center sees itself as the representative of “democracy” in a struggle against “anti-democrats.” This is nonsense, of course, because the AfD also wants to pour its system-supporting demands into laws. That is as democratic as things in the Federal Republic have always been. Its mix of nationalism, authoritarianism, chauvinism, neoliberal economic policy, and sanctimonious moralizing is simply distributed a little differently and expressed more bluntly than by the “old parties.”
CDU in blue
Neither mainstream nor alternative media like to talk about how much less the AfD’s program differs from the CDU’s than many assume. One striking example sounds as if copied directly from one of the Christian Democratic parties: the AfD wants to “give special support to Christianity” – in the very federal state with the lowest proportion of church members, at not even 14%.
Like the CDU, the AfD demands unpaid compulsory work for asylum seekers. But in parts of Saxony-Anhalt, this already exists. Municipalities happily replace regularly paid jobs, for example in park maintenance, with unpaid labor from refugees and the unemployed. It also wants Ukrainians no longer to be recognized as war refugees, fully aware that the CDU has already pushed this through the EU and that those sent back will be forced by Ukraine to the front against Russia. That fits its supposedly anti-war line just as badly as its demands – entirely compatible with the ‘old parties’ – for more rearmament, more military industry, and more simplified weapons exports across the world.
In May, for example, the AfD voted together with the CDU in the town council of Sangerhausen, a small town in Saxony-Anhalt, in favor of bringing in the Israeli arms company Elbit Systems – genocide in Palestine and possible business with Ukraine notwithstanding. None of that concerns us in Germany at all, Hans-Thomas Tillschneider admitted openly in an interview with Compact magazine. The only things that mattered were the 400 promised jobs and extra tax revenue. What he did not say: he means the taxes paid by workers, which in any case only flow to the federal level, because the AfD would prefer to cut corporate taxes.
Market-radical delusions
On taxes, Siegmund’s party appears to have borrowed heavily from American tech oligarchs. It even wants to “examine special economic zones in Saxony-Anhalt.” That means areas where corporations pay little or no tax and where normal labor rights for employees would no longer apply. Under current law, this is not enforceable. But laws, of course, can be changed later.
Special economic zones are a fetish of so-called market libertarians – neoliberal extremists like tech billionaires Elon Musk and Peter Thiel. And who would have thought it: in the CDU-linked Konrad Adenauer Foundation, such market-radical fantasies are highly popular as well. There, common ground is easy to find.
More of the same
On many issues, the AfD merely goes a little further than the governing parties in Saxony-Anhalt – the CDU, SPD, and FDP. It wants to force teachers and public servants into patriotic declarations, arm the police even more heavily than they already are, and largely prevent investigations into officers even after deadly use of firearms. The executive branch is to become an untouchable authority, which in reality it already almost is – no surprise when the police investigate themselves.
The AfD also calls for a ‘voluntary citizens’ guard,’ meaning a private vigilante force supported by municipalities. Such a force could, for instance, help the police ‘catch’ student councils, which the AfD wants to ban, or “put Antifa back in its place.” It wants to classify the latter as a terrorist organization – greetings from US President Trump. Since there is no actual group by that exact name, any number of political dissidents could then be branded with the label. How convenient. This fits its desire for prison sentences for anyone who “disparages Germany.” That, too, is almost infinitely open to interpretation.
The conclusion is obvious: for both sides, freedom of expression means above all freedom for their own opinions and suppression of those who think differently. The two camps are not actually that far apart.
Millions for the rise
So much for the claim that the AfD is less neoliberal than the CDU, Greens, SPD, or FDP. This is entirely compatible with an authoritarian state, as we can already observe in part. Wealthy industrial donors likely want exactly that. The AfD already has plenty of such backing: last year, in large donations above €35,000, it came in second place directly behind the CDU, with nearly €5.15 million in income, while the CDU collected €6.35 million. That figure does not include all smaller donations.
The AfD received its largest donation from Henning Conle, a German-Swiss real estate shark who has heavily financed the party since its founding, up until 2021 together with the now-deceased billionaire August von Finck Jr. Millions flowed into the AfD’s coffers over the years, often more or less covertly via shell companies, think tanks, and advertising agencies. Not that things are so very different with the ‘old parties’, they are just better at not getting caught.
Such huge sums from circles of capital, intended to enable a party’s rise, do not really fit the myth of some kind of fundamental opposition on behalf of the ‘little people’. Whoever gives that much is pursuing something that certainly does not lie in the interest of the majority. In that respect, it is no different from the other parties.
Collusion with the old parties and corporate bosses
And yet the story of the one and only true opposition party stubbornly persists. That is due above all to the scaremongering of the self-appointed ‘true democrats’ in politics and the media. For Saxony-Anhalt’s AfD lead candidate himself likes to blurt out what they do not want to hear. Recently podcaster Benjamin Berndt asked him about the Potsdam ‘remigration meeting’, which some media outlets inflated into a new Wannsee Conference.
Siegmund laughed it off: it had merely been one of many meetings with cadres from various parties, including the CDU, and influential business figures. That, he said, is how the AfD forges “networks” with the economy and other political factions – and collects donations at the same time.
In saying this, he spoke aloud what anyone in Saxony-Anhalt who wants to know it knows. It immediately reminded me of 2017: in Oebisfelde, a small town near Magdeburg, the AfD invited people to an election event disguised as a “citizens’ regulars’ table.” Volkssolidarität provided the hall, there were free drinks, complimentary snacks, and a podium. Sitting on that podium were not only AfD members, but influential businessmen and CDU and FDP politicians who – to everyone’s amazement – openly campaigned for voting AfD and boasted of their donations to it. There was no sign of exclusion even back then, nine years ago – and nothing has changed since.
The AfD regularly stages such meetings in eastern Germany. Any journalist on the ground could have found that out. But the press prefers to feign outrage over isolated incidents. Thus, for example, the regional news outlet Volksstimme blathered in 2022 about a “secret meeting” and sanctimoniously asked: “Were the CDU and AfD in Saxony-Anhalt making common cause?” More recently, the Tagesspiegel cooked up a new scandal: a CDU politician had donated €10,000 euros to the AfD. Well, fancy that?
Escape from reality
This ‘business as usual’ is probably rather embarrassing even to the self-proclaimed ‘center democrats’ themselves. In reality, they have been colluding with the AfD so actively for so long that even the Left, sitting at the children’s table, can no longer fail to notice it. Yet the Left is just as eager to flee from the truth and courts the CDU in a manner as embarrassing as it is futile, hoping that it will finally tear down the only truly existing firewall it has – the one against the Left.
Anyone who refuses to pick a side can only feel like a misplaced extra in the midst of a mad shadow-fight between two camps, each trapped in its own parallel reality: two camps that inflate tiny differences, spread panic, talk nonsense, blank out reality, deceive workers, make the poor poorer (or want to), and stir up the aggression already visible on the streets.
All Siegmund has to do is show up, smiling, and churn out culture-war phrases about banning gender asterisks, “leftist terrorists,” and compulsory German flags – all of which explains neither how people are supposed to pay tomorrow’s rent with money they do not have, nor how their lives are to improve. But then, the others do not explain that either.
The frustration in the German state with the highest average age was thus inevitable. And Siegmund apparently sees it coming. In the above-mentioned podcast, among other things, he tries to prepare for it accordingly: he stressed that he could not change very much very quickly because the CDU had left him with a pile of shattered glass. Naturally – voters have to be kept on the hook for longer than a single election campaign.
The pile of broken shards is real. And Siegmund knows, just like the “old parties,” that a harder-edged CDU policy will not improve the lives of the majority. But whoever wants to administer the system had better not talk about the system’s causes. In inventing problems to distract from the real ones, they all outdo one another. In Saxony-Anhalt, capital is merely rehearsing a test run – with new protagonists.

DRC to move embassy to Jerusalem in move to 'court' Trump
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05

Breadcrumb
DRC to move embassy to Jerusalem in move to 'court' Trump, Israel
The Democratic Republic of the Congo will be moving its embassy in Israel from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem in what analysts argue is an effort to "court" the United States to help its war effort against the M23 in the country's east.
DRC President Felix Tshisekedi announced the planned relocation on Thursday during an official visit to Israel, where he met with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. He said both countries would take steps towards making that happen.
The move comes as the DRC's military struggles to contain the Rwandan-backed M23 rebel group, which has seized and continues to hold large parts of the country’s volatile, mineral-rich east, including the provincial capitals of Goma and Bukavu.
According to Owen Bonertz, Africa Editor at intelligence platform Factal, the reason behind Tshisekedi's decision had to do with the "courting" of Washington in order to obtain "American defence assurances in their war against the M23".
"In general, the DRC is trying to move towards the United States for some sort of guarantee of weapons or more direct military aid in their war against M23, and this Israeli announcement is kind of an easy, symbolic way for the DRC to make Trump happy in this instance," Bonertz told The New Arab.
Bonertz said US policy towards the DRC had shifted since Donald Trump returned to the presidency in January 2025, citing the lifting of restrictions on cooperation imposed over the country’s record of using child soldiers in conflict, alongside new US investment in its mining sector.
The mining agreement was part of a broader US push to reduce China’s dominance of strategic mineral supply chains, he said, adding that closer ties among the three countries could also bring further "positive impacts" for US and Israeli mining interests in the DRC.
The embassy move is the latest in a series of international relocations following the United States’ 2018 decision to recognise Jerusalem as Israel’s capital and move its embassy there.
Colombia announced plans to relocate its embassy to Jerusalem in recent weeks, joining Fiji, Guatemala, Honduras, Papua New Guinea and Paraguay, which have established embassies in the city. Argentina’s President Javier Milei has also pledged to move his country’s embassy.
Jerusalem’s status remains contested: Israel initially occupied and later annexed East Jerusalem after the 1967 war, while Palestinians claim it as the capital of a future independent state.

Former NSC adviser explains why Iran could face internal upheaval within months - interview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
16:04:08 UTC
01:04:08 KST

Brig.-Gen. (res.) Prof. Jacob Nagel estimates that six to nine months of sustained economic pressure could create the conditions for an effective popular uprising in Iran during an interview with 103fm.
Nagel, a senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies (FDD), previously served as national security adviser and head of the National Security Council.
He said the US is pursuing a strategy of applying sustained economic pressure on Iran rather than immediately launching further strikes, arguing that Washington is seeking to weaken Tehran by targeting its main sources of revenue.
"The United States is a superpower that can almost do whatever it wants," Nagel said, adding that the approach is to "choke Iran’s economy, but we will really choke Iran’s economy."
At the same time, he acknowledged that Iran continues to export fuel despite the pressure, though he questioned the accuracy of reported figures. "I do not believe the exact numbers, but let’s assume they are exporting half the amount of fuel they exported before the war. Instead of 20 million barrels, 10 million barrels, they are managing," he said.
Nagel argued that the pressure on Iran’s economy is targeting its primary source of revenue and could eventually fuel domestic unrest.
"They are choking the Iranian economy, including their main source of cash flow, which is fuel that the Iranians are struggling to sell, and Iranian money is about to run out. Inflation is terrible," Nagel said.
Expert says economic strain could push Iranians back to streets
He predicted that prolonged economic pressure could push Iranians back into the streets.
"With six to nine months of this kind of pressure, I would bet that the people will return to the streets. They will not agree to be without electricity, without water."
However, Nagel warned that an uprising would remain difficult due to the regime’s history of suppressing protests.
"When the public takes to the streets and rebels, either they are shot in the street, or they end up hanging from the gallows," he said. He added that after months of economic pressure, "even the Basij will not want to fight," saying, "I hope the Basij will join the people."
Nagel said concerns over Iran’s ability to retaliate are among the reasons the US has so far avoided targeting the country’s energy sector. He said Tehran could still strike US allies in the Gulf, including Saudi Arabia, Bahrain and Qatar.
"At this stage the Iranians still have enough power to respond," Nagel said.
Trump advisers warn against targeting Iran’s energy infrastructure
Nagel said this is also the view of advisers close to US President Donald Trump, who he said have warned against targeting Iran’s energy infrastructure because of the potential consequences for regional allies and global oil prices.
"The advisers sitting next to Trump, the advisers who made the agreements: Kushner, Witkoff, and Vance, they tell him: 'This is not good. If we destroy them, they will destroy the energy reserves of Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Kuwait, and the Emirates, and then the price of oil will be $200 dollars.'"

Israel claims control of Lebanon’s key Ali al-Taher ridge: What that means

Israel claims control of Lebanon’s key Ali al-Taher ridge: What that means
Israeli Defence Ministry asserts operational control over strategic highland; Hezbollah yet to comment.
Israel this week has claimed to have established operational control over the strategically vital Ali al-Taher ridge in southern Lebanon, after an extended operation against positions of the Lebanese armed group Hezbollah.
In a statement on Friday, Defence Minister Israel Katz claimed Israeli forces had driven Hezbollah fighters out of what he said was a network of tunnels under the contested highland, 15km (10 miles) from the border.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Israel releases five detainees to Lebanon after US-mediated negotiations
- list 2 of 4October 7 attack shapes Israel’s elections and fuels political blame
- list 3 of 4Israeli strike kills three in southern Lebanon amid ongoing escalation
- list 4 of 4Israeli drones drop bombs on southern Lebanon’s Mansouri
“Prime Minister Netanyahu and I are leading a clear and uncompromising policy, reinforced every day by the [Israeli military]: Israel will not withdraw from the security zone in Lebanon until Hezbollah is disarmed throughout Lebanon and the threats to the residents of the Galilee are removed,” he was quoted as saying by Israeli media. “The capture of Ali Taher is an important step towards achieving this goal.”
Iran-backed Hezbollah has yet to formally comment on the Israeli claims. However, hours before Katz’s comments, Reuters news agency reported that Iran had warned the United States last month that it would respond forcefully if Israeli attacks on the ridge, which rises 600 metres above sea level (1,970 feet), continued.
Israel and Hezbollah have been fighting, with varying levels of intensity, since October 2023. Israel has twice escalated the conflict – first in September 2024 and then in March this year, following the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Israel has been working to embed its occupation of southern Lebanon since the latest escalation, when it announced the creation of a “security” or “buffer” zone, which rights groups say has involved the deliberate destruction of civilian infrastructure – potentially a war crime – and is responsible for the displacement of hundreds of thousands of Lebanese.
Israeli strikes and ground operations around the Ali al-Taher ridge continued despite a ceasefire agreed in June, after Israel gained control of nearby Beaufort Castle and part of the higher ground overlooking much of southern Lebanon and northern Israel.
According to Mohanad Hage Ali, of the Carnegie Middle East Centre, Israel’s success has partly been down to technological superiority but also due to the complete absence of “inhibition” in their assaults upon Lebanese towns and villages, which have often accrued daily casualty rates of dozens of people.
“There aren’t any consequences to their actions,” he said. “They can demolish entire villages and wipe out whole societies in a way they could never do before. It’s ethnic cleansing.”
Politics of resistance
Pitched as a measure to protect citizens of northern Israel, who Israeli analysts such as Ori Goldberg described as being owed an electoral debt by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ahead of crucial elections later this year, the occupation is also a means of exerting additional pressure on the government in Beirut.
“The Israeli ‘operational control’ over the ridge is no doubt a tactical, even strategic, gain, enabling Israel a better control over southern Lebanon,” said Ahron Bregman, an Israeli security analyst and senior teaching fellow at King’s College London. “From an Israeli perspective, it is a way to put pressure on the Lebanese government: Tackle Hezbollah head-on, or we stay here.”
Nicholas Blanford, a non-resident senior fellow at the Atlantic Council and an authority on the group, said Hezbollah’s lack of comment on the Israeli claims raised a number of questions.
“It could be that a deal’s been done. It could be that Israel is exaggerating what it means by ‘operational control’,” he said, noting that neither the extent of Israel’s military control over the ridge, nor the infrastructure contained within it, is known.
“What we do know is that Hezbollah appears ready to get back into the resistance business, but no longer seems to be making the decisions,” he said. “Those are coming from Iran, who appear to want to keep things quiet for now.”
Analysts also suggested that a lack of a response from Tehran may frustrate Netanyahu, who has invested much of his electoral stock in finishing the war with Iran, an opponent he has characterised as posing an existential threat to the country since at least the early 1990s.
Katz has described an attack against Israel as freeing its military “from all constraints”, and that in such a scenario, the military would “strike all infrastructure – including energy infrastructure – and return Iran to the Stone Age and darkness”, all of which would almost certainly constitute war crimes.
However, how far Israel – diplomatically, economically and militarily dependent upon the US – can proceed beyond rhetoric is open to question.
With Netanyahu predicted to struggle in October’s elections, what happens in southern Lebanon may prove crucial.
“Will Iran come to Hezbollah’s aid?” Bregman asked. “One person for sure – a certain Benjamin Netanyahu prays that they do – as it could even postpone the forthcoming elections in Israel in which, if judged by current polls, he will be defeated.”

Rome and Athens: Israel’s unlikely new gateways to North America - comment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
16:03:48 UTC
01:03:48 KST

In a cab to Ben-Gurion Airport on my way to the States, the driver asked me the inevitable question: “Terminal One or Three?”
Terminal Three provided the stark images for a recent article in this paper titled, “Chaos ensues at Ben-Gurion Airport after staff strike grinds Israeli air travel to a halt.” Terminal One, on the other hand, is the nostalgic airport of my youth.
I began this piece in homage to the Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist who popularized the cab-driver conversation device to advance his multiple causes, from support of the two-state solution to critiques of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
What I really wanted to tell my driver, however, was “Terminal Four” – which is why I am now proposing the immediate inauguration of “Terminal Four” and “Terminal Five.”
No construction budget is required. “Terminal Four” is known internationally as FCO – Rome Fiumicino Leonardo da Vinci International Airport. “Terminal Five” is ATH – Athens International Airport Eleftherios Venizelos.
The new route to North America
It seems like almost everyone flying to North America this summer passed through a European hub, with ATH and FCO ranking among the most popular. This is not due to any sudden urge to explore the historical connection between the Jewish people and the Greeks or the Romans. It is simply because US carriers were not flying to Israel.
As a result, travelers to North America faced sky-high prices and severely limited availability on the few direct routes served by Israeli carriers.
In case you have not experienced this pain personally, New York, Miami, Los Angeles, and Boston were the only nonstop summer destinations operating out of Ben-Gurion.
A sample of economy-class summer direct fares showed New York hovering around $2,500, while the other North American destinations were going for over $6,000 for the lowest-cost seat.
Shockingly, at those astronomical prices, seats were still scarce. While this has been the absurd reality for most of the past three years, the highly anticipated, step-by-step return of US legacy carriers will continue to be reported in The Jerusalem Post Travel section.
Compare that to the brief golden period between the end of COVID-19 restrictions and October 7, 2023, when those exact same flights hovered around the thousand-dollar mark.
Furthermore, the prolonged absence of Delta, United, American, and Air Canada completely stripped my fellow travelers of nonstop service to the San Francisco Bay Area, Chicago, and the entirety of the Great White North.
Thus, we return to the “Terminal Four” and “Terminal Five” designation. Geographical accuracy and tongue-in-cheek branding aside, no one expects European aviation authorities to permanently rewrite their signs.
Yet, in an era where Florida has officially renamed West Palm Beach to President Donald J. Trump International Airport, and Tennessee is moving to honor Dolly Parton at Nashville International, a little creative renaming isn’t entirely without precedent.
And for my fellow travelers heading to North America, these unorthodox hubs remain a highly relevant, de facto reality – so much so that summer travelers report Hebrew has almost become the lingua franca at selected European airports.
How to make use of a European stopover
The reality of how “Terminals Four and Five” operate as impromptu hubs is still relevant and quite straightforward, as follows:
FCO and ATH are served from Israel by multiple Israeli, European, and low-cost carriers. Landing in Rome or Athens, the world is your oyster. From there, 11 additional North American cities are served nonstop by seven different airlines, with round-trip transatlantic fares sitting comfortably around $1,000.
Given that a European stopover on the way to North America introduces additional scheduling flexibility alongside potential cost savings, it becomes a viable travel strategy.
As an added feature, why not make a day of it? Leave the airport. Hit the beach in 10 minutes, zip off to the Colosseum in 45 minutes, or make it to the Acropolis in an hour. Enjoy excellent dining in Rome, kosher or otherwise.
Experience an authentic meal of carciofi alla giudia (Jewish-style artichokes) in the historic Jewish Ghetto. You can even bring a dense, sweet cake of Pizza Ebraica home to your family in Teaneck, NJ.
They say Rome was not built in a day, but you can certainly see a lot of it in one. If you want to stay close to FCO, venture no more than 10 minutes from the terminal to the beaches of Lido di Ostia, or explore the world-class ruins and Europe’s oldest synagogue at Ostia Antica.
If your schedule requires an overnight stay, book an airport hotel or a cozy guesthouse in nearby Fiumicino, Italy, or Artemida, Greece.
Once your sightseeing is done, utilize your airline lounge access or buy a day pass to relax, recharge, and shower before boarding your transatlantic flight.
Convinced? Just remember to plan ahead, especially if traveling with children. Make sure your schedules align well. Because you may be self-connecting across multiple airlines, leave plenty of time between flights – no tight connections, please. You will likely need to collect your bags in FCO or ATH, so locate luggage storage facilities in advance.
Book convenient lodging, map out your transportation plan, and check opening hours, as Italian cultural sites do not always operate on a 365-day schedule. My personal advice for the day excursion: travel light or ultra-light.
Get off the plane excited to explore. By the time you upload photos of your kids climbing on 2,000-year-old Roman ruins to your social networks, you will be boarding your next flight feeling rested, invigorated, and a bit more well-traveled.
The long absence of American carriers was disturbing, yet the crisis has left us with what may be a better way to travel to North America. A well-planned stopover isn’t a compromise; it is a creative travel opportunity.
Even as more direct routes open up, do not be surprised if the savvy traveler who has opted for a day in Rome is greeted by a sign that reads: “Terminal Four – FCO – Benvenuti a Roma! Bruchim HaBa’im.”
The writer is an occasional contributor to the Post from Ra’anana. In his day job, he is CEO of Coworking Israel.

====================================================================================================

Hangzhou offers a glimpse of China’s journey from silk to silicon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
16:03:20 UTC
01:03:20 KST

Hangzhou may be celebrated by leisure travelers for its trio of UNESCO World Heritage Sites, but for Western visitors making the journey today, it is likely household names from the tech sphere that ring most familiar. Chief among them is e-commerce giant Alibaba and its global subsidiary, AliExpress.
For the past three decades, these titans have come to symbolize Hangzhou’s meteoric ascent as a powerhouse of innovation, transforming both the urban landscape and the local community.
While nature still frames the metropolis, encircled as it is by lush forested hills, serene lakes, and winding rivers, this bustling city of 13 million souls has evolved far beyond its picturesque geography. Today, it stands proudly as a magnet for cutting-edge technological investment, forward-thinking educational initiatives, and top-tier IT talent drawn from every corner of the globe.
The Wensan Future Technology Experience Center is the perfect starting point for understanding how far technology has come and where it’s likely to go. Dozens of robots and AI-based technologies perform practical everyday tasks as well as entertaining activities in this visitor center. From exoskeletons to fighting robots, one can experience the very best that Hangzhou and China have to offer in this hands-on experience.
The headquarters of Alibaba affords another view into the world of hi-tech in China. In 1999, Jack Ma and 17 friends created a small company that eventually became Alibaba. Today, the group employs around 200,000 people around the world, across a variety of brands and subsidiaries, and has a whopping $140-billion turnover.
AliExpress, familiar to pretty much all Israelis, is just one part of this mega-corporation’s influence on international commerce, finance, and trade. Indeed, the company enjoys a strong investment relationship with Israel, particularly via its collaboration with Jerusalem Venture Partners.
The company’s sprawling visitor center offers a peek into the life of Ma and his colleagues through explanatory panels in a huge atrium, which is surrounded by offices of the conglomerate. Nestled at the center of the atrium is a replica of the Hangzhou apartment where the company began.
Among the technologies on display and indeed in practical use in the headquarters is facial recognition for vending machines. Simply looking at the machine engages an unlocking mechanism, items are removed, and the purchase price is automatically debited from the bank account, with a receipt automatically appearing on one’s phone.
“This is a glimpse into the future,” notes tour guide Carl Gao as the system clears another transaction. “These technologies are here now and will be everywhere soon.”
Inspiration by the water
Just steps from the urban rush lies West Lake, a tranquil expanse of water that has inspired travelers for centuries, balancing history with everyday life. In the morning, locals practice Tai Chi by the water and traditional musicians play in the pavilions, while just minutes away, the modern city hums along.
Among the historical landmarks surrounding the water is the Broken Bridge, situated at the end of the Bai Causeway. Despite its name, the bridge is structurally intact and derives its identity from an optical illusion created in winter when melting snow clears unevenly on its arch, making parts of it appear disconnected.
Historically, it served as the primary setting for the famous romantic tragedy of the White Snake, symbolizing enduring devotion and the meeting place of myth and reality.
Further out on the water stand the Three Pools Mirroring the Moon, located on a small artificial island in the southern sector of the lake. This site features three hollow stone mini-pagodas erected during the Ming Dynasty, designed with holes that allow candlelight to mix with moonlight on autumn nights.
Today, the location represents classical Chinese garden design and holds national recognition as the imagery featured on the back of the Chinese one-yuan banknote.
Overlooking the southern shore stands the Leifeng Pagoda, originally built in the 10th century by the King of Wuyue to consecrate Buddhist relics and celebrate a royal birth.
Although the original structure collapsed in 1924 due to structural decay and relic scavenging, a modern reconstruction now houses the old ruins beneath protective glass while offering a comprehensive museum space. The tower symbolizes the turbulent intersection of historical preservation and modern architectural rebuilding, providing an elevated vantage point over the entire lake basin.
West Lake sits right on the edge of the city, serving as a gateway to the broader, picture-postcard beauty of Zhejiang province.
The historic Silk Road
Some 64 million people call this wider region home, yet much of the landscape remains covered by cultivated tea plantations, mulberry bushes, and wilder vegetation climbing over mountains, hills, and a flat river delta. For centuries, tea, silk, and ceramics served as the major Chinese goods exported westward along the historic Silk Road toward Istanbul and Rome.
Today, the province also produces the deliciously fresh Nongfu Spring bottled water, a brand associated with sourcing water from protected natural environments, including the Thousand Island Lake area.
At its visitors’ center, one can observe highly automated production systems designed to bottle and distribute water and a variety of the brand’s other beverages, which include teas, vitamin drinks, and juice products, on a national scale.
The region is blessed with an ample water supply. Zhejiang features a humid subtropical monsoon climate, receiving high annual rainfall that typically ranges between 1,000 and 1,900 mm, roughly 39 to 75 inches, depending on the specific terrain.
Its often wide or powerful rivers are not only a vital source of water but also a major engine for energy. The Xin’an River Hydropower Station stands as one of the landmark engineering projects of modern China, playing an essential role in regional development by generating electricity and managing water resources to support economic growth across Zhejiang.
The project also led to the creation of the vast Thousand Island Lake reservoir, where visitors today can witness firsthand China’s ongoing efforts to balance infrastructure, industry, and environmental stewardship.
The lakeside town of Chun’an
Leaving the dam behind, the road winds along the shoreline toward Chun’an, offering wide, striking vistas across the vast lake. The surrounding hills are mostly blanketed in dense trees that give the landscape a textured, rounded look, occasionally interrupted by patches of tea plantations.
Amid the stunning scenery, a solitary fisherman stands balanced on a long, flat wooden boat, net in hand, carrying on a traditional way of life on waters that were shaped just decades ago by this modern, seemingly never-ending reservoir.
As daylight begins to fade, the lakeside town of Chun’an offers an ideal stopping point for a sunset dinner and an overnight stay. Waterfront restaurants serve fresh catches alongside local specialties, providing a relaxed atmosphere as the sky turns orange and purple over the water. It is a quiet place to rest before continuing the journey.
An hour west of Chun’an lies Xiajiang. Tucked into the hills of Zhejiang province, the village feels less like a traditional ancient hamlet and more like a carefully polished showcase. Decades ago, it was a typical, impoverished mountainside community, but heavy government investment turned it into a poster child for rural modernization.
Today, Xiajiang features neat rows of uniform whitewashed guesthouses, pristine stone paths, and an immaculate river running through the center, functioning almost as an open-air exhibition of modern Chinese country life where visitors come to see how rural tourism and state-backed revitalization intersect. Farmers dry hot peppers and corn kernels on the sidewalks and squares, just as their ancestors did, before the tourists arrived.
Wuzhen lies to the north of Hangzhou, on the way to Shanghai. It’s a canal town that wears its history on its sleeve, yet runs with the precision of a modern theme park. Located in the northern reaches of Zhejiang, this ancient water settlement dates back well over a thousand years, originally serving as a vital trading post where boats navigated a dense web of stone-lined waterways.
Today, it stands as one of China’s most famous preserved historic towns, divided administratively into distinct zones that cater directly to cultural tourists and conference-goers alike, while also taking into account the life patterns of its citizens.
Approaching the historic core, the landscape shifts abruptly from modern concrete highways to a labyrinth of weathered gray-brick buildings, black-tiled roofs, and crisscrossing arched stone bridges.
The water of the canal system laps directly against the foundations of two-story wooden houses; their balconies draped with laundry and traditional lanterns swaying gently in the breeze. Flat-bottomed wooden passenger boats, propelled by boatmen standing at the stern using a single long oar, glide quietly beneath low bridges, carrying visitors past narrow alleyways and old stone wharves.
A living museum
What makes Wuzhen unique in the modern tourism landscape is its meticulous management. Rather than remaining an entirely organic, lived-in community, the historic district underwent a massive, state-backed restoration project starting in the late 1990s, transforming it into a living museum.
Historic workshops and old merchant houses were carefully restored to showcase traditional crafts that once sustained the local economy. Visitors can walk through operational indigo fabric-dyeing yards where yards of deep blue cloth hang drying on high bamboo poles, or stop by small, family-run distilleries producing traditional rice wine that hangs in the humid air.
At the same time, the town has embraced an entirely different kind of prominence in recent years. Just on the edge of the historic water town sits a sprawling, ultra-modern convention center featuring massive glass domes and hi-tech facilities. This venue serves as the permanent home of the World Internet Conference, drawing global tech executives, cybersecurity experts, and government officials to debate the digital future.
As daylight fades, Wuzhen undergoes a dramatic transformation. The crowds of day trippers disperse, and thousands of red lanterns ignite along the water’s edge, casting long, shimmering reflections across the dark canals.
The atmosphere turns remarkably still, broken only by the occasional splash of an oar or the muffled murmur of diners gathered in small waterside restaurants. It is a commercialized slice of the past, certainly, but one executed with an undeniable aesthetic appeal that captures the enduring romance of China’s watery southern landscapes.
Perhaps the most striking thing about traveling through Hangzhou and the surrounding countryside is the sense that China is not choosing between its past and its future. It is attempting, sometimes with breathtaking ambition, to embrace both.
Technology is a philosophy of possibility
In Hangzhou, technology is not presented simply as a tool but almost as a philosophy of possibility. Artificial intelligence, robotics, facial recognition and vast digital enterprises are woven into everyday life with a confidence that reflects a belief in progress, efficiency and human ingenuity.
Yet only minutes away, people gather beside West Lake to practice Tai Chi, listen to traditional music or simply contemplate the water. Ancient stories and legends remain embedded in the landscape, while Buddhist and Confucian traditions continue to provide a backdrop through which people understand harmony, balance and their relationship with the world around them.
That same determination to reconcile old and new is visible beyond the city. Zhejiang’s spectacular mountains, tea plantations, rivers and lakes provide a reminder of the extraordinary natural beauty that has shaped life here for centuries.
At the same time, villages such as Xiajiang reveal another side of contemporary China: a recognition that decades of urbanization have left rural communities behind, and an ambitious attempt to reverse that process through investment, infrastructure and tourism.
The result may sometimes feel carefully curated, even theatrical, but beneath the polished facades lies a seemingly genuine desire to give rural communities a viable future.
Perhaps that is the enduring impression of this journey. China is changing at extraordinary speed, but it does not necessarily see modernization as an act of erasing what came before.
Instead, it appears to be constantly reinventing the relationship between tradition and innovation, countryside and city, nature and technology. The journey from silk to silicon is not a rejection of the past, but its reinvention.
In Hangzhou and its hinterland, the result is a landscape where ancient waterways can lead to internet conferences, tea fields coexist with cutting-edge industry, and centuries-old beliefs sit comfortably beside visions of an AI-powered future. It is a fascinating and often beautiful glimpse of a country trying to carry its past into tomorrow.
The authors were guests of the Embassy of the People’s Republic of China in Israel (travelchina.org.cn/en).

Australian man charged over alleged antisemitic threats against Zionist council

2026-09-05
16:03:20 UTC

A 52-year-old man from northern Queensland, Australia, has been charged with two hate crime offenses following alleged antisemitic threats targeting the Queensland Zionist Council.
Chris McComb, a resident of Mossman, is accused of calling for Jews and Israelis to be expelled from Australia, among other demands.
The Queensland Zionist Council confirmed that it received the message. In a statement quoted by The Courier-Mail, the council said it received an online message through the contact form on its website in early July 2026 that contained "explicit threats."
Police took steps to protect the identity of the council representative who received the message. The council and the Zionist Federation of Australia said they supported the decision not to disclose the person's identity.
The council used the case to warn about what it described as a growing and dangerous trend: the use of terms such as "Zionists" and "anti-Zionism" as a cover for statements that are, in practice, directed at Jews and Israelis.
Anti-Zionism: a tool for a modern Jewish hatred
"Anti-Zionism has increasingly become a tool for a modern form of anti-Jewish hatred," the council said. It added that such rhetoric "presents itself as political commentary, while in practice it is used as a means of threatening, defaming, and intimidating Jews and Israelis."
The council added that the case "reflects a broader pattern" and said it has been warning government officials, police, and online platforms about it for some time.
Australian Police arrested McComb on August 27 in an area north of Cairns. The newly established joint hate crime team of Queensland Police and the Australian Federal Police is carrying out the investigation. The team combines investigators from Queensland's counterterrorism unit with Australian Federal Police national security investigators.
McComb himself, however, has not been charged with any terrorism offenses at this time.
"The harm to social cohesion at the local community level ultimately affects Australia's national security," Australian Federal Police Detective Superintendent Anthony Conway said. "We will not allow divisive and hateful rhetoric to grow and spread."
The case comes amid a sharp increase in reports of antisemitism in Queensland. Jason Steinberg, president of the Queensland Jewish Board of Deputies, told The Australian that more than 100 reported antisemitic incidents have already been recorded in the state this year.
"It is deeply concerning to know that antisemitism, hatred, and the intent to harm Jews have not stopped in our country," he said.
Paul Myers, a Jewish community leader, told The Courier-Mail that the charges show that when hatred moves from words to threats, the law takes action. He said it was particularly concerning how normalized this type of hatred has become and "how often it is now hidden behind the language of political opinion."
