====================================================================================================

First human trial of psilocin since the 1960s reveals better tolerability than psilocybin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
14:00:55 UTC
23:00:55 KST

Recent research suggests that consuming psilocin, the active compound in “magic” mushrooms, might cause fewer side effects than taking psilocybin. The study also explored taking the drug under the tongue, finding it well tolerated though less intense at the tested doses. The findings were published in Journal of Psychopharmacology.
Psilocybin is a naturally occurring compound found in certain hallucinogenic mushrooms. In recent years, it has gained attention as a potential treatment for mental health conditions. For example, a study covered by PsyPost in 2021 noted that psilocybin therapy could offer symptom relief comparable to some conventional antidepressants.
However, psilocybin itself does not directly cause psychedelic effects. It is a prodrug, meaning the body must break it down to activate it. When a person swallows psilocybin, enzymes in the gut and liver strip away a phosphate molecule, converting it into a new chemical called psilocin.
Psilocin is the active substance that enters the brain and alters perception. In fact, a 2019 study indicated that the intensity of a person’s psychedelic experience closely matches the concentration of psilocin circulating in their blood. Because the body’s conversion process can vary from person to person, standard oral psilocybin often yields unpredictable results and tends to cause unpleasant side effects.
“Nearly every modern psilocybin trial has used the same thing: synthetic psilocybin, 25 mg, in a capsule,” Josh Woolley, an associate professor of psychiatry at the University of California, San Francisco and director of the Translational Psychedelic Research Program, told PsyPost. “There are reasons to think other options might work better. Psilocybin is a prodrug, so the body has to convert it to psilocin, and people vary a lot in how efficiently they do that. That may be part of why responses to a fixed dose are so variable.”
Researchers wanted to know if administering psilocin directly would skip this metabolic step, potentially offering a gentler and more predictable experience. They also wanted to test a sublingual route, which involves placing a dissolving tablet under the tongue. Sublingual administration allows a drug to absorb directly into the bloodstream through the tissues of the mouth, completely bypassing the digestive system.
“Nobody had given psilocin directly to a human since the 1960s, and nobody had tried a sublingual formulation of any of these compounds,” Woolley noted.
Additionally, the research team used botanical extracts rather than lab-made synthetic chemicals. These whole-mushroom formulations contain natural trace compounds, known as alkaloids, alongside the primary drug. Alkaloids are naturally occurring chemical compounds found in plants and fungi that produce physiological effects on the body, and some researchers suspect they might influence the overall experience. “Mushrooms contain other alkaloids besides psilocybin, and standardized botanical extracts now make it possible to test whole-mushroom formulations under pharmaceutical conditions, which hadn’t been done,” Woolley said.
The research, led by Marlene L. Tai and Woolley, aimed to compare these different methods in a controlled setting. The scientists recruited 20 healthy adults between the ages of 25 and 50. All participants had prior experience with psychedelics and reported mild feelings of social disconnection. The study used a crossover design, meaning each person received multiple different treatments on separate days to compare the effects within the same individual.
Participants attended up to four drug administration sessions spaced four weeks apart. During these sessions, they received either an oral capsule of psilocybin (25 milligrams), an oral capsule of psilocin (17.5 milligrams, a dose designed to match the psilocybin strength), or a sublingual tablet of psilocin. The initial sublingual dose was set low at 2.18 milligrams and later increased to 4.36 milligrams or 8 milligrams to assess safety and tolerability.
All sessions took place in a comfortable clinic room where participants wore eyeshades and listened to music. A therapist and an assistant stayed in the room to provide psychological support. Throughout the day, the research team measured blood pressure and heart rate, while participants rated the intensity of the drug’s effects every 15 to 30 minutes.
At the end of each session, participants completed several questionnaires. These surveys measured the emotional and psychological qualities of their experience, including feelings of unity, emotional breakthroughs, and challenging states like fear or paranoia.
When comparing the two oral capsules, the scientists found that psilocin produced a psychological and physical journey that was very similar to psilocybin. The onset time, peak intensity, and duration of the experiences were mostly indistinguishable. Both drugs reliably produced deep psychological insights and mystical-type experiences.
“We expected psilocin to come on faster, since it skips a metabolic step, and it didn’t,” Woolley explained. “The two were hard to tell apart on almost every measure.”
However, oral psilocin was associated with a lower overall burden of adverse side effects. While almost all participants experienced mild issues on both drugs, oral psilocybin was linked to more moderate and severe events. These included headaches, anxiety, and one instance of transient loss of consciousness. Interestingly, gastrointestinal issues like nausea were similar between the two oral drugs, suggesting that stomach upset is not solely caused by the body breaking down psilocybin.
“The tolerability difference was modest, not dramatic,” Woolley said. “Fewer and milder adverse events on average, mostly headache and anxiety, rather than a categorical improvement. Whether that matters clinically depends on the setting. In a treatment where one session already requires eight hours of monitoring, small reductions in burden can add up. But this was 18 people per condition, so it’s a signal worth following, not an established difference.”
The sublingual psilocin tablets proved safe and were well tolerated by the participants. But the physical and psychological effects were much milder than the oral doses. The subjective intensity and cardiovascular responses were noticeably lower, indicating that less of the drug made its way into the systemic circulation at the tested amounts.
“At the cautious doses we used with FDA input, we clearly didn’t reach the exposure needed to test whether the route has real advantages,” Woolley noted. “This is an early study in 20 healthy volunteers. It’s a first look, not a verdict.”
Despite the milder overall intensity, sublingual psilocin still facilitated notable psychological responses. Participants reported scores on measures of emotional breakthrough and psychological insight that rivaled those typically seen with much higher oral doses. The authors noted that this suggests even mild psychedelic exposures might offer some therapeutic benefit.
“One result we’re still thinking about,” the researcher stated. “Even the very mild sublingual doses produced emotional breakthrough scores comparable to the full 25 mg doses. That could be a false positive, or an effect of the psychotherapy rather than the drug. But if it holds, it raises a real question about whether an intense psychedelic experience is necessary for the psychological benefits people are after.”
In an exploratory analysis, the researchers also compared their botanical mushroom extracts to data from a separate trial that used synthetic psilocybin. The psychological effects were broadly similar. This provides evidence that standardized whole-mushroom extracts function much like lab-made versions, offering a viable alternative for future treatments.
“On the botanical question, our comparison was with data from a previously published trial of synthetic psilocybin, not with a synthetic arm in our own study,” Woolley explained. “Two different populations, two different settings. So the fair statement is that we saw nothing that would suggest a big difference, not that we ruled one out. Testing the ‘entourage effect’ properly would require a head-to-head comparison in the same trial.” This entourage effect is the theory that multiple natural compounds within a plant or mushroom work together synergistically to produce stronger or different effects than an isolated chemical alone.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The study included a small group of healthy, highly educated volunteers who already had experience with psychedelics. Because of this, it is not guaranteed that people with severe mental health conditions or those entirely new to psychedelics would respond in the exact same way.
The researchers also emphasized the strict clinical environment used during the trial. “The main one is that nothing here suggests people should be taking mushroom extracts on their own or trying to convert psilocybin to psilocin at home,” Woolley warned. “These were pharmaceutical grade products made to Good Manufacturing Practice standards, given under continuous medical supervision with a licensed therapist present throughout. That matters. One participant briefly lost consciousness during a psilocybin session, which we’ve reported separately, and it was handled because clinicians were in the room.”
The trial also lacked a pure inactive placebo group. Because the sublingual doses produced noticeably milder physical sensations than the oral capsules, participants and therapists were often able to guess which treatment had been administered. This awareness could have influenced the subjective survey responses.
Finally, the research team did not collect blood samples during the sessions. Without measuring the actual concentration of psilocin in the blood, it is difficult to know exactly how much of the sublingual drug was absorbed or how individual metabolisms processed the oral capsules. Future studies will need to incorporate blood testing and try higher sublingual doses to fully evaluate this delivery method.
“Measuring actual psilocin levels is what would let us link formulation to exposure to effect, and its absence was our main limitation here,” Woolley observed. “Sublingual psilocin needs a proper dose-ranging study at higher doses. And eventually this has to be tested in people with the conditions these drugs might treat, not just healthy volunteers.”
Moving forward, the team intends to share additional findings from the current participants. “We have a companion paper in preparation from this same trial looking at longer-term psychological outcomes, including loneliness, out to six months,” Woolley, who also serves as a staff psychiatrist at the San Francisco VA Medical Center, added. “That’s the other half of the story and we’ll have more to say when it’s out.”
The study, “A randomized crossover trial comparing the acute physiological and psychological effects of botanical formulations of oral psilocybin, oral psilocin, and sublingual psilocin,” was authored by Marlene L. Tai, Balázs Szigeti, Amanda E. Downey, Jacob S. Aday, Lisa Fredenburg, Kimberly Sakai, Cesar Molina, Gisele Fernandes-Osterhold, Ellen R. Bradley, Maddie Pantoni, Ryan Moss, Benjamin Lightburn, Franziska Plessow, Aoife O’Donovan, and Josh D. Woolley.

IFAD, Equity Group launch 200 mln USD climate finance mechanism for East African farmers
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
22:00:44 CST
23:00:44 KST

KIGALI, Sept. 5 (Xinhua) -- The International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD) and Equity Group on Friday launched the Africa Rural Climate Adaptation Finance Mechanism (ARCAFIM), a 200-million-U.S.-dollar financing mechanism aimed at expanding access to climate adaptation finance for smallholder farmers and rural businesses in East Africa, IFAD said in a statement.
The financing mechanism was launched on the sidelines of the Africa Food Systems Forum in the Rwandan capital Kigali. It is designed to address the persistent gap between climate finance commitments and the capital reaching rural communities, according to the statement.
It is being implemented by IFAD and Equity Group, with support from the Green Climate Fund, the Ministry for Foreign Affairs of Finland, the Nordic Development Fund, Denmark and the European Union.
The 12-year mechanism comprises 180 million U.S. dollars in lending capital and about 20 million U.S. dollars for technical assistance, with the lending capital expected to generate about 266 million dollars in loans through four investment cycles.
ARCAFIM will operate in Rwanda, Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania, with the ambition of reaching about 260,000 smallholder farmers and 500 rural micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs), according to the statement.
At least 50 percent of the intended beneficiaries will be women and 30 percent youth. The initiative is expected to strengthen food security for about 1.2 million people and benefit an estimated 1.5 million people directly and indirectly by supporting investments in climate-resilient agriculture and rural businesses.
Speaking at the launch, IFAD Vice President Gerardine Mukeshimana said the success of climate adaptation finance would depend on turning global commitments into tangible investments in rural communities.
"ARCAFIM's ambition is to make rural climate adaptation a recognizable, viable and sustainable business line for African financial institutions. It will support tailored financial products and a climate adaptation financing taxonomy, so that participating institutions gain the experience, systems and confidence to continue expanding adaptation finance," Mukeshimana is quoted as saying in the statement.
James Mwangi, Chief Executive Officer of Equity Group Holdings, said the mechanism would help change the way financial institutions view smallholder farmers by treating them as entrepreneurs and bankable clients.
He said Equity Group's commitment of 90 million U.S. dollars from its own balance sheet would help build a sustainable market for climate-resilient lending rather than a temporary financing program. ■

====================================================================================================

‘The chancellor is in a bind’: is No 11 at odds with Burnham’s big vision?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
14:00:38 UTC
23:00:38 KST

Until now, Andy Burnham has been a lucky prime minister. In office for just over six weeks, no major domestic crisis derailed his plans over the summer, Reform has been on the back foot, and he arrived back at Westminster with his personal approval ratings soaring and optimism undampened.
But underneath the sense of relief that many Labour MPs are feeling that their high-stakes gamble of ousting Keir Starmer appears – for now – to have paid off, there is an unease that Burnham’s premiership is yet to make contact with economic reality.
In their early weeks in office, his team were able to point to some inherited green shoots: below-forecast inflation figures, sustained growth, signs that sluggish productivity could be starting to turn around. All despite the economic turmoil unleashed by the Iran conflict.
This week, all that changed. With the end of summer recess came a global bond sell-off amid anxiety over oil prices, sticky inflation and pressure to ramp up defence spending, which pushed government borrowing costs to their highest since the 2008 financial crash.
It makes the backdrop to John Healey’s first budget as chancellor a difficult one. Economists reckon about half of the £24bn fiscal breathing space his predecessor Rachel Reeves had built up at her spring forecast has since been wiped out by higher inflation and interest rates, severely limiting Healey’s room for manoeuvre.
Among the more experienced hands in government, there is a firm view that the new administration cannot return to the days of slim headroom given Reeves’s experience last year, which led to more brutal proposed welfare cuts and ultimately a backbench rebellion last summer.
Healey has just returned from the G20 finance ministers’ meeting in North Carolina and is acutely conscious of factors beyond his control that will hit the Office for Budget Responsibility’s forecasts, including the rising cost of oil after bombing resumed in Iran.
It is little surprise, then, that he has repeatedly stressed that fiscal responsibility is the “bedrock” of his approach and he will stick to Reeves’s fiscal rules.
But his cautious tone jars uncomfortably with the prime minister’s large – and costly – policy vision: more public control of utilities, reform of the broken social care system and a mass social home building programme.
“[Healey] is in a bind,” one Treasury source said. “His instinct is to keep things steady, especially while the OBR does its snapshot, but that’s not Andy’s gameplan for his first week back.”
Indeed, Downing Street has been eager to ensure Burnham’s vision stays front and centre. In a mammoth three-and-a-half-hour Commons session on Tuesday, he repeatedly promised to deliver the “much more substantial change” the country was crying out for.
Among Burnham’s closest allies, there have been some mutterings that Healey could, like chancellors before him, be in danger of being “captured” by the Treasury and its more orthodox arguments. “John did not exactly show in the Ministry of Defence that he was good at questioning internal departmental wisdom and pressures,” one government aide said.
The friction between the two operations burst into the open last week when Healey suggested in a television interview that Burnham was running a “continuity” government.
No 10 insiders pushed back hard. “Nobody listening to Andy and his plans for growth could think he is just about continuity,” said one senior figure. “He’s going to change things.”
A timely report that suggests Manchester’s economic success – one of Burnham’s biggest legacies – could be replicated across England to unlock untapped growth potential of up to £80bn is released this weekend.
Mandala Partners, a global economic research consultancy that was led by Nick Williams – a former Downing Street economic adviser who is now working for the first secretary, Louise Haigh – found that housing, transport and health devolution would be crucial to achieving the prime minister’s aim of “growth in every postcode”.
Of these, the impact of following Manchester’s housing investment model is most striking. The report found that an £8.5bn programme of revolving public risk capital across mayoral strategic authorities could unlock almost 100,000 additional homes, crowd in more than £20bn of private investment and support more than 70,000 jobs.
While not commissioned by No 10, Mandala’s study nevertheless bolsters Burnham’s central growth argument that learning from the success of Manchester’s devolution model could deliver far-reaching economic benefits and release the country from its low-growth chokehold.
The chancellor has privately acknowledged there is room for modest additional borrowing to fund investment given Reeves’s rule change in 2024, which allowed the Treasury to offset financial assets against government debt.
However, there is little sense of a radical new perspective emerging from the new regime at No 11. On Monday, Healey will give a speech on the government’s mission for growth, which is expected to stress the importance of devolution and public investment – both themes Reeves repeatedly returned to.
The chancellor will emphasise the need to give the private sector the confidence to invest – raising doubts about whether he is likely to go ahead with one of the big revenue raisers that progressive economists and the TUC have called for: a windfall tax on banks.
Treasury sources have declined to say whether Healey will stick to Reeves’s intention of holding only one major “fiscal event” each year, with the spring forecast a much more low-key affair. That would leave open the possibility of using his 28 October statement to fund the gaps in the defence investment plan and make more progress on tax devolution, while leaving the weightier tax and spending decisions until the spring.
Labour MPs are anxious for change as quickly as the government can deliver it. They applaud Burnham’s ambition and the sense of hope he fosters but worry that the economic realities will drag him down.
Tan Dhesi, the Labour chair of the Commons defence committee, summed up the mood when he suggested at PMQs that “vibes alone just will not be enough”. While he was referring to military spending, the sentiment is shared across the backbenches.
Burnham has repeatedly said he will be relentless in fulfilling his priorities. But some of his MPs are already worried that his promise to repair the crumbling state and offer “breathing space” on the cost of living could be hard to reconcile with promises of fiscal responsibility.
Downing Street sources argue, however, that it is only by improving infrastructure and devolving power that the British economy can grow as fast as Manchester’s. They cite Burnham’s visit to Cornwall this summer, where businesses told him it was taking them a year to connect to the grid.
Healey’s economic instincts are less clear. When asked what would be the main difference between him and his instinctively prudent predecessor, one adviser said: “To be honest, I think he will actually be more cautious.”
Despite his apparent wariness, government aides insist the chancellor is fully onboard with Burnham’s vision. One said: “There will always be tensions between the different parts of government, but John is aligned with Andy’s agenda. And he knows who is boss.”

23:00:10 KST

KIGALI, Sept. 5 (Xinhua) -- Rwanda on Friday named 22 baby mountain gorillas born over the past 12 months during the 21st edition of the annual gorilla naming ceremony, known locally as Kwita Izina.
The event, held at the foothills of Volcanoes National Park in Musanze District, northern Rwanda, brought together local communities, conservationists, partners, and guests from Rwanda and around the world to celebrate the country's mountain gorillas and the continued success of its conservation efforts.
"A name for us is more than a celebration; it is a promise, and the promise we make to these gorillas is that they will have the protection, habitat, and conditions they need to grow, thrive, and reproduce," said Rwandan Prime Minister Justin Nsengiyumva while presiding over the event.
Speaking at the ceremony, Jean-Guy Afrika, Rwanda Development Board (RDB) chief executive officer, said that Rwanda's conservation model is built on a simple principle: protecting nature and improving people's lives must go together.
"Kwita Izina helps us share this vision with the world. It showcases Rwanda's conservation model, our tourism offering, and the partnerships that continue to position our country as a destination for sustainable, high-value travel and investments," he said.
The event was held under the theme, "Conservation is Life: Sustaining the Future." With 22 babies named this year, the total number of mountain gorillas named through Kwita Izina since it became an official annual event in 2005 now stands at 460.
More than 1,060 mountain gorillas now live in the wild across the Virunga Massif and Bwindi ecosystem. Mountain gorillas remain the only great ape whose population continues to grow, following decades of collaboration between governments, conservation organisations, researchers, veterinarians, rangers and communities, according to RDB. ■

How Asian shipyards in Japan, Korea and Philippines keep US warships battle ready
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
14:00:06 UTC
23:00:06 KST

How Asian shipyards in Japan, Korea and Philippines keep US warships battle ready
Legal flexibility and regional partnerships allow US Seventh Fleet vessels to undergo complex overhauls closer to potential conflict zones
The facility is among the repair and maintenance hubs the US Navy has been developing in the region, strategically pushing for allies to perform major maintenance, repair and overhaul (MRO) work on US naval vessels given the decline of its shipbuilding base at home.
The repair work on the Benfold in the Philippine port took about 10 days before it resumed operations.
While US law mandates that major warships be built domestically, outsourcing MRO to foreign yards offers more flexibility, especially for forward-deployed vessels.
Naval vessels homeported outside the United States are not strictly prohibited from receiving foreign MRO services and deployed US-homeported ships may also be serviced by foreign workers under specific conditions.
The capacity of regional allies in the western Pacific, including Japan and South Korea, is particularly vital, given their distance from the continental US as well as Washington’s intensifying strategic competition with Beijing.
“By establishing the ability to repair and sustain larger numbers of ships closer to potential conflict areas in the Indo-Pacific, the United States could potentially support extended deployments – including during wartime – by reducing the need to recall ships to the US mainland for repairs,” the Washington-based think tank Centre for Strategic and International Studies said in a recent report.

Painting looted by Nazis to be returned to collector's heir
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
13:58:31 UTC
22:58:31 KST

"Portrait of a Lady," Italian painting looted by Nazis, ordered returned to Jewish collector's heir
A 17th-century Italian painting looted by Nazis from a prominent Jewish Dutch art collector must be returned to the rightful owner's heir, a judge in Argentina ruled on Friday.
Judge Santiago Inchausti approved a deal in which the daughter of a fugitive Nazi official agreed to give up her claim to the painting rather than face trial. This paves the way for the long-sought return of "Portrait of a Lady" to Maril von Saher, the sole surviving heir of art dealer Jacques Goudstikker. His much-celebrated collection of 1,100 paintings was sold under duress to Nazi officials after Adolf Hitler's Germany invaded the Netherlands in 1940.
The painting was recognized by the Dutch newspaper Algemeen Dagblad in a photo of a house for sale in the Argentine seaside resort of Mar del Plata in August 2025.
The painting was hanging above a green sofa in the living room of Patricia Kadgien, whose father, Friedrich Kadgien, was a financier for the Nazi SS paramilitary organization. He was one of the several high-ranking Nazis to escape to the South American country after World War II.
Patricia Kadgien and her husband, Juan Carlos Cortegoso, were charged with aggravated cover-up last year after authorities said they hid the 18th-century painting despite knowing Argentine and international investigators were seeking it.
Under the agreement, a copy obtained by The Associated Press, the couple agreed to give up any claim to the work and consent to its return to von Saher in exchange for avoiding a criminal trial and spending two years under court supervision. During that time, they must make payments to a hospital in Argentina's coastal city of Mar del Plata, where they live, and keep authorities informed of their whereabouts.
For decades, the portrait had been identified as a work by the Italian Baroque painter Giuseppe Vittore Ghislandi. It appeared under that attribution in Goudstikker's collection records and was exhibited as a Ghislandi in Amsterdam before the war. But a court-ordered examination by Argentina's National Academy of Fine Arts reached a different conclusion, attributing the work to the Italian artist Giacomo Antonio Melchiorre Ceruti.
Experts authenticated the painting as part of Goudstikker's collection and estimated its value at about $290,000.
Goudstikker was one of Europe's leading art dealers before World War II, known for a collection that included works by Rembrandt and Vermeer. He died in a shipwreck while fleeing Amsterdam with his family as German forces swept into the Netherlands in May 1940.
An estimated 1,100 works from his collection were illegally sold to Hermann Göring, known as Hitler's right-hand man, who amassed a vast art collection during the war. It remains unclear exactly how "Portrait of a Lady" came into the possession of Kadgien, Göring's financial adviser, who handled foreign currency, precious metals and the sale of confiscated property for the Nazi regime.
Kadgien fled Europe after Germany's defeat, first to Switzerland and later to Argentina. He died in the South American country in 1978 without having been arrested or charged with war crimes.
Lawyers for von Saher, who now lives in Greenwich, Connecticut, and spent decades trying to recover her family's looted art, said she has agreed to let the painting be exhibited in Argentina before being returned to her.
During last year's raids on homes owned by Kadgien and her sister in Mar del Plata, Argentine police also seized two 19th-century paintings, along with other prints and engravings. Authorities are still investigating whether any of them may also have been looted during World War II.

U.S. forces destroy three Iranian oil tankers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
13:57:14 UTC
22:57:14 KST

- CENTCOM disabled or destroyed three Iranian oil tankers on September 5 after Iran fired ballistic missiles at two U.S. Navy ships, which evaded the attacks unharmed.
- The strikes follow a pattern since February's Operation Epic Fury, including a fragile June ceasefire and a July strike on more than 80 Iranian targets.
U.S. Central Command forces struck and disabled three Iranian oil tankers on September 5, hours after Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps fired ballistic missiles at two U.S. Navy warships patrolling the region, according to a CENTCOM statement.
Both American vessels, an aircraft carrier and a guided-missile destroyer, evaded the Iranian missiles, and no U.S. personnel were harmed, CENTCOM said. The command did not name the two ships involved.
In response, American forces permanently disabled two Iranian crude oil carriers, the M/T Downy off Kharg Island and the M/T Stark 1 near Jask, and completely destroyed a third, the unladen M/T Kylo, also known as the Noxen, in the Gulf of Oman. CENTCOM said forces struck the Kylo in multiple critical locations after its crew was ordered to abandon ship, rendering the vessel inoperable.
CENTCOM described the three tankers as part of what it called a multibillion-dollar shadow fleet that generates revenue for the IRGC and its regional proxy groups, adding that Iran had no way to defend the ships once they were targeted.
“Let the message to the IRGC be clear: If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost, taking out three of yours,” said Adm. Brad Cooper, CENTCOM commander. “We will not hesitate to defend American forces, and if necessary, destroy Iran’s limited and exposed oil fleet.”
The strikes are the latest exchange in a conflict between the United States and Iran that began February 28, when the U.S. launched Operation Epic Fury. American forces have since enforced a naval blockade meant to cut off Iran’s oil exports, repeatedly disabling tankers that attempted to defy it. In May, an F/A-18 launched from the USS Abraham Lincoln (CVN 72) disabled the tanker M/T Hasna’s rudder with cannon fire near an Iranian port, and jets from the USS George H.W. Bush (CVN 77) later disabled two more unladen tankers, the M/T Sea Star III and M/T Sevda, attempting the same route.
A ceasefire took hold by early June, though CENTCOM described it as fragile at the time and publicly disputed Iranian claims that its forces had fired on U.S. Navy ships in the Gulf of Oman, saying doing so would have violated the truce. The uneasy calm broke down further in July, when Iran struck three commercial tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, prompting CENTCOM to hit more than 80 targets across southern Iran overnight, including air defense systems, command-and-control networks, coastal radar sites and more than 60 IRGC small boats.

Fact check: Germany's postal voting system isn't rigged
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
13:55:00 UTC
22:55:00 KST

Fact check: Germany's postal voting system isn't rigged
September 5, 2026
Stakes are high in Germany's three September state elections. In Saxony-Anhalt, where voters go to the ballot boxes on Sunday, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) could make history in by winning an outright majority.
The AfD's Saxony-Anhalt branch, which has been classified by the domestic intelligence agency as a "confirmed right-wing extremist organization", could become Germany's first far-right state government since World War II.
Mail-in voting, or "Briefwahl," has become an increasingly common feature of German elections. But the rise in mail-in ballots has been followed by a renewed wave of speculation and claims questioning the security and integrity of postal vote.
DW Fact check examined a sample of claims circulating online and assessed what the available evidence shows.
Does postal voting manipulate election results?
Claim: Cases of fraud involving postal ballots prove that postal voting is unreliable.
This claim recurrently appeared in posts about postal voting that DW Fact check reviewed on social media platforms including TikTok, X and Facebook.
Some posts point to individual cases of electoral fraud involving postal ballots and present them as evidence that the system as a whole is flawed. One verified account on X using the AfD logo, for example, cited two cases — a mail-in vote being cast on behalf of an elderly woman with dementia, and hundreds of voters in Magdeburg receiving multiple ballots — before calling postal voting defective and demanding immediate reforms.
DW Fact check: Misleading. Individual cases of fraud, errors or violations do not demonstrate that the entire postal voting system is unreliable or that it has affected the outcome of an election.
The post by the X account with the AfD logo refers to two real incidents, but does so in a misleading way. The claim about an elderly woman may refer to a case in Dessau, where police recently investigated an alleged vote cast on behalf of a 95-year-old woman with "severe dementia" but found no evidence of manipulation. The other incident occurred in Magdeburg, where 440 voters did receive duplicate ballots for the September 6 election ; however, the duplicates were invalidated and could not be used to cast additional valid votes.
Cases of electoral misconduct involving postal ballots have occurred in postal voting, as they have with voting at polling stations. In one case in Dresden, a man manipulated absentee ballots during the 2024 local and state elections, primarily in favor of the far-right Free Saxons party as well as the AfD. And in Bavaria, a former mayor was accused of manipulating postal voting documents in a March 2026 local election.
There have also been documented mistakes, administrative problems and delays in the handling of postal ballots in previous German elections. A 2021 study examining postal voting in German federal elections between 1998 and 2017 found that these weaknesses were primarily related to organization and logistics. Researcher Daniel Hellmann of the Martin Luther University Halle-Wittenberg said, however, that the research was still ongoing.
But such problems are not evidence of widespread fraud or of postal ballots being manipulated on a scale capable of changing an election result.
The 2021 study concluded that postal voting in Germany was secure overall. It found that none of the incidents examined could have changed an election result by even a single seat.
"If problems have occurred, they have generally been reviewed through legal channels and proportionate consequences have been imposed," Lukas Stötzer, an election researcher at the University of Witten/Herdecke in western Germany, told DW. "The postal voting system works and is secure, and that's why it is becoming more popular."
Postal voting easy to manipulate?
Claim: Postal votes are easily manipulated during counting.
"It can be assumed that postal voting in Saxony-Anhalt will massively distort the election result, This is also relatively easy to do, and the checks on postal voting are laughable," wrote one user on X with about 130,000 followers on August 14.
This claim was also a recurring theme among the posts reviewed by DW Fact check, with some of the content presented in satirical, AI-generated cartoons. The AI-generated video depicted here on TikTok and labelled satire, for example, shows a man involved in counting ballots simply altering the votes from AfD to the center-right CDU party, and then calling a man named "Friedrich" — presumably Chancellor Friedrich Merz — to say that he had "everything under control."
DW Fact check: False. Germany has detailed procedures governing the handling and counting of postal ballots. Postal votes are transported, stored and opened according to established rules, and their counting takes place publicly.
Members of the public are generally allowed to observe the election process, including the counting of votes, without having to demonstrate a particular interest or affiliation. This applies to postal ballot counting as well.
That means election officials do not simply open postal ballots and count them behind closed doors. The process is conducted by election boards, whose work can be observed by members of the public and each parties' representatives.
In an interview with German public broadcaster ARD Christa Dieckmann, Saxony-Anhalt's state election commissioner, pointed to public observation as an important safeguard. "The best way to ensure the fairness of the election is to come to the polling station as an observer for elections as the basis for choosing a legitimate government," she said.
DW Fact check also encountered numerous claims promoting what has been dubbed the "nursing home theory," which alleges that elderly people who are unable to vote in person may not be casting their ballots freely, but could instead be pressured or influenced by certain political parties or caregivers.
DW Fact check has investigated similar claims in the past, many of which have been promoted by AfD politicians. It has found no substantial evidence to support the broader allegation that postal voting in nursing homes is systematically manipulated or that elderly voters are routinely pressured into voting for particular parties.
A familiar claim beyond Germany
The doubts surrounding postal voting are not unique to Germany. Similar claims have surfaced during elections in other democracies, often becoming entangled with broader political battles over the legitimacy of elections.
During the 2020 US presidential election, President Donald Trump repeatedly claimed that expanded mail-in voting would lead to widespread fraud. Fact-checkers documented and debunked repeated false and exaggerated claims about the security of mail ballots. Ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, the Trump administration is again seeking to impose new restrictions on mail-in ballots, measures that have faced repeated legal challenges.
Election researcher Stötzer said such claims can become part of a broader political strategy to undermine trust in democratic institutions.
"Right-wing populist parties strategically fuel these doubts," Stötzer said, adding that such claims can later be used to justify electoral law changes that benefit those parties.
He said the immediate impact of such allegations may be limited. But if they are repeated election after election, the longer-term consequences could be more serious.
"Public trust in electoral institutions could suffer," Stötzer said. Election results that are considered undesirable could then routinely be attributed to alleged irregularities in postal voting.
This is a collaborative project between ARD-faktenfinder, and DW Fact check.
Edited by: Martin Kuebler

Why has the Trump administration ordered staff to take polygraph tests?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
13:54:33 UTC
22:54:33 KST

Why has the Trump administration ordered staff to take polygraph tests?
Reports of dwindling US weapons stocks have triggered an unusually sweeping hunt for leakers inside the Pentagon.
In a major crackdown on information leaks, the Trump administration has ordered dozens of Pentagon officials to undergo polygraph tests amid media reports of dwindling United States weapons stockpiles in the Middle East.
About 50 military officers and civilian officials working with the US military’s Joint Staff were subjected to polygraph examinations – commonly known as lie-detector tests – in August, The New York Times (NYT) has reported.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Trump sends envoys to Russia, Ukraine with new peace plan
- list 2 of 3Oil and politics: What Trump’s ‘historic’ deal means for Venezuela
- list 3 of 3Why is Trump threatening to strike Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain again, now?
CBS News separately reported that several dozen people underwent polygraph examinations earlier in the summer, including some US Central Command (CENTCOM) officials.
As US President Donald Trump accused unknown staff of making “treasonous statements” to journalists earlier this week, an ongoing investigation into information leaks also involves the Department of Justice and the FBI.
Here’s what we know about the polygraph tests.
Why are Pentagon staff undergoing polygraph tests?
This is part of a wider investigation into suspected leaks of classified information about US weapons stockpiles to journalists after news reports emerged in July that supplies of some critical munitions, particularly long-range missiles and Patriot interceptors, were running low. The reports coincided with the US halting attacks on Iran.
The Trump administration has strongly denied that it is low on weapons, saying it has “massive amounts” of weaponry available.
However, investigators have asked Joint Staff personnel undergoing polygraphs whether they provided classified information to the news media, particularly about declining US munitions stocks, according to the NYT.
CBS News reported that the polygraphs covered a range of national security matters. Two sources told the broadcaster that nobody failed the questions intended to establish whether officials had leaked information to the media.
The NYT reported that the investigation was intended not only to identify potential leakers but also to deter others from disclosing information in the future.
Between 1,500 and 2,000 military officers and civilian officials work for the Joint Staff, which helps coordinate military operations, policy and war planning with US combatant commands around the world.
General Dan Caine, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, was among senior officials who were not tested.
The Pentagon has not publicly confirmed details of the polygraph tests. “The Department does not comment on internal personnel or investigative matters but takes all leaks of classified national security information extremely seriously and investigates accordingly,” chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said.
Why are the weapons leaks so sensitive?
The level of US weapons reserves available to its forces stationed in the Middle East has become an increasingly sensitive issue as the US continues strikes on Iran using sophisticated munitions that are difficult and time-consuming to replace.
Iran has excelled at depleting expensive US defensive systems, such as Patriot missiles, by bombarding US targets in the Gulf with volley after volley of cheap, mass-produced Shahed drones.
For the US, information suggesting that its supplies are running low could give adversaries insight into how long Washington can sustain military operations and where its capabilities may be under strain. As well as launching sporadic strikes on targets in Iran, the US is maintaining a naval blockade on Iranian ports in and around the critical Strait of Hormuz, which Iran closed to traffic in March.
The president has gone further in attacking the reporting by news outlets, calling accounts of dwindling stocks “treasonous statements”. He has pledged that the people behind leaks will be “hunted down” and warned they could face lengthy prison terms.
Trump has also sought to reassure Americans that supplies are being replenished. “Additionally, large amounts are being manufactured and shipped to the US as needed,” he wrote on Truth Social last month.
Does the Pentagon have a problem with leaks?
The polygraph tests are part of a broader effort by the Trump administration to prevent sensitive information from leaving the Pentagon.
Under Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, the department has opened multiple investigations into leaks and taken steps to limit journalists’ access to military officials and information. Current and former officials have described growing mistrust inside the Pentagon, according to the NYT.
Hegseth has also overseen significant changes among the military’s senior ranks. At least 80 generals, admirals and other officials have been removed or had their promotions blocked during his tenure, the newspaper reported.
The Pentagon’s campaign against leaks became more formalised in July, when Hegseth created a task force with the Department of Justice to speed up investigations into unauthorised disclosures. The Pentagon’s lawyers were also given expanded authority to obtain records and seek assistance for such inquiries.
Hegseth said the aim was to get information to federal law enforcement, including the FBI, more quickly when suspected leaks occurred.
“Leaked information risks lives,” he said.
The polygraph operation is separate from that process, however. Military investigators carried out those examinations without FBI involvement, according to the NYT.
At the same time, Hegseth’s relationship with journalists covering the Pentagon has become increasingly strained. He has not held a Pentagon news briefing on the Iran war since May 5 and has introduced restrictions on journalists’ access to parts of the building, which the NYT is challenging in court.
The Pentagon last month also dismissed the publisher and editor-in-chief of Stars and Stripes, the government-funded newspaper covering the US military.
Hegseth has himself faced scrutiny over the handling of sensitive military information. Last year, details about planned US attacks in Yemen were shared in a Signal group that included a journalist.
When else has the Trump administration used lie detectors?
The Pentagon’s latest operation is part of a history of the Trump administration’s use of polygraphs in investigations into suspected leaks.
One of the first examples came shortly after Hegseth took charge of the Pentagon. In March 2025, his chief of staff launched an inquiry into what the department called “unauthorised disclosures of national security information”, with Sky News reporting that employees could be required to take lie detector tests.
The inquiry came after reporting that Elon Musk was due to receive a classified briefing about how the US military would respond to a potential conflict with China.
Both Trump and Musk denied the report. Musk dismissed it as “pure propaganda” and called for those responsible for providing the information to journalists to be prosecuted.
Trump, however, separately acknowledged the potential sensitivity of giving Musk access to information concerning China because of his business interests there. “Elon has businesses in China, and he would be susceptible, perhaps, to that,” he said.
Lie detectors have also been deployed elsewhere in the administration. In May 2026, FBI Director Kash Patel reportedly had more than two dozen current and former members of his security detail undergo polygraphs during an investigation into leaks from within the bureau.
How extraordinary is the use of polygraphs?
The use of lie detectors is not, by itself, unusual within the US national security system. Its use on this scale among senior military personnel is, however.
Officials entrusted with some of the government’s most sensitive secrets can already face polygraph examinations. That includes personnel working with certain special access programmes, where testing can form part of the security procedures surrounding access to classified material.
But those routine security checks are different from assembling dozens of military and civilian officials for questioning as investigators try to establish whether information has been passed to journalists.
The NYT reported that nothing comparable has been carried out across the upper ranks of the US military in modern history.

US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have ended their meeting in Moscow with President Vladimir Putin as the White House renews efforts to end Russia's war against Ukraine, with the US pair set to visit Kyiv afterward.
Russian state news agency RIA Novosti reported that talks lasted approximately three hours, with the US envoys leaving the Kremlin at about 11 p.m. on September 5.
There was no official Kremlin or US comment immediately after the meeting.
As the session started, RIA Novosti quoted Putin as saying the three men would have to address a "difficult situation" during their discussions at the Kremlin.
Earlier, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Putin had ordered a three-day halt to Russian strikes on Kyiv starting at midnight ahead of the US envoys' planned visit to the Ukrainian capital, which Russia has hammered with attacks for a week.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had accused Russia of deliberately targeting Kyiv's two airports in September 4-5 overnight attacks in an attempt to disrupt the US envoys' visit. Other Russian attacks across Ukraine killed at least five people.
Prior to the envoys' arrival, US President Donald Trump said Washington had "an idea for peace" and that his team was "bringing with them a proposal to end the war," now in its fifth year since Putin launched the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
"I sent them over to see whether or not we can get something done, and there may be a good chance that we'll do it," Trump told reporters at the White House.
He gave no details. Putin has shown no sign of compromise in recent comments, among other things insisting that Russia must control all of eastern Ukraine's Donetsk region, including the parts its forces have failed to capture in years of heavy fighting.
Responding to increasing concerns in the West that Russia could attack a NATO member to test the alliance's resolve, Trump again said he doesn't believe Putin is planning such a move.
"I speak to him. I know him very well. Putin's not looking to attack NATO territory," Trump said.
Zelenskyy said on September 4 that "today it has been clearly determined that American representatives will be in Ukraine and in Russia in the coming days" and he called for a pause in air strikes by both sides to facilitate any meetings.
He added that the US team had informed him that Witkoff and Kushner would visit Kyiv on September 6, a day after their talks in Moscow.
Zelenskyy Calls For Pause In Air Strikes
Zelenskyy said Ukrainian forces would "ensure the normal functioning of Russia airspace so that the negotiators can arrive there safely" and demanded that Moscow reciprocate.
"There will be no air strikes from our side, and Russia must also refrain from conducting air strikes for the time needed to hold these negotiations."
Putin's order for a halt to strikes on Kyiv from September 6-8 came the following day. Peskov made no mention of other parts of Ukraine when he told Russian media about the decision, which came amid reports that Russia continued its attacks elsewhere in Ukraine ahead of the planned pause.
Zelenskyy said on September 5 that Russian forces had targeted Kyiv's Zhulyany and Boryspil airports, accusing Moscow of seeking to create uncertainty over the US envoys' planned journey to Ukraine.
"Clearly, these Russian strikes on the airports are a reaction to the discussions and preparations for the possibility of the US side using an aircraft to travel to Ukraine," Zelenskyy said on X , adding there would be "no threats to diplomacy" from the Ukrainian side.
Flying into Kyiv would be highly unusual. Ukrainian airspace has been closed to regular civilian flights since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022, and visiting foreign leaders and officials have generally reached the capital by train.
The visit would come just days after a Russian drone strike hit the headquarters of Ukraine's domestic security service -- known as the SBU and a key agency that would be responsible for the US envoys' safety during a visit.
Despite Zelenskyy's call for a mutual pause ahead of a fresh round of diplomacy, Russia continued to target places across Ukraine on September 5, killing five people and wounding five at an industrial facility in the Dnipropetrovsk region, according to regional authorities.
Two people were also wounded in the Kyiv region and two others in the southern Mykolayiv region, according to reports. The Ukrainian military said that, in its overnight strikes, Moscow used Iskander-M ballistic missiles and at least 167 drones, around half of which were jet-powered.
New Diplomatic Push
The US envoys' visit to Kyiv would mark their first visit to Ukraine since taking leading roles in the administration's efforts to end the war and come amid a renewed diplomatic push aimed at reaching a peace agreement.
Trump made ending the largest war in Europe since 1945 a priority when he took office in January 2025, but an agreement has been elusive and diplomacy had been largely stalled since the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran in late February.
Despite the renewed diplomacy, fundamental differences between Moscow and Kyiv remain. The Kremlin said on September 4 that Putin's position that Ukraine should cede the entirety of the four mainland regions claimed by Russia -- Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhya, and Kherson -- and abandon its ambition to join NATO remained "unshakeable."
Kyiv has voiced willingness to hold talks with the front lines frozen in place, but has repeatedly rejected giving up its territory to Russia and has insisted on security guarantees as part of any peace settlement.
CIA Director John Ratcliffe on August 25 met with the heads of the Russian intelligence and security services in Moscow. The US spy agency did not disclose the full agenda, but the Kremlin said Ratcliffe did not meet with Putin.
Analysts say Washington's broader approach to the conflict remains difficult to discern.
Heather Conley, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute (AEI) and a former senior State Department official, said "it's not clear if the US is willing to place pressure, more pressure on Russia," citing confusion over a Russian sanctions bill currently on an uncertain course in the US Congress and uncertainty over potential licensing of the production of Patriot missiles to Ukraine.
"There's just a lack of clarity right now on on how the US is planning to proceed," she added.

Echoes of the past: Ceremonial dress of a Safavid noble
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
13:54:18 UTC
22:54:18 KST

Echoes of the past: Ceremonial dress of a Safavid noble
The National Museum of Iran preserves a red-ground silk robe whose material and formal characteristics locate it firmly within the Safavid textile tradition.
Woven in Yazd and dated to the 11th century AH, this long-sleeved, ankle-length garment with slits at the sides and cuffs measures ninety-seven centimeters in height. Its construction, the tailored fit, the choice of silk, the employment of metallic-woven trims, and the structural lining of blue cotton was deliberately orchestrated to produce a lively, dignified silhouette upon the wearer.
A distinct visual rhythm animates the fabric's surface. An underlying network of hexagonal compartments, set against a subtly dissolving ground, frames identical but isolated floral sprays. This systematic repetition of plant motifs in white, blue, green, and brown against the red field accomplishes more than mere ornament; it converts the garment's two-dimensional plane into a modulated three-dimensional surface, establishing geometric coherence and a measured, almost architectural, sense of balance. The chromatic contrast, in particular, heightens the botanical forms, rendering them legible from a distance while rewarding close inspection with fine brush-like delineation.
Ornamental elaboration further distinguishes the robe's ceremonial function. Gold-woven bands (zarbaft), embroidered with foliage and blossoms in red, green, purple, and white, edge both sides of the chest opening, the lateral slits, and the cuffs. These metallic accents, juxtaposed with the silk ground, impart a lustrous, courtly opulence. Seventeen silver buttons—sixteen conical ones along the left chest opening and five smaller specimens on one sleeve—serve simultaneously as fastenings and as integral elements of the decorative scheme. Their presence reinforces the garment's formal, official character and aligns it with the protocol of Safavid court dress, where such details signified rank and ceremonial readiness.
The Safavid court's sustained patronage of textile arts provides the essential historical framework for this piece. Royal support encouraged the convergence of painting, architecture, calligraphy, and weaving within the royal workshops. In this environment, textile designers often worked across media, and certain painters themselves assumed the loom, weaving the luxurious silks and brocades they had originally drafted on paper. Weaving centers in Tabriz, Qazvin, Isfahan, Yazd, and Kashan consequently produced velvets, satins, multi-layered silks, and brocades that were unrivaled in chromatic variety and figural invention. These fabrics were not confined to domestic consumption; they entered long-distance trade networks as prized Iranian exports, reaching markets from the Ottoman Empire to the European continent.
Ultimately, this red silk qaba synthesizes several distinct strands of Safavid material culture: the weaver's technical expertise, the painter's eye for spatial patterning, the tailor's concern for bodily form, and the court's demand for visual markers of rank. It remains a concrete, tangible document of a period when Persian dress achieved a distinctive stylistic unity and asserted its place among the most sophisticated textile traditions of the early modern world.

Earlier in June, Salehi-Amiri announced that the government would pursue a program to expand domestic and international markets for handicrafts, increase exports, support artisans and develop a complete value chain for the sector.
Speaking at a ceremony marking National Handicrafts Week in Isfahan, the minister said Iranian handicrafts continued to receive international recognition and cited growing foreign interest in Iranian artistic products.
He added that the government aimed to establish Iranian handicrafts marketplaces in capitals around the world and was working to remove barriers to international market access.
According to the minister, strengthening the sector requires completion of the entire value chain, from raw material supply and production to marketing, sales and exports.
He said the ministry had held discussions with domestic and international companies in recent months to facilitate broader access for Iranian handicrafts to global distribution networks.
A total of 299 handicraft branches are currently practiced across the country, which is home to 17 cities and villages designated by the World Crafts Council as world craft hubs.

Ritual marking anniversary of Fatima Masumeh’s arrival in Qom added to national heritage list
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
13:52:49 UTC
22:52:49 KST

Ritual marking anniversary of Fatima Masumeh’s arrival in Qom added to national heritage list
TEHRAN – The ritual marking the anniversary of the arrival of Fatima Masumeh (S.A.), sister of the eighth Shia Imam, Imam Reza (A.S.), in the Iranian city of Qom has been inscribed on the national list of Iran’s intangible cultural heritage, a senior cultural heritage official said.
Ali Darabi, deputy minister of Cultural Heritage, Tourism and Handicrafts, said the annual observance commemorating Fatima Masumeh’s arrival in Qom has been an important historical and cultural event for the city and that its registration would contribute to safeguarding Qom’s intangible heritage and historical identity.
The anniversary falls on 23 Rabi al-Awwal in the Islamic lunar calendar and has also been designated as Qom Day. The period between Qom Day and the anniversary of Fatima Masumeh’s death on 10 Rabi al-Thani is known as the Masumeh Days, Darabi said.
He added that the inscription would help preserve, document and transmit the tradition to future generations, while reflecting greater attention to the living and spiritual heritage of local communities.
“Registering the ritual on the national list of intangible cultural heritage is an effort to commemorate a historical and cultural event and preserve the connection between heritage, identity and the everyday life of people,” Darabi explained.
The Fatima Masumeh Shrine, the mausoleum of Fatima bint Musa, is one of the most prominent religious and cultural landmarks in Qom.
The shrine is an important pilgrimage site for Shia Muslims and draws large numbers of pilgrims and visitors each year. Qom is also one of Iran’s major religious centers and is home to numerous seminaries and religious schools.
The shrine was itself registered on Iran’s national heritage list in 1931 (1310 in the Iranian calendar), according to Darabi.

About 110km southeast of London, Dover handled more than nine million passengers and two million freight vehicles last year, according to the port’s website.

Ukraine confirms combat flights of its new radar plane
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
13:50:46 UTC
22:50:46 KST

- Ukraine's defense ministry confirmed a Swedish-supplied ASC 890 radar aircraft has flown combat missions since March 2026, after Sweden announced the transfer in May 2024.
- The Saab 340-based aircraft carries an Erieye radar capable of detecting air and sea targets at up to 280 miles, feeding data to Ukraine's F-16, Mirage 2000 and Gripen fighters.
Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense has confirmed that a Swedish-supplied Saab 340 airborne early warning aircraft (AEW&C), known as the ASC 890, has been flying combat missions over Ukraine since March 2026, according to information the ministry released detailing the country’s expanding fleet of Western combat aircraft.
Sweden first announced it would transfer the aircraft in May 2024, as part of its 16th and largest military aid package to Ukraine at the time, worth roughly $1.25 billion. The Ukrainian government said the transfer was confirmed in August 2025, and the plane’s first documented combat sorties over Ukraine followed roughly seven months later. Independent reporting had already suggested the aircraft was operating in Ukrainian airspace before the government’s confirmation: footage that surfaced on a Russian Telegram channel on March 20, 2026, appeared to show the plane in level flight, with background voices speaking Ukrainian, though the exact date and location of that video could not be independently verified at the time.
The ASC 890 is built on the Saab 340 regional airliner airframe and carries Saab’s Erieye radar in a distinctive rectangular fairing mounted above the fuselage, sometimes described as a “balance beam.” The radar uses active electronically scanned array technology and can detect and track aircraft and ships at ranges up to roughly 280 miles (450 kilometers), typically while the plane cruises at around 20,000 feet. A crew of six operates the aircraft, including a mission control officer, a combat control operator and a surveillance operator.
In practice, the aircraft is meant to work as a flying radar and command post. It can spot Russian aircraft, cruise missiles and drones from far outside the reach of ground-based radar, then pass that tracking data to Ukrainian fighter pilots so they can intercept threats without needing their own radars active, which would otherwise expose their position. Sweden’s defense minister said at the time of the 2024 pledge that the aircraft would give Ukraine “a new capability against both airborne and maritime targets.”
The Swedish Air Force operated two ASC 890 aircraft before the transfer, and both are understood to have gone to Ukraine, leaving Sweden temporarily without its own airborne early warning capability until replacement aircraft arrive. Delivery had been tied in part to modifications needed to make the plane’s data-sharing systems work with Ukraine’s fleet of F-16 fighters, according to Swedish defense officials who addressed reports of delay in March 2025.
Ukraine’s defense ministry described the ASC 890 as one piece of a broader air combat network built around Western fighter aircraft. The country’s F-16 fleet, the first jets of which arrived in 2024 from Denmark, the Netherlands, Norway and Belgium, forms the core of that network, with pilot training conducted partly in Romania.
Ukraine has also begun receiving Mirage 2000 fighters from France starting in 2025 and expects up to 16 Gripen C/D fighters from Sweden, provided at no cost, with a newer Gripen E variant planned for delivery by 2030. Ukrainian officials say combining the ASC 890’s radar coverage with these fighter types is intended to bring Ukraine’s air defense closer to a NATO-standard, networked approach to air combat, rather than relying on individual aircraft operating with limited situational awareness.

Civilians among at least 60 killed in Yemen as ground fighting escalates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
13:47:19 UTC
22:47:19 KST

Clashes between Yemen’s Saudi-backed government forces and the Iran-aligned Houthi rebel movement have killed more than 60 people, including civilians, as the Houthis pushed forward with a military offensive on Yemen’s western coast.
Twenty-six government troops and 31 Houthi fighters were killed during several hours of fighting in the country’s south-west on Saturday, medical and military sources told Agence France-Presse (AFP). A missile strike also killed six civilians and injured seven others travelling by bus in the city of Taiz.
The killings were the latest in a series of bloody clashes in recent days as the Houthis continued an offensive in western Taiz and southern Hodeidah along the Red Sea coast. On Friday, 129 were killed in fighting between rebel and government forces, according to an AFP tally.
The fighting is some of the deadliest in years, after the collapse in July of the 2022 ceasefire. The truce fell apart after an Iranian plane attempted to land in Houthi-controlled Sana’a, triggering attacks by the Yemeni government on the airport.
The Houthis are trying to beat back governmental troops to capture strategic hills overlooking Bab al-Mandeb in order to advance towards port cities on the coast. So far, they have managed to capture areas in western Taiz.
In Taiz, a government military officer said the “coming hours will be decisive” as the Houthis had taken positions near the city a day before. They added that reinforcements had been arriving from Aden to try to stem the Houthi advance.
On Friday, government forces said that they had recaptured the al-Khazan and al-Makahna hills west of Taiz, two strategically important areas for controlling the region.
The Houthis had previously controlled the port city of al-Makha overlooking Bab al-Mandeb, before being pushed out by government forces backed by the Saudi-led coalition.
The Bab al-Mandeb strait is a crucial maritime chokepoint for ships heading to the Suez canal. About 10% of global maritime trade passes through the strait. Saudi Arabia has been using the strait to export oil for months after the start of the US-Iran war.
If shipping is disrupted in Bab al-Mandeb, it will only further raise the cost of global goods, which has already rocketed as a result of the virtual closure of the strait of Hormuz since March 2026.
If the Houthis manage to recapture the port city and take key areas along the Red Sea coast, it will help them control naval traffic in the Red Sea. In July, the Houthis declared a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia, and they have repeatedly disrupted traffic in solidarity with Gaza since the start of the war there in October 2023.
Yemen has been embroiled in a civil war since 2014, when the Houthis and allied forces took the capital city of Sana’a and pushed the then government out of power. A Saudi-led coalition then began a military intervention to support the Yemeni government and fight the Houthis, a strategic ally of Iran.
At least 150,000 people in Yemen have been killed in the fighting, and hundreds of thousands more have died from related causes such as hunger and diseases. About 4.5 million people have been displaced by the fighting and more than 18.2 million are in dire need of humanitarian assistance, according to the UN.

Parent body of Epsilon-Perseid meteor shower has still not been identified
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
13:45:00 UTC
22:45:00 KST

MOSCOW, September 5. /TASS/. The parent body of the Epsilon-Perseid meteor shower, observed from September 5 to 21, has still not been identified. Scientists suspect it may be an unknown long-period comet, Yevgeny Burmistrov, an expert in astronomy at Perm National Research Polytechnic University, has told TASS.
The Epsilon-Perseid meteor shower is one of the fastest, but relatively weak, showers. This year, the Epsilon-Perseids will reach their peak activity on the night of September 9-10. Astronomers predict up to eight flashes per hour.
"The parent body for this meteor shower has not been determined with any certainty. It is presumably an unknown long-period comet, whose complete orbit around the Sun takes more than two centuries. As it approaches the Sun, its nucleus heats up and releases dust and ice particles, which remain in its orbital trajectory, forming a dust trail. When our Earth crosses this trail, we observe the meteor shower," he added.
In the absence of data on the parent comet, scientists were able to detect the shower through regular observations: in early September, meteors emerged from an area then associated with the star Epsilon Persei every year at the same speed.
"This coincidence testifies to their common origin, which allowed us to identify them as a separate cosmic phenomenon and calculate its orbit. The speed of the falling meteors will reach approximately 64 kilometers per second - one of the highest speeds among meteor showers," Burmistrov said.

Fighting between Yemen's Saudi-backed government forces and the country's Houthi rebels killed more than 60 people on Saturday, including civilians, medical and military sources told AFP.

On Friday, the fighting killed 129 people, according to an AFP tally compiled from several sources.
With Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz to commercial ships, the Bab al-Mandab chokepoint has gained importance as a transit route for oil from Saudi Arabia, the world's biggest exporter of crude.

In July, a fragile truce between the Houthis and Yemen's government fell apart after the rebels welcomed an Iranian plane to the capital Sanaa, setting off a spate of attacks.

Swedish-supplied ASC 890 early warning aircraft has been conducting combat missions in Ukraine, says Kyiv
Kyiv has said that an ASC 890 airborne early warning and control (AEW&C) aircraft supplied to Ukraine by Sweden has been carrying out combat missions in Ukraine.
Source: Ukrainian Ministry of Defence in a report on the Air Force Capability Coalition, which brings together countries supporting Ukraine's air force
Details: The Ukrainian Ministry of Defence said the ASC 890 (also known as the Saab 340 AEW&C) had carried out its first combat sorties over Ukraine in March 2026.
Quote: "This aircraft is capable of detecting aerial assets at considerable range, coordinating the actions of combat aircraft and enhancing the effectiveness of fighter aircraft operations."
More details: The Ministry of Defence explained that the AEW&C system is a key element of a NATO-standard air combat system, working alongside F-16, Mirage 2000 and Gripen fighter jets, which Kyiv's partners have pledged to provide to Ukraine.
Sweden announced in May 2024 that it would provide Ukraine with two ASC 890 aircraft and confirmed in August 2025 that the transfer was proceeding as planned. The aircraft are manufactured by Swedish defence company Saab.
According to Ukrainian military news outlet Militarnyi, the aircraft has a crew of seven: three crew members and four operators of the radar and airspace management system. It can carry out patrol missions at a speed of around 300 km/h at altitudes of 2,000 to 6,000 metres.
More details: The long-range radar detection aircraft is equipped with an FSR 890 Erieye radar, which can track up to 500 surface targets and 1,000 airborne targets simultaneously. The radar can detect targets at altitudes of up to 20 km and has an instrumental detection range of 450 km.
Background: Ukrainska Pravda previously reported that the UK, in partnership with Sweden, would provide €300 million in support for the supply of 16 modern aircraft to Ukraine.

Russia launched 2,800 jet-powered drones on Ukraine in August; combat colonel takes charge of Close Air Defence
A Ukrainian military official has revealed that Colonel Oleksandr Dmukhovskyi has recently been appointed commander of Ukraine's Close Air Defence, the branch responsible for protecting troops and critical facilities against aerial threats at short range.
Source: Colonel Yurii Ihnat, spokesperson for the Ukrainian Air Force, in a comment to Ukrainska Pravda
Details: Yurii Cherevashchenko, Deputy Commander of the Air Force, will oversee Ukraine's Close Air Defence and coordinate this area within the Air Force.
According to Ihnat, the role of Close Air Defence is becoming increasingly important as Russia steps up its use of attack UAVs, particularly jet-powered drones, prompting the military leadership and Ukrainian defence industry to seek effective and practical ways to counter them.
The spokesperson said Russia launched around 350 jet-powered UAVs on Ukraine in June, 1,500 in July and more than 2,800 in August.
Quote: "The statistics speak for themselves – the enemy is ramping up the production and numbers of jet-powered UAVs. Countermeasures are being taken – all available assets and personnel are being deployed to shoot down or neutralise jet-powered drones, including fighter aircraft, short- and medium-range anti-aircraft missile systems, and electronic warfare systems.
Of course, the Close Air Defence – mobile fire groups and anti-aircraft interceptor drone crews – remains part of the integrated air defence system. There are certainly plenty of aerial targets for them. After all, reconnaissance UAVs, 'classic Shaheds' equipped with internal combustion engines, Gerberas and Parodiyas have not disappeared. There are fewer of them now, but a significant number are still being launched.
Personnel changes in the leadership are a normal and ongoing process, particularly during wartime. Brigade commanders and those appointed to higher posts are officers who have gained substantial experience in combat operations, demonstrated effectiveness, delivered results on the battlefield, understand the inner workings of the organisation, and are able to apply this experience on a larger scale. Take, for example, Oleksandr Dmukhovskyi, who was recently appointed commander of the Close Air Defence; prior to this, he led one of the finest regiments – the 1020th Anti-Aircraft Missile and Artillery Regiment, which boasts some of the highest records for shooting down enemy attack drones."
Details: According to Ihnat, the state leadership and the Ukrainian defence industry have come up with innovative ways to counter jet-powered UAVs, and these have already been unveiled. The Air Force will, of course, provide the facilities needed to test them, particularly jet-powered interceptors.
Read also: Life in Kyiv amid constant air-raid warnings as Russia shifts to jet-powered drones
Background:
- During Mykhailo Fedorov's tenure as Defence Minister, the Close Air Defence, which was being formed under the leadership of Pavlo Yelizarov, Deputy Commander of the Ukrainian Air Force, was headed by Colonel Yevhen Khliebnikov.
- In late August, Ukraine's new Defence Minister, Yevhen Khmara, said Ukraine already has four potential interceptors capable of shooting down jet-powered Shaheds, all of which have undergone field trials.

U.S. Army Ordered First Batch of TITAN Reconnaissance Systems
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
13:30:57 UTC
22:30:57 KST

The U.S. Army has moved the TITAN system into mass production by awarding two contracts totaling $192 million.
This was reported on the official website of the U.S. Army.
Under the contracts, the first eight production systems—four TITAN Advanced and four TITAN Basic—are scheduled to be manufactured and integrated.
The TITAN is a mobile ground-based intelligence station designed to collect and process data from various sensors. The system uses artificial intelligence and machine learning to fuse intelligence information and more quickly determine target coordinates.
The Advanced version is a more powerful variant intended for division-level units and above, with direct access to space-based intelligence. The Basic version is a simplified variant for lower-level units, which receives this data through ground-based centers. They are scheduled to be delivered over the next 18 months.
Palantir Technologies and Anduril Industries received $127 million and $65 million, respectively.
The new systems will supplement the nine prototype TITAN systems that the U.S. Army is already using in operational units.
The TITAN can transmit the collected data to weapons systems, reducing the time between target detection and opening fire. The system is designed to support multi-domain operations and long-range, high-precision strikes.
Palantir notes that the TITAN combines sensors, networks, and automated data processing. The system’s software generates an intelligence picture and guidance data while simultaneously reducing the workload on operators.
The U.S. Army is expected to begin placing additional production orders for the TITAN as early as fiscal year 2027.
Palantir is responsible for the overall production and integration of the system. L3Harris Technologies, Sierra Nevada Corporation, Strategic Technology Consulting, and World Wide Technology are also involved in the program. Anduril will supply hardware components and integrate the equipment into secure modules.
As a reminder, Palantir CEO Alex Karp will become the first investor in Mykhailo Fedorov’s own defense company.
