Aeon discloses new specs for its Zeus tactical missile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
10:21:09 UTC
19:21:09 KST

- Aeon disclosed new details about its Zeus tactical missile, including a stated speed exceeding Mach 0.65 and a 6-pound warhead payload, in a LinkedIn post.
- The company has said Zeus costs roughly $50,000 per unit and holds eight-figure contracts with the Department of War, though new specifications remain unverified.
Aeon, a Texas-based defense manufacturer, disclosed new technical details about its Zeus tactical missile system in a public post from Chief Growth Officer Wes Shover, including a stated speed of more than Mach 0.65 and a 6-pound (2.7-kilogram) warhead payload.
The Defence Blog first reported on Zeus in April, when Aeon founder and CEO Naweed Tahmas gave an exclusive look at the system, describing it as a software-defined, modular guided weapon priced at roughly $50,000 per unit, with a target production rate exceeding 10,000 units a year. Zeus sits in the same rough weight class as an unguided AT4 rocket but is designed to deliver precision guidance closer to a Javelin-class system, at a fraction of the cost of legacy anti-armor missiles.
Shover’s statement added company details not previously disclosed publicly. He described Zeus as built around a “Modular Seeker Interface,” letting operators swap the sensor package to engage different target types, and an “Open Warhead Design” that Aeon says can carry a 6-pound payload. He also said the missile can interface with “legacy systems” already fielded by the military, rather than requiring new supporting infrastructure, and that the company maintains a “transparent” bill of materials for the system, meaning it discloses the parts and costs that go into building each unit.
“When we speak to end users, Program Offices, Integrators, and Customers the message is clear,” Shover said. “Zeus fits into a giant gap that exists in the Defense Industry where a fresh approach has been needed for decades.”
Aeon has grown quickly since its 2023 founding. The company has raised $18.6 million in venture funding from investors including Quiet Capital, Silent Ventures and 1789 Capital, and it is relocating its headquarters and manufacturing operations from Austin to nearby Cedar Park, Texas, where the city council approved a $1.5 million economic development agreement in May tied to Aeon creating 135 jobs with a combined annual payroll of roughly $16.5 million by the end of 2029. Aeon has also moved beyond developing Zeus alone. In August, Tahmas hosted four congressional appropriations staffers for a tour of the company’s fuze production line, telling them Aeon would deliver nearly 1,000 fuzes the following week to support the Pentagon’s Drone Dominance program, a roughly $1 billion push to buy more than 200,000 small, lethal drones by 2027.
That fuze work reflects a manufacturing strategy Aeon has applied to Zeus as well. The company has said it produces its own solid rocket motors and fuzes in-house rather than sourcing them from outside suppliers, a choice it frames as protection against the kind of supply chain disruptions that have affected larger, more traditionally structured defense programs.
Zeus itself is designed for both dismounted infantry use and mounted employment on manned and unmanned ground vehicles and surface vessels, with operators able to switch between roles by attaching or removing a shoulder mount, according to Aeon.
The company has said it holds an active integration partnership with one of Ukraine’s largest drone manufacturers to enable Zeus to be fired from quadcopter platforms, along with a separate Ukrainian partnership covering integration onto ground vehicles and boats. The weapon’s targeting runs on what Aeon calls ODIN, a proprietary software-defined architecture the company says supports multiple targeting modes, engagement beyond the operator’s direct line of sight, and integration with battlefield command-and-control networks through the Android Team Awareness Kit, a mapping and coordination app used across the U.S. military.
Based on public contracting records reviewed by The Defence Blog in April, Aeon holds contracts worth eight figures with the Department of War for production and fielding of the Zeus system. The company has not disclosed the exact contract value, delivery schedule, or which military units or programs are receiving the weapon.

Sanctions or illusion? US claim on Iran’s financial lifeline
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
10:19:34 UTC
19:19:34 KST

In his latest remarks, the US Treasury Secretary has once again presented an exaggerated picture of Washington’s ability to collapse Iran’s economic network, claiming that by sanctioning a Turkish bank, the United States has cut “Iran’s vital financial arteries”—a claim that, rather than reflecting a decisive development in Iran’s economy, reflects the Donald Trump administration’s effort to instill the impression that sanctions are on the verge of completely paralyzing Iran’s economy.
Scott Bessent, the US Treasury Secretary, announced on Friday that Washington has sanctioned the investment bank “Golden Global” and two of its subsidiaries in Turkey. The US Treasury Department claims that this group has played a role in transferring Iran’s oil revenues from China to Turkey and converting part of these resources into cash and gold, and has also provided banking services to some Iranian entities. At the same time, Bessent warned that another bank may be targeted by sanctions next week and even spoke of continuing this process until other countries stop economic cooperation with Iran.
The sanction itself is, of course, a reality and cannot be denied. The United States has placed a financial institution based in Turkey on its sanctions list, and this action severely restricts its access to the dollar-based financial system. But there is a very large gap between “sanctioning a bank” and “cutting a country’s financial arteries.” That gap is precisely where the Trump administration’s propaganda rhetoric enters the scene.
Iran has been under the harshest US sanctions regime for years and has redesigned an important part of its financial and trade network to cope with these very pressures. Tehran is not dependent on a single bank, a single money transfer route, or a single country to continue its foreign trade. Exchange networks, indirect trade, barter, the use of non-dollar currencies, intermediary companies, and cooperation with various trading partners are part of the mechanisms that have been developed over recent years to reduce the impact of sanctions. Therefore, even if one channel is closed, it does not mean that all of Iran’s financial flows have stopped.
More importantly, the very sanctioning of Golden Global shows that Washington is still identifying and targeting Iran’s financial “channels”; that is, if all of Iran’s financial arteries had truly already been cut, there would have been no need to discover and sanction new routes. The fact that the US Treasury Department goes after new banks, companies, and intermediaries every week actually shows that Iran’s trade and resource-transfer network remains active, and Washington is trying to restrict it step by step.
On the other hand, another part of Bessent’s remarks about oil prices is also significantly out of step with market reality. He predicted that an increase in global supply could bring crude oil prices down to the range of $40 to $50. But with military and geopolitical tensions in the Middle East continuing, the oil market is not currently confirming such a picture. Brent crude traded at around $95 in Friday’s trading and rose more than 6 percent over the course of a week. More simply, the current market is not only not in the $40 to $50 range, but is almost double the level the US Treasury Secretary is talking about.
This gap between claim and reality is highly significant. The Trump administration is trying to convey two messages at the same time: first, that US economic pressure against Iran is choking the country’s economy; and second, that Washington is capable of sharply lowering oil prices by increasing energy supply. But the oil market is not subject to the decisions of a single government. War, geopolitical risk, shipping routes, the security of the Strait of Hormuz, the export volumes of major producers, and market expectations all play a role in determining oil prices.
Even from a political perspective, the claim of “cutting Iran’s financial arteries” is more of a threatening message to foreign banks and companies than a report on the collapse of Iran’s economy. The United States wants to convince banks and financial institutions in Turkey, the UAE, China, and other countries that cooperating with Iran will come at a heavy cost. In fact, the main goal of secondary sanctions is precisely this: Washington wants to extend the power of its sanctions beyond US borders and force companies in other countries to choose between trading with Iran and access to the US financial system. This policy undoubtedly creates costs for Iran, and the effects of financial and banking sanctions cannot be minimized. The narrowing of money transfer routes, the increase in the cost of foreign trade, the greater difficulty of repatriating export revenues, and the increased risk for banks and companies doing business all create real pressure. But economic pressure is not the same as economic collapse, and sanctioning one bank is not equivalent to destroying a country’s financial network.
Even inside Iran, economic officials have emphasized in recent days that the country’s economy, despite the pressure of sanctions and restrictions caused by the war, still has resources and tools for managing the foreign exchange market. The governor of the Central Bank of Iran has also announced that the country has sufficient foreign exchange resources and that the central bank is ready to intervene to manage the market. Of course, these statements do not mean there are no economic problems; rather, they show that the image of a “collapsed economy” raised in Washington’s rhetoric is far from the complex reality of Iran’s economy.
Ultimately, what Bessent calls an “economic isolation operation” should be seen more as a maximum-pressure campaign and a continuous economic war against Iran, rather than a final blow intended to disable the country’s economy. The United States can raise the cost of trading with Iran, sanction banks, and target financial routes one after another; but to conclude from these measures that “Iran’s financial arteries have been cut” is a claim far larger than the reality that the available evidence shows.
The main problem with such claims is that, through repetition, economic pressure is mistaken for strategic success. Washington may be able to remove a bank from the dollar financial system, but it still has to prove that it can disable all of Iran’s networks of trade, exports, resource transfers, and economic relations with foreign partners. Until that happens, phrases like “cutting Iran’s vital arteries” are more a part of the Trump administration’s psychological operation to display the power of sanctions than an accurate description of Iran’s economic situation.

NEW DELHI: Lashkar terrorist Yasir, a Pakistani national linked to Hafiz Saeed's outift, was killed by security forces in the higher reaches of Yusmarg in central Kashmir, on Saturday.He was suspected of being involved in several major terror attacks in Jammu and Kashmir in 2024, including the ambush of an Indian Air Force convoy in Poonch and the killing of soldiers and civilian workers near Gulmarg.
Yasir was gunned down on Friday during Operation Ashdar, launched after security forces received intelligence about the movement of a group of terrorists through the Pir Panjal mountains. Jammu and Kashmir Police identified the slain terrorist as Yasir and said he was affiliated with the banned Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT).The police also posted a message on X after the operation, saying, "You Can Run But You Can't Hide!"
Yasir's role in the 2024 attacks
Security agencies had first detected Yasir's presence in the region in 2024. Officials said intelligence inputs pointed to his involvement in at least three major terror attacks that year.The first was the ambush of an IAF convoy in Poonch on May 4, 2024. Terrorists opened fire on the convoy near Shahsitar in the Surankote area as the personnel were returning to their base at Sanai Top. One IAF member was killed and four others were injured.Yasir was also suspected of involvement in the October 20 attack at Gangangir near Sonamarg, where terrorists killed seven people, including a local doctor.
Four days later, on October 24, terrorists attacked an Army vehicle in Bota Pathri near Gulmarg. The attack killed five people, including three soldiers and two civilian porters. Officials said Yasir was part of the group behind the attack.
Link to Lashkar
Yasir was reportedly operating with a Lashkar-e-Taiba group led by commander Junai Ahmed Bhat. Bhat was killed by security forces in the Dachigam forest on the outskirts of Srinagar on December 3, 2024.After the Bota Pathri attack, Yasir and another Lashkar terrorist, identified as Musa, are believed to have remained hidden in the Yusmarg and Pulwama areas. Officials said they later crossed to the Jammu side of the Pir Panjal range before returning to the Valley earlier this month.
The latest operation began after security forces tracked the movement of the terrorist group from Ashdar Gali in Poonch towards Pakherpora in Pulwama through Yusmarg.The Army, J&K Police and CRPF established a cordon in the area on September 1. They made contact with the terrorists on September 3 at Ashdar Gali, a remote mountain ridge. Yasir was eventually killed in the exchange of fire. An AK rifle was recovered from the site.The operation is still continuing as security forces search for Musa, who is believed to be hiding among large boulders and natural caves. The encounter site lies between 12,000 and 15,500 feet in the Pir Panjal range, where heavy rain and visibility of as little as five metres have made the operation particularly difficult.

Taiwan defense institute reports overseas cyber intrusion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
10:12:17 UTC
19:12:17 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — More than 200 old procurement notices were sent to vendors after a hidden administrative interface on the National Chung-Shan Institute of Science and Technology’s procurement system was breached from an overseas IP address.
The intrusion activated a scheduled command that resent earlier quotation notices, while NCSIST said the original developer had built the interface for maintenance convenience, per Liberty Times.
NCSIST initially attributed the Aug. 28 incident to an AI cybersecurity agent that went beyond its permissions during testing. The institute later said a full report from the developer showed the hidden scheduling function, rather than the AI test, was the cause, per CNA.
A Ministry of Digital Affairs document provided to KMT Legislator Wang Hung-wei (王鴻薇) said an external party had brute-forced a login and activated the scheduled command. The Investigation Bureau’s Taipei City Field Office has opened an investigation, while NCSIST said no other information was leaked, per UDN.
The procurement system long predates NCSIST’s 2025 software-supply-chain rules, and the institute said it never subjected the older system to a comparable review. NCSIST said that omission exposed a weakness in its management controls.
NCSIST said it is strengthening safeguards on the procurement system and requiring the developer to fully document its software components. New controls will be designed to detect abnormal outbound activity and automatically restrict or halt network service, while the institute reviews responsibility for the failures that led to the incident.

Horse smuggling exposes cracks in US defenses against screwworm
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
10:11:54 UTC
19:11:54 KST

Horse smuggling exposes cracks in US defenses against screwworm
REDFORD, Texas, Sept 5 - When sheriff's deputies intercepted a trailer carrying six horses near the border town of Redford, Texas, they uncovered more than a livestock violation. The animals had crossed the Rio Grande illegally from Mexico through a shadowy smuggling network, bypassing the veterinary inspections, health certifications and quarantine measures that the U.S. requires for livestock.
Smuggled animals are coming into focus as possible hosts for New World screwworm. The flesh-eating parasite began infesting U.S. cattle in June despite efforts to halt the spread, such as a U.S. ban of more than a year on Mexican livestock, a team of government inspectors on horseback and a swarm of sterile flies.
The horses caught near Redford in late May were not infested, but the case highlights a little-enforced part of the U.S. response to the threat. As U.S. authorities restricted cattle imports and disrupted billions of dollars in trade to contain the fly, a cartel-linked trade in horses and other animals continued moving through remote stretches of the border.
For more than a year, U.S. officials have argued that illegal livestock trafficking from Central America helped carry screwworm north. But Reuters found illicit animal movements have also persisted along parts of the U.S.-Mexico border, often taking the same routes used to smuggle drugs and people.
The stakes are enormous. A previous screwworm outbreak killed thousands of animals in the U.S. before the pest was declared eradicated in the 1960s. In Texas, where authorities confirmed the first new U.S. animal cases this year, experts estimate a widespread outbreak could cost the economy up to $1.8 billion.
The Trump administration has partially reopened the border to Mexican livestock to bring relief to U.S. consumers, with beef prices at record highs after the ban, despite rising infestations in Mexico.
U.S. Department of Agriculture officials, law enforcement and animal-industry experts said smuggled animals range from high-value horses bought for racing and rodeos to dogs used in illegal fighting rings and cattle. Authorities have also intercepted exotic animals, including primates, bears and tigers in recent years.
Mexico's animal health agency Senasica has confirmed over 2,000 equine cases of screwworm since the outbreak started in 2024.
"These kinds of movements represent a risk because they allow the fly to travel much faster than it could move naturally," said Oscar Rico, a researcher at Universidad Nacional Autonoma de Mexico, who co-authored a study predicting how animals could spread screwworm.
BORDER PATROLS REVEAL SMUGGLING SCALE
During a week in August, Reuters visited three remote communities along the Texas-Mexico border, joined patrols with local officers and interviewed sheriffs, veterinarians and former Border Patrol agents. They described the challenge of policing hundreds of miles of rugged terrain where animals, drugs and people can cross undetected.
Presidio County Sergeant Deputy Sheriff Jaime Sanchez, who investigated the Redford case, said trafficked horses can fetch at least $30,000 on the black market, with smugglers able to undercut legal sellers by avoiding import paperwork, taxes and veterinary requirements. Smugglers often take the horses to Houston and Dallas, where they sell them for farm work, racing or charrería, Mexico’s traditional equestrian sport.
Sanchez's department has intercepted more than 50 smuggled horses in the past two years by pulling over horse trailers, an unusual sight in the dry, border community of Presidio, Texas.
Redford, historically known as "El Polvo" (the Dust), is a near-ghost town, with roads lined by abandoned homes and a shuttered school. With fewer than 20 families living there, the community has become a vulnerable corridor for illegal crossings controlled by Mexican cartels, where vast stretches of isolated terrain can provide cover, Sanchez said.
On a scorching day in August, he pointed to a shallow stretch of the Rio Grande where smugglers walked the horses across the river and through the private property of an older resident before loading them into a trailer.
"It's easy for them to pay someone $500 or $1,000 per horse to cross it, load it onto the trailer, and drive off," he said.
Presidio County is working with federal officials to curb animal smuggling, which Sanchez attributed to La Linea, a cartel that the Trump administration designated a Foreign Terrorist Organization in July. The FBI also linked the group to criminal activity along the border.
"Since these are security matters, the issue of screwworm always comes up because it can hit economies very hard," Sanchez said. "In reality, we are very concerned."
Mexico's environmental regulator Profepa said in a statement that it cooperates with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to share information on "trafficking cases, coordinated enforcement operations, and the return or repatriation of live wildlife specimens."
Spokespersons for Mexico's security, agriculture and foreign ministries declined to comment.
UNDOCUMENTED CROSSINGS EVADE INSPECTIONS
U.S. officials have not linked any of the country's 48 confirmed screwworm cases to smuggling. Many experts think that is likely an undercount since wildlife and smuggled animals evade scrutiny. The USDA has not identified how screwworm first reached the U.S., saying in a statement that epidemiological investigations are ongoing.
Scientists, veterinarians and epidemiologists interviewed by Reuters said undocumented animal crossings present the same types of disease-transmission risks that officials have linked to illegal cattle movements originating in Central America, because animals moving outside regulated channels may avoid inspections and treatment that could identify infections.
USDA Inspector General John Walk said the recent smuggling at the U.S. southern border "seems more pronounced" and that animal trafficking is not just an agricultural concern, but a national security issue heightened by screwworm.
"It could be a vector," Walk said at his office in Washington, D.C.
In July, Walk traveled to Brownsville, Texas, to alert local law enforcement to the risk animal-trafficking networks pose of spreading screwworm. U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins said on X in early August that the department was "cracking down" on illicit livestock movements in a post about the U.S. screwworm response.
Ricardo Ramirez, 57, has spent his life watching cattle roam across his sunbaked ranch in Zapata County, about 500 miles (805 km) southeast of Presidio, where his family has owned land since the 1940s.
Screwworm "didn't affect us for the last 50 years and lo and behold, here we are again with this thing upon us," Ramirez said from beneath the sparse shade of a tree on his ranch.
FOCUS ON HORSE TRAILERS
One August morning, Zapata came alive with the sound of engines, radios and speedboats. About 80 law enforcement officers with Operation Lone Star Task Force, a state law enforcement coalition to deter illegal crossings and smuggling, converged for a coordinated sweep. Patrol trucks rolled along highways and back roads, while officers searched waterways for signs of illegal activity.
Among the vehicles drawing investigators' attention are horse trailers, which blend into rural life.
Hours later, as Goliad County deputies launched a drone into the dark sky to scan remote areas along the border, they pointed to a 2024 case that they say demonstrates how smugglers can deploy trailers. Officers stopped a livestock trailer and found 14 people inside, alongside a neglected horse. Investigators determined the vehicle was connected to human smuggling, and the driver told authorities he was paid $10,000.
"Most people, when they think about the cartel, they think about either drugs or illegal aliens," Goliad County Sheriff Roy Boyd said. "The revenue streams for the cartels are far more diverse than people have ever suspected."
In Terrell County, Texas, where the U.S.-Mexico border cuts through rocky desert terrain, Sheriff Thaddeus Cleveland gestured from his pickup truck at a herd of feral cattle slowly crossing the river. Plastic water bottles and discarded clothing litter the landscape, traces of people who crossed the border illegally.
"A lot of times the smugglers would use horses to bring the drugs across the border due to the terrain," said Cleveland, a former Border Patrol agent, adding that the animals were often turned over to the USDA for mounted agents to use.
Animal-smuggling routes present a particular challenge for screwworm control because infected animals may never come into contact with veterinarians.
Tawnee Preisner, founder of the Tennessee-based Horse Plus Humane Society, said her organization has found horses with neck wounds, metal tracheotomy tubes and deep tissue pockets, raising concerns that smugglers may be hiding drugs or contraband inside the animals. The FBI contacted the organization in 2025 for information on horse smuggling, she said.
"When horses are being used to move drugs and humans, if a horse gets (screwworm), they're not going to report it," Preisner said, adding, "They're just going to shoot the horse, bury it and keep going." REUTERS

Taiwan launches 'non-red' testing platform for drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
10:11:45 UTC
19:11:45 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Industrial Technology Research Institute has completed Taiwan's first verification platform designed to assess whether drones and components meet “non-red” supply chain and cybersecurity requirements.
The platform was developed with US partners after ITRI became the first organization outside the US to be authorized in June to conduct Green UAS evaluations, per Fount Media. It digitizes the process of tracing suppliers, checking component origins, and evaluating cybersecurity risks.
More than 20 domestic drone manufacturers and key component suppliers have requested assessments covering drone systems and batteries. Companies from Japan, Australia, and the Philippines have also inquired about the service.
Chien Jui-hung (錢睿宏), director of ITRI’s Smart Machinery Promotion Office, said many domestically made drones are already technically mature, but companies often struggle to demonstrate that their products can be trusted, Fount Media reported. Firms previously had to compile extensive documentation and trace components through multiple supplier layers without a standardized system.
The new platform lets companies trace key components, identify documentation gaps, and flag potential Chinese suppliers before formal certification. It can help them address problems before testing and avoid repeated reviews.
The platform is also designed around requirements associated with the US Defense Innovation Unit’s Blue UAS framework, according to Fount Media. Green UAS is primarily aimed at commercial and non-US defense markets, while Blue UAS is used for drones considered for US defense applications.
Obtaining Green UAS certification does not automatically make a drone Blue UAS-approved or guarantee US military contracts. Instead, it allows Taiwanese companies to establish supply chain and cybersecurity evidence at home before pursuing additional US government or defense-market requirements.
The nation’s drone exports are expanding rapidly, with complete-drone exports reaching NT$3.64 billion (US$115 million) in the first quarter of 2026, exceeding the NT$2.95 billion recorded for all of 2025, Fount Media reported. The top three markets were the Czech Republic, Poland, and the US. More than 267 local companies have entered the drone industry, covering complete systems and component manufacturing.
ITRI hopes to eventually integrate Taiwan’s broader drone testing capabilities, per CNA. Chien said a single-window system that coordinates testing resources across different organizations would help establish a more comprehensive drone verification system.

New images show China’s largest stealth drone in testing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
10:11:31 UTC
19:11:31 KST

- New satellite images show China's largest known stealth drone, unofficially called the WZ-X, undergoing testing at Malan Air Base in Xinjiang.
- Analysts estimate its wingspan at about 52 meters, wider than a B-2 bomber, with a range exceeding 20,000 kilometers, though China has not confirmed the aircraft's existence.
New satellite images have surfaced showing China’s largest known stealth drone undergoing testing at a secretive air base in China’s Xinjiang region, according to analysts tracking the program on social media.
Aviation researcher Andreas Rupprecht posted on LinkedIn that two new images had leaked showing the aircraft, known unofficially as the WZ-X, at what appears to be Malan Air Base. A separate image cited by defense outlet The War Zone and shared on social media showed the aircraft’s trailing edge in detail, describing it as “shallowly serrated,” a shaping technique used to reduce a stealth aircraft’s radar signature.
Neither China’s government nor its military has confirmed the aircraft’s existence, name or purpose. Everything known about the WZ-X comes from commercial satellite imagery and the analysts who study it.
Malan Air Base, located in the Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, has become the Chinese air force’s primary test site for uncrewed aircraft, according to Rupprecht, who has researched Chinese military aviation and aircraft serial numbers for years. The base also hosts the 178th UAV Brigade. Satellite imagery dating back to 2022 shows the site expanding steadily, with new hangars and taxiways that analysts believe are tied to the WZ-X and a second, still-unidentified stealth combat drone known as the GJ-X. Rupprecht compared Malan to Area 51 in the United States, both for its remote desert location and for its role housing China’s most secretive aircraft programs.
The WZ-X was first identified in satellite imagery in 2024, with additional images captured through 2025 and 2026. Analysts describe it as a twin-engine flying-wing design, similar in overall layout to the U.S. Air Force’s classified RQ-180 drone but considerably larger. Estimates place its wingspan at roughly 52 meters (173 feet), wider than a B-2 Spirit bomber, with a length of about 14 meters (46 feet).
The War Zone has reported that its wingspan makes it the largest Chinese flying-wing design identified to date.
Rupprecht said the aircraft’s two engines appear to draw air through a single intake mounted on top of the fuselage, reportedly shielded with a conformal mesh intended to reduce the aircraft’s radar cross-section. Analysts estimate the drone’s range at more than 20,000 kilometers (12,400 miles), with a normal cruising altitude between 18 and 20 kilometers (59,000 and 66,000 feet) and a cruising speed of roughly Mach 0.5 to 0.65. Some sources have suggested the aircraft was developed by Nantong University in Jiangsu province, though this has not been independently confirmed.
Satellite imagery from Malan has also shown a second large flying-wing aircraft nearby, described by analysts as a heavier “cranked-kite” design with a wingspan of roughly 42 meters (137 feet), likely intended for lower-altitude missions and potentially capable of both surveillance and long-range strike. The War Zone has also identified a smaller, tailless drone resembling China’s sixth-generation fighter designs parked at the same base, alongside a Y-20 heavy transport aircraft, suggesting Malan supports multiple secretive aircraft programs simultaneously rather than a single project.
Analysts caution that appearing in satellite photos does not mean the WZ-X is an operational weapon. Its exact role, whether reconnaissance, communications relay or long-range strike, along with its manufacturer and formal designation, remains unconfirmed.

The Venezuelan billionaire the US investigated for money laundering now has a Pentagon oil deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
10:06:34 UTC
19:06:34 KST

The Venezuelan billionaire the US investigated for money laundering now has a Pentagon oil deal
CARACAS/MIAMI, Sept 5 - The billionaire who helped broker the Trump administration’s sweeping long-term oil deal with Venezuela was until recently a target of U.S. money-laundering investigations involving funds embezzled from the state-owned oil company PDVSA. Now, after assisting U.S. authorities ahead of the capture of authoritarian leader Nicolas Maduro, Alejandro Betancourt is Washington’s key partner in an unusual oil agreement with Caracas.
According to last week’s announcement, the U.S. gains access to about one-fifth of Venezuela’s crude reserves for decades. The Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital takes a 35% stake in North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP), Betancourt’s company and a known crude producer in Venezuela. The State Department gets the right to buy 20% of NABEP’s oil at cost, and preferential access to the remaining 80% of output.
The deal marks a striking change of fortune for Betancourt, who four people familiar with U.S. policy in Venezuela said was key to U.S. strategy and planning in the lead-up to the January 3 operation that removed former President Maduro from power and flew him to New York to face charges of drug-trafficking, which Maduro denies.
Asked about the investigations of Betancourt, a U.S. official who declined to be named said most of the legal challenges were nearly a decade old — and that he currently has no legal problems in the United States. NABEP’s record of pumping oil in Venezuela made Betancourt the best partner to help boost output under the arrangement, the official said.
Reuters could not determine precisely when U.S. federal prosecutors paused their investigation into Betancourt or whether it came in exchange for his cooperation with the Trump administration.
Sarah Chouraqui, NABEP’s lawyer, said Betancourt had a strong record of operating in complex energy markets. “The allegations in question have been examined extensively by authorities in multiple jurisdictions, and no charges have been brought against him,” she said in an email.
Chouraqui did not address questions about his assistance to the Trump administration or his legal cases.
INFORMATION THAT HELPED ENFORCE U.S. BLOCKADE
In the months before Maduro’s capture, the billionaire provided information that helped enforce a U.S. naval blockade targeting sanctioned oil tankers operating in Venezuela, which led to the seizure or interdiction of more than a dozen vessels, according to the four people who spoke on condition of anonymity. He also facilitated negotiations with officials including Delcy Rodriguez, who became interim president after Maduro’s capture.
The Venezuelan government did not respond to requests for comment.
After Maduro’s removal, Betancourt’s role as a key intermediary continued, helping broker oil deals and other partnerships and continuing to assist communications between Washington and Caracas to kickstart Venezuela’s economy, according to seven sources.
In January, Betancourt helped broker a key oil trading agreement that has led to the export of more than 135 million barrels of crude and fuel to the United States, Europe, India and the Caribbean so far, according to vessel monitoring data and six people with knowledge of the negotiations. That’s about half of all oil exports through the end of August.
Reuters could not determine his exact role in the discussions.
Betancourt has also popped in on meetings at Venezuela’s Miraflores presidential palace, according to two people familiar with the matter. He was also at Miraflores during this week’s visit by U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright, Wright told reporters, though Betancourt did not appear with Wright and Rodriguez at a signing ceremony for oil deals.
Betancourt has been investigated in the United States, Spain and Switzerland but never indicted.
Earlier this year U.S. federal prosecutors in Florida paused their investigation into Betancourt in connection with an alleged plan that involved embezzling over $1 billion from Venezuela’s state-owned oil company and laundering it through real estate in Miami and bank accounts in Malta and Switzerland.
Two of those people said U.S. prosecutors had been subsequently discouraged by supervisors from investigating Betancourt further.
Prosecutors on the case were not given a rationale, four people familiar with the case said.
After the investigation stalled, U.S. officials pressured the Swiss government to ease its inquiries into the tycoon, said four people familiar with the matter. Switzerland, which was also investigating Betancourt for money-laundering, dropped its request to extradite him from the United Kingdom in May, said the sources.
The Zurich Public Prosecutor’s Office declined to comment on whether the United States influenced the decision to withdraw its extradition request, but said the case against Betancourt was still proceeding.
"The extradition request was withdrawn because of particular aspects of UK extradition law, which we cannot discuss in detail,” the Office said. “This step concerns only the extradition proceedings in the UK. The criminal proceedings against the accused are otherwise unaffected and will continue."
The withdrawal was unusual, said Mark Pieth, a Swiss legal scholar and anti-corruption expert. “You would not do that if the case is continuing,” he said.
The United Kingdom’s Home Office declined to comment.
A YOUNG GENERATION OF BUSINESS LEADERS
Betancourt is a prominent member of the so-called Bolichicos — a younger generation of business people who amassed fortunes during the administration of former Venezuelan leader Hugo Chavez. His company Derwick Associates won roughly $2 billion in government contracts to build power plants during the country's electricity crisis in the 2010s — some without competitive bidding — despite having little construction experience.
Government data later showed many of the plants operated at a fraction of their intended capacity or not at all, as Venezuela's power grid continued to suffer widespread blackouts. Betancourt and Derwick have repeatedly denied wrongdoing and said the facilities were completed and that later failures resulted from mismanagement by state authorities. Rodriguez told a press conference on Wednesday that all legal proceedings against Betancourt’s companies in Venezuela were dismissed years ago.
In 2012, Betancourt entered into a partnership with state-controlled company PDVSA to operate mature fields in western Venezuela. These would eventually become the core production of NABEP, which Betancourt co-founded with Florida billionaire Harry Sargeant in April 2024. Sargeant sold his shares in NABEP last month.
Mauricio Claver-Carone, a Miami businessman and former Trump administration adviser who implemented U.S. policy in Caracas in an unofficial role, told Reuters last month that Betancourt is a useful intermediary between the Trump administration and Rodriguez because he understands the oil business in both countries. He added that Betancourt had been helpful to the first Trump administration.
But several former U.S. intelligence officials, prosecutors and diplomats privately expressed concern regarding Betancourt's influence on U.S. policy, because of the previous investigation in the U.S. and ongoing investigation in Switzerland, as well as his proximity to high-ranking officials from the former Hugo Chavez and Maduro governments.
Federal prosecutors are “scratching their heads,” said one former prosecutor with knowledge of the situation.
Before the Miami-based investigation into Betancourt was put on hold, six sources said he had been identified as an unnamed unindicted co-conspirator in an alleged plan by former Venezuelan energy officials and their associates to launder more than $1 billion misappropriated from the state-owned PDVSA oil company. Ten people have been indicted since 2018.
In Spain, authorities launched a new investigation into Betancourt for money laundering last year involving $4 billion allegedly embezzled from PDVSA, according to Spanish newspaper El Pais.
Reuters was unable to determine if he remained under investigation.
Spain’s National Court and the Venezuelan state oil company did not respond to requests for comment.
Once he was free to leave the UK, Betancourt traveled to Venezuela in late June and again in July, both times departing from West Palm Beach, Florida, according to flight manifests seen by Reuters.
Betancourt’s lawyer Chouraqui did not comment on his travel. REUTERS

====================================================================================================

Census 2027: The 14 questions and why opposition fears an NPR 'backdoor'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
10:06:05 UTC
19:06:05 KST

Opposition is raising questions over the methodology of population enumeration, alleging that it too has a “deeper nefarious purpose”
NEW DELHI: Although six years late, enumerators have started knocking on doors for the decennial headcount in Ladakh and snowbound regions such as Jammu and Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand starting September 1.But doubts and fears have preceded the Census, turning what was meant to be a routine exercise to track population growth and aid policy planning into a fresh political flashpoint.
Until now, the caste census had been the main point of contention between the opposition and the government. The opposition had questioned the intent and methodology of an exercise being conducted in the country after almost 100 years.The contention has now moved beyond the caste census, and the opposition is also raising questions over the methodology of population enumeration, alleging that it too has a “deeper nefarious purpose”.
What is the controversy?
On August 14, the Centre notified the list of questions that officials will ask during population enumeration. The questionnaire, however, contains 14 new or modified questions compared with the 2011 Census.These include spouse's name, nationality as declared, father's particulars, mother's particulars, SC/ST/caste, literacy and digital literacy, highest educational level attained and stream/discipline, place of Covid-19 vaccination, total number of bank accounts, mobile number, Aadhaar number, voter ID number, passport number for Indian passport holders, and availability of a driving licence.
Interestingly, several of these questions, including details of a person's father and mother and their places of birth, were also part of the National Population Register (NPR) schedule notified in 2020.Moreover, the Union Budget presented on February 1 this year allocated Rs 6,000 crore for the NPR and Census 2027, even though the government has not yet notified any schedule for the NPR.The Budget document said the allocation included provisions for the Office of the Registrar General and Census Commissioner of India and various schemes of the Registrar General of India, with Rs 6,000 crore earmarked for NPR and Census 2027.
What are the opposition's charges
Following the notification of the questionnaire, the opposition has accused the Centre of turning the Census exercise into a “backdoor for the NPR, and eventually, NRC”.Congress Rajya Sabha member Jairam Ramesh said the methodology of asking questions in Census 2027 is flawed and alleged that questions on religion, date of birth, place of birth and parents' details had never been asked in previous enumerations.“Census is confidential. Clearly, Census 27 has a deeper nefarious purpose,” he said in a post on X.Similarly, former West Bengal chief minister Mamata Banerjee alleged that the Centre was planning to conduct the Census in the form of NPR.“They have started the census. Census in the form of NPR. You have to provide your bank account number, mobile number and Aadhaar number. You must disclose the full details of all family members,” Mamata said.“No political party has been informed. At least the Trinamool Congress was not informed. Nobody knows whose name will be deleted. Is it going to be another SIR? Who knows,” she added.Even during the run-up to the Bengal assembly elections, she alleged that the Centre was planning to 'take away' people's citizenship in the name of NRC.Former Kerala chief minister Pinarayi Vijayan also raised questions over the inclusion of the new questions, arguing that the Census should not be used to divide people.“The reported inclusion of questions about parents’ place of birth and religion in the upcoming Census is deeply troubling. The Census must not become a backdoor for the NPR and, eventually, the NRC. Citizenship cannot be tied to religion, and no census should be used to divide our people. The Union Government must immediately drop such divisive questions. Secular forces must stand united against this dangerous move,” Vijayan said.
Difference between Census and NPR
Census and NPR differ in their legal basis, objectives and the nature of information they are designed to collect.The Census is a statistical exercise meant to produce data on population, literacy, occupation, migration, housing and, in 2027, caste. It is used for making policies, allocating resources and delimitation.On the other hand, the National Population Register is a continuously updated register of “usual residents” created under the Citizenship Act, 1955.It is designed to maintain an identifiable database of people who have lived in a locality for at least six months or intend to stay there for the next six months, irrespective of their citizenship.
The NPR collects detailed identity information, including names, parents' particulars, place of birth, nationality as declared, address and identity documents such as Aadhaar, voter ID and passport, as well as mobile numbers. The data collected through NPR is linked to the proposed National Register of Citizens.Under Rule 3 of the Citizenship Rules, the Centre may order preparation of the National Population Register, from which the Local Register of citizens is prepared after verification.Rule 4 provides that individuals whose citizenship is doubtful can be flagged in the Population Register for further enquiry.The NPR data was first collected in 2010 alongside the 2011 Census house-listing exercise and updated through a door-to-door survey in 2015.However, both the Census and NPR are conducted by the Office of the Registrar General and Census Commissioner, under the Union Ministry of Home Affairs.
What the law says
Can Census data be shared?
The inclusion of the new questions has raised a larger question: Can information collected during the Census be accessed or used by government agencies for purposes beyond the exercise itself?The law says no. Section 15 of the Census Act, 1948 provides a strong legal shield around personal information collected during the Census.“No person shall have a right to inspect any book, register or record made by a census-officer in the discharge of his duty,” the Act says.“No entry in any such book, register, record or schedule shall be admissible as evidence in any civil proceeding whatsoever or in any criminal proceeding other than a prosecution under this Act or any other law for any act or omission which constitutes an offence under this Act,” it further says.This means that the information collected through the census cannot be used by other government agencies to determine the citizenship of a person.Speaking to The Times of India, advocate Ajinkya Udane said it would therefore be incorrect to accuse the government of divulging information collected through the Census.“Through the census, private information of people is being asked. However, the Census Act bars the government from divulging this information to its agencies,” Udane said.“So, to accuse the government of doing something which the law bars it from doing is not correct,” he added.Cyber and privacy law expert advocate Prashant Mali, however, stressed that Census data must remain a statistical instrument and “not become a backdoor for state surveillance”.“Section 15 of the Census Act creates a strong statutory confidentiality barrier. Individual census records are not open to inspection and are not admissible as evidence. Therefore, census information cannot legitimately be converted into an evidentiary database for citizenship determination merely because another government authority wants to use it,” Mali said.
Census data must remain a statistical instrument and “not become a backdoor for state surveillance”.
He said that even if a census record, or personal information traceable back to it, is accessed or used in a manner prohibited by Section 15, describing it as “independent intelligence” would not cure the underlying violation.“Substance must prevail over form. If the underlying census record or identifiable information has been accessed or used contrary to Section 15, I feel calling it independent intelligence does not cure the problem,” he said.“I feel the State cannot do indirectly through a citizenship inquiry what Section 15 of the Census Act prohibits it from doing directly through the Census record. A lawful purpose for processing does not automatically create a lawful source of data,” he told The Times of India.During the conversation, Mali said that the interaction between the Digital Personal Data Protection Act (DPDPA) and the Census Act will also be interesting to watch during the exercise.“DPDPA (Digital Personal Data Protection Act) Sections 3–17 are scheduled to come into force 18 months after 13 November 2025, i.e. 13 May 2027, while Census 2027 field operations occur around that period,” Mali said.
“This makes the interaction between the Census Act and DPDPA particularly interesting for the 2027 exercise,” he added.The Digital Personal Data Protection Act (DPDPA) is primary law which will dictate how the personal data is collected, processed and stored.It sets out obligations for entities handling personal data - such as obtaining consent, limiting use to the stated purpose, and ensuring data security - and grants individuals rights over their own data, including access and correction.
Rohitashwa Ranjan is a digital journalist with The Times of India, where he decodes Indian politics as a carefully staged production with scripts, subtext and everything behind. His stories track elections, party dynamics and the things that often are buried beneath the headlines. When not parsing vote shares or alliances, he is usually reading between the lines, where the real story tends to reside.

Russia’s elite drone unit says it used 1 million FPV drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
10:04:55 UTC
19:04:55 KST

- Russia's Rubicon drone unit claims it used over 1 million FPV drones and struck 280,000 targets in Ukraine from January 2025 to August 2026, an unverified, self-reported figure.
- Independent analysts say Rubicon grew from 1,450 to about 5,000 personnel by 2026, but that Ukraine has since regained an edge in mid-range drone warfare.
Russia’s Rubicon Center for Advanced Unmanned Technologies claims its operators used more than 1 million First-Person-View (FPV) drones and struck over 280,000 targets in Ukraine between January 2025 and August 2026, according to a statement the unit posted to its official Telegram channel. The figures come only from Russia’s elite drone unit itself and have not been independently verified.
Rubicon said the 20-month total makes it “the undisputed leader” in FPV drone use among all Russian units fighting in Ukraine. The unit also said it has published more than 45,000 videos of strikes on its Telegram channel, with new footage posted daily showing operations, tactics and the unit’s history.
As with the strike and drone-use figures, these numbers are self-reported by the unit and cannot be independently confirmed.
Rubicon was established on August 2, 2024, by order of Russian Defense Minister Andrei Belousov, according to reporting by the newsletter Two Marines, run by analyst Rob Lee and Ukrainian marine drone operator Dmytro Putiata. The center was created partly in response to Ukraine’s own specialized drone units and its “Drone Line” initiative, and was designed to centralize Russian research, procurement and combat deployment of drones, ground robots and unmanned boats under one command, rather than leaving that work scattered across volunteer-funded projects.
An investigation by Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty identified the unit’s commander as Colonel Sergei Budnikov, a 37-year-old former artillery and marine officer, with facilities including a training site at Patriot Park near Moscow.
Independent reporting has documented Rubicon’s rapid growth. The unit expanded from roughly 1,450 personnel in 2025 to about 5,000 by 2026, organized into battalion-sized detachments that each field dozens of quadcopter and fixed-wing strike teams, according to the Foreign Policy Research Institute’s analysis of the Two Marines data. That same analysis cautioned that Rubicon’s fast expansion has strained its recruitment pipeline and diluted the specialized training that made its early detachments effective.
Rubicon first drew significant attention for its role helping Russian forces cut off Ukrainian supply lines during the fighting in Russia’s Kursk Oblast in late 2024 and early 2025, after Ukraine’s surprise incursion there in August 2024. Ukrainian commanders quoted in independent reporting described the unit’s fiber-optic guided drones, which resist electronic jamming, as a serious problem, and Rubicon has continued operating on active fronts including the Kupiansk axis, where a Ukrainian brigade officer told Ukrainian outlet Suspilne in October that the unit’s use of remote mining and FPV drones was disrupting Ukrainian logistics.
Independent assessments diverge from Rubicon’s own self-promotion, however. While the unit’s tactics contributed to Russian gains around Pokrovsk, Myrnohrad and Kostyantynivka in 2025, the Foreign Policy Research Institute’s analysis found that Rubicon did not fundamentally change the broader stalemate in drone warfare along the front, and that by 2026 Ukraine had regained an edge in mid-range drone operations. Neither Rubicon’s claimed strike totals nor its claim of “undisputed” leadership among Russian drone units have been corroborated by Ukrainian officials or independent battlefield analysts.

Health warnings could reduce youth’s hours spent on social media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
10:02:10 UTC
19:02:10 KST

Pop-up messages that warn of the harms of social media could help reduce youth’s social media use, a new study found.
Alcohol and tobacco products have health warnings about the negative impacts. Researchers say that social media could benefit from similar warnings too, such as “Using social media causes sleep problems. This is bad for your health,” and “Social media is associated with significant mental health harms for children and young adults.”
Exactly such pop-up messages showed up in a study published on JAMA Health Forum. The messages informed about the harmful impact of social media — such as depression, anxiety, worsened body image and sleep disruption. Researchers hope this could be yet another tool in the toolbox aimed at managing youth’s social media time more healthily.
“With substances like tobacco and alcohol, we find, on average, that well-designed warning labels change behavior,” lead study author Anna Grummon, assistant professor of paediatrics, said. As social media is a completely different product compared to cigarettes or alcohol, “where you just put the warning on the product and it lives there,” these warnings have to be “basically pop-ups,” Grummon said.
Researchers saw that over 1,000 youth aged 13 to 29-years increased their understanding of social media risks to their mental well-being after being exposed to 14 warnings on six health topics while scrolling. The warnings covered social media addiction, negative body image, sleep disruption, depression, anxiety, overall mental health harms and the fact that social media has not been proven safe for young people.
Participants consistently reported that the warning messages would reduce their social media use, authors said.
Youth rated each message in response to two questions: “How much does this message discourage you from wanting to use social media?” and “How much does this message increase your awareness of the harms of using social media?”
The messages that worked the best were those that warned about mental health harms, such as depression and anxiety, except the addiction warning.
While the data does not show why those messages performed best, “if I were to speculate, I would say that these are harms that resonate with people,” Grummon said. “People may think, ‘That’s right, I can see that happening to my friends or to me,’ and these are outcomes people care about.”

US ambassador visits Palestinian town amid rise in West Bank settler violence
US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee met on Saturday with Palestinians, including the families of US citizens killed by Israeli settlers, in a Palestinian town in the occupied West Bank that has been the target of repeated settler attacks.
Settler violence in the West Bank has risen sharply since Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition government, the most right-wing in Israel's history, took office in late 2022.
During the visit, Huckabee said that there was no plan underway to force Palestinians out of Gaza, after Israeli ministers laid out ideas on how to expel the war-battered territory's two million people.
"I can tell you categorically there is no plan of the Israelis to displace people out of Gaza against their will," Ambassador Mike Huckabee told reporters as he visited Palestinian-Americans in the West Bank.
Several settlements have been established around Turmus Ayya, the Palestinian town near Ramallah that Huckabee was visiting on Saturday. Its residents say that harassment by militant Israeli settlers is common and that they are unable to stop them from entering the town and damaging their homes.

"One of the messages that we have been sending and we will continue to send is that people in these communities have a right to live with a level of security and safety, and that the government has a responsibility to make sure that that happens," he told reporters.

Israeli settlers accused of carrying out attacks in the West Bank targeting Palestinians are rarely prosecuted.
"We are hoping that (the ambassador) will do something for us regarding these lawless settlers," Turmus Ayya resident Sameer Hazama said ahead of the meeting with the ambassador.
Huckabee visited Taybeh, one of the only Christian villages remaining in the West Bank, in June 2025 after a church there was vandalised. Huckabee said at the time that the desecration of a place of worship was an act of terror and a crime.

====================================================================================================

Over half the risk for postpartum psychosis is tied to genetics, large study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
10:00:35 UTC
19:00:35 KST

New research published in Molecular Psychiatry indicates that postpartum psychosis is heavily influenced by both common and rare genetic factors, with about half of the risk tied to genetics. The study also identified a specific gene involved in cholesterol production that provides evidence for shared biological pathways between postpartum psychosis, schizophrenia, and certain autoimmune conditions.
Postpartum psychosis is a rare but severe mental health emergency that occurs in roughly 1 to 2 out of every 1,000 mothers shortly after childbirth. It involves an abrupt onset of symptoms like mania, severe depression, confusion, and psychosis, which is when a person loses touch with reality through hallucinations or delusions. The condition poses heavy risks to both the mother and the infant, often requiring immediate medical hospitalization.
Earlier research established that this vulnerability has deep biological roots. A 2001 study showed that the tendency to experience a severe psychotic episode triggered specifically by childbirth runs strongly in families. Moving beyond familial history, a 2013 study discovered that women experiencing their first episode of postpartum psychosis show disruptions in their immune systems.
Alongside these immune factors, metabolic changes have also been implicated, as a 2017 meta-analysis suggested that people going through their first psychotic episode tend to have altered cholesterol levels. These findings paved the way for large-scale genetic sequencing to pinpoint the exact genes and shared biological pathways involved. To build on these insights, researchers led by Seulgi Jung and study co-author Behrang Mahjani, an assistant professor at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai who directs the Mahjani Lab, aimed to detail the specific genetic architecture of postpartum psychosis.
“Postpartum psychosis is a severe but understudied psychiatric disorder,” Mahjani told PsyPost. “Our previous study showed that sisters of women with postpartum psychosis have a markedly elevated risk, but its heritability had not been quantified and no specific risk genes had been identified. We therefore examined the contribution of both common and rare genetic variation to the disorder.”
The researchers first used data from Swedish national registers to estimate the overall genetic risk of the disorder. They examined health records from over 1.6 million mothers who gave birth to their first child between 1980 and 2017. Among this massive group, 2,514 mothers, or 0.15 percent, developed postpartum psychosis.
By tracking the health records of the mothers’ sisters and cousins, the researchers estimated the heritability of postpartum psychosis to be 55 percent. This indicates that more than half of the variation in who develops the condition can be attributed to genetic factors, a rate similar to that of bipolar disorder.
“The genetic contribution is substantial,” Mahjani explained. “Heritability in this range means that inherited variation accounts for a large share of the differences in vulnerability between individuals, comparable to what is seen for bipolar disorder and schizophrenia.”
“This supports the view that postpartum psychosis reflects an underlying biological vulnerability rather than being simply a psychological reaction to the stress of childbirth,” he added.
To see how much of this heritability comes from common genetic variations, the team turned to the All of Us Research Program, a large national database of genetic and health information. They focused on whole-genome sequencing data from 198 mothers of European ancestry who had experienced postpartum psychosis, comparing them to 2,013 matched controls.
The team found that common genetic variants explained about 45.6 percent of the risk for postpartum psychosis. Because this is slightly lower than the 55 percent heritability estimated from family histories, it suggests that rarer genetic variations also play a role in the disorder.
The researchers then looked closely at rare genetic changes, specifically focusing on protein-truncating variants. These are severe mutations that essentially break a gene, preventing it from producing a functional protein. They analyzed a larger sample of 461 cases of postpartum psychosis and 4,610 unaffected controls.
Women with postpartum psychosis had an unusually high number of these disruptive mutations in genes that are generally highly constrained, meaning the genes do not usually tolerate mutations well without causing major biological problems. Based on these mutation patterns, the researchers estimated that there are around 81 specific genes that contribute to the risk of postpartum psychosis.
When analyzing which individual genes were most affected, the gene HMGCR stood out strongly. This gene contains the instructions for making a key enzyme that controls how the body produces cholesterol. A second gene, DNMT1, which helps maintain how DNA is regulated and read by the body, also showed a possible, though less certain, link to the disorder.
“The rare variants in HMGCR have large effects in the people who carry them, which is what allowed us to detect the gene despite a relatively modest sample,” Mahjani noted.
However, he cautioned against oversimplifying this connection. “HMGCR should not be read as ‘the postpartum psychosis gene,'” he said. “It is one of the many genes contributing to risk, and like other severe psychiatric disorders the condition is highly polygenic.”
To explore the broader impact of these genes, the researchers checked for mutations in HMGCR and DNMT1 across hundreds of thousands of individuals in two large medical biobanks. They found that rare mutations in HMGCR were also linked to conditions like vascular dementia and unspecified mental disorders, indicating the gene influences brain health outside of the postpartum period.
Finally, the researchers compared their list of genetic risk factors for postpartum psychosis against genes known to cause other illnesses. They found that a substantial percentage of the top risk genes for bipolar disorder and schizophrenia were also linked to postpartum psychosis. Additionally, they noted a genetic overlap with autoimmune diseases like rheumatoid arthritis, myasthenia gravis, and Crohn’s disease, with HMGCR appearing as a top risk gene for both schizophrenia and rheumatoid arthritis.
“The results were largely consistent with what genetic studies of related psychiatric disorders would predict,” Mahjani said.
There are a few things to keep in mind regarding this study. First, definitions of postpartum psychosis can vary across different medical records. The registry data used in the study often lacked the precise end dates of episodes, which makes it harder to classify the exact duration of the illness.
The researchers also did not separate women whose postpartum psychosis was their very first psychiatric episode from those who had a pre-existing condition, such as bipolar disorder. As a result, some of the genetic patterns they found might reflect severe mental illness in general rather than factors entirely unique to the postpartum period.
Additionally, the genetic sequencing data relied heavily on individuals of European ancestry, meaning the results might not fully capture the genetic risk factors present in other populations. Future studies with more diverse groups will help provide a more complete picture of the condition’s genetic roots.
“Our immediate priority is to replicate these findings in larger samples,” Mahjani said of the team’s next steps. “Beyond that, we want to understand how the genes we identified actually function in the disorder, and how genetic vulnerability interacts with the hormonal and immune changes that occur during and after pregnancy.”
“Mainly that postpartum psychosis has been remarkably understudied relative to its severity,” he concluded. “Progress will depend on continued access to the kind of large-scale genomic resources that made this work possible, such as the All of Us Research Program, and on studies large enough to identify additional risk genes with confidence.”
The study, “Genetic architecture of postpartum psychosis: from common to rare genetic variation,” was authored by Seulgi Jung, Madison Caballero, Adrianna Kępińska, Shelby Smout, Trine Munk-Olsen, Thalia K. Robakis, Veerle Bergink, and Behrang Mahjani.

Captain calamity: Pete Hegseth under fire for ‘inept’ leadership of US military
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
10:00:35 UTC
19:00:35 KST

In a different Washington, under a different president, a return to the well-worn playbook of all-out sanctions to counter Iran might have been the signal for a publicity-hungry US secretary of defense to adopt a lower profile.
But these are no ordinary times. And Pete Hegseth is no ordinary defense secretary.
Barely a week after the treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, unleashed a supposed “economic D-day” aimed at crushing the regime in Tehran under the weight of commercial pressures, Hegseth once again returned to the limelight – and the center of controversy.
The former Fox News host usurped Bessent from center stage as the conflict with Iran reverted to open warfare and discontent at the Pentagon was laid bare once more.
Turf wars within Hegseth’s own fiefdom resurfaced with the resignation of the army secretary, fresh revelations of blocked promotions and leaked disclosures of resistance from military top brass of extended deployments to the Middle East.
While the Pentagon insists that any suggestion the defense department is in disarray under Hegseth is “completely baseless”, alarm over his conduct in the role – and the implications – has not merely been expressed by Hegseth’s political opponents.
“The secretary of defense is a clear and present danger to the national security of the United States and the world,” said Randy Manner, a retired major general in the US national guard – in which Hegseth also served – and member of National Security Leaders for America (NSL4A), a group of former military leaders. “He has done more harm to the national security of the United States than any secretary of defense since the country was created.”
Thom Tillis, the Republican senator from North Carolina, who is stepping down from the US Senate after clashes with Donald Trump, bluntly urged the US president this week to fire his defense secretary.
“I have never witnessed more inept management of the brave men and women who serve our country,” Tillis wrote on social media. “He is intimidated by competence and retreats to ginning up culture wars instead of soberly attending to the vital work of our national defense and the health and wellbeing of our fighting force.”
After a month-long lull, the resumption of strikes on Iranian targets near the strait of Hormuz meanwhile renewed questions over just what the US wants to achieve in its war with the Islamic regime, which Trump and his defense secretary once loudly vowed to topple.
The strikes, on mainland Iran as well as Iranian islands in the Gulf, caused multiple casualties. In one incident, Iranian media reported that five people, including a six-year-old child, were killed in the southern city of Kuhestak when a missile struck a wedding party.
Iranian authorities labelled the deaths a war crime. The episode had echoes of strikes in the city of Minab on the first day of the war on 28 February, when more than 150 people, including 120 children, were killed when missiles hit an elementary school. The US has not formally admitted responsibility, although officials have said the incident is under military investigation.
The latest strikes were quickly followed by disclosures that Hegseth had extended military deployments in the Middle East, where the US currently maintains 50,000 troops and 19 warships – partly to enforce a naval blockade on Iran – into the middle of next year.
The extensions were ordered even after several commanders in other sectors voiced objections, formally known as “non-concurs”, to the deployments, arguing that they could leave the US at risk of being unable to meet its commitments in other areas, while subjecting forces to the additional strain of being at sea for too long.
The non-concurs were recorded in the Secretary of Defense Orders Book of 14 August, a classified document whose contents were leaked and reported by the Washington Post.
‘The past six months has failed’
“I’m not sure what the strategy is here,” Kevin Carroll, a former army colonel and military intelligence officer who served in the offices of the defense secretary and joint chiefs of staff, said of the war on Iran. “What’s the enemy’s center of gravity that we’re going after?
“We tried decapitating their leadership. That didn’t work. We tried going after their missile program. We were not able to destroy it. Tried sinking the navy, but they still maintain a mining capability.
“We could easily take out their energy infrastructure. But that would drive the price of oil much, much higher, and lead to retaliatory attacks on the energy infrastructure of our Gulf allies. It’s not clear what this target set is intended to do.”
Nate Swanson, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council and a former White House and state department adviser on Iran, said Hegseth’s long-term deployment orders reflected the administration’s decision to embrace a policy of long-term economic blockade.
“It’s a recognition of the fact that the past six months has failed, but they don’t know what to do,” argued Swanson, who suggested that Trump was attracted by the idea of abandoning the conflict, but wanted to do so in way that enabled him to project strength.
As the war drags on, Hegseth stands accused of being insufficiently engaged with such grave policy matters, preferring instead to focus on “cultural” issues – sacrificing the careers of talented career officers in the process – and his future political ambitions.
The defense secretary, who has evaded awkward questions or scrutiny by not holding a formal Pentagon briefing since 5 May, has reportedly told associates that he is considering a bid for the 2028 Republican presidential nomination.
In the midst of a burgeoning trade war between the US and Canada, Hegseth – who has previously railed against “fat” generals and instituted testosterone tests for service personnel – found time to wade in by apparently “body shaming” two Canadian female teenage cadets.
The social media post attracted a storm of criticism. In a podcast, Joe Walsh, a former Republican congressman who is now a Democrat, accused Hegseth of “fucking online harassment” and denounced the defense secretary as a “punk”.
Tensions over Hegseth’s priorities reached a head this week when the army secretary, Dan Driscoll – a friend and ally of Vice-President JD Vance – resigned after repeatedly clashing with Hegseth over blocked promotions and purges of senior commanders on flimsy pretexts.
A large proportion of those blocked or fired have been black or female, in line with Hegseth’s vocal crusade against “woke” DEI (diversity, equity and inclusiveness) initiatives. In the latest of a series of purges, the New York Times reported that Hegseth had blocked the promotions of seven officers to the two-star general rank.
In submitting his resignation, Driscoll – who has spearheaded efforts to modernize the army, including through embracing drone warfare – voiced concerns “surrounding Army transformation and readiness and Hegseth’s blocking those efforts specifically by firing the generals who were responsible”, a source told CNN.
Driscoll’s departure – and the reasons for it – aroused anger even among Republicans, most notably Tillis, the outgoing GOP senator. “Dan was the right man at the right moment to lead our Soldiers and Army civilians,” wrote Tillis.
The withering verdict is seconded by some retired generals, who say misgivings over Hegseth’s leadership are quietly shared by many serving officers who remain.
Manner said Hegseth was depriving other parts of the armed forces to fund the Iran war out of “readiness accounts”. “These are for training the rest of the force,” he said. “So the rest of the force is losing training hours, equipment and money for maintenance and operations. The rest of the military is significantly degraded.”
Manner also said his conversations with serving officers bore out the leaked concerns voiced in the Secretary of Defence’s Orders Book. “I have firsthand knowledge of people who are serving on active duty who echo the exact same concerns that we are headed to a situation where we can no longer defend Taiwan, that we are very unlikely to be able to defend even, quite frankly, South Korea,” he said.
‘Infinitely worse’ than Rumsfeld
Hegseth, who has drawn accusations of war crimes for ordering a succession of strikes on alleged drug-ferrying boats off the coasts of South America, is not the first US defense secretary to come under a harsh spotlight over the conduct of a far-off American war.
Robert McNamara, defense secretary under Lyndon Johnson, became a lightning rod for criticism during the Vietnam war before eventually undergoing a crisis of conscience and being moved to a new role as head of the World Bank.
During George W Bush’s administration, Donald Rumsfeld became the target of fierce criticism after failing as defense secretary to plan adequately for the occupation of Iraq after the initial invasion to topple Saddam Hussein.
But Paul Eaton, a retired major general who trained Iraqi troops after the invasion and is now an adviser to VoteVets – an advocacy group for progressive military veterans – said Rumsfeld’s failings paled in comparison with Hegseth.
“Rumsfeld had ‘next war-itis’, which was a contributing factor to Bush firing him after the shellacking that the Republican party had in the [2006] midterms,” Eaton said. “All this sounds faintly familiar with what we’re going through right now.
“But this is infinitely worse because we had a lot of other very smart people to corral the bad ideas coming out of Rumsfeld. [This time] we’ve had the whole removal of seasoned men and women who have learned things the hard way most of the time in combat.
“If you fail to plan, plan to fail, and what we’re seeing in the Iran war is just evidence. The frustration is, we’re better than this in the uniformed military but we got handed a terrible set of guidance from our civilian leadership.”
Michael O’Hanlon, a defense and strategy expert at the Brookings Institution, argued that the armed forces had enough “bench strength” to survive Hegseth’s purges without imminent collapse, but lamented the loss of certain key individuals who could not be easily replaced.
He singled out Gen Chris Donahue, who recently stepped down from his post as head of the US land command in Europe and Africa.
“We haven’t had a TV talkshow star with a strong partisan and cultural agenda wind up as secretary of defense,” said O’Hanlon. “There may be some echoes of previous secretaries, but the political and culture stuff is Pete Hegseth through and through.”
Hegseth was “not going to wind up leaving a major mark”, O’Hanlon predicted. “He’s going to wind up being known as the guy who fought Trump’s culture wars for him – and maybe failed to help Trump stay out of trouble in the Iran war, depending on how bad that gets.”
This article was amended on 5 September 2026. An earlier version erred in saying that Robert McNamara became head of the International Monetary Fund; he was head (as its president from 1968 to 1981) of the World Bank, the IMF’s sister organization.
