Putin refused to make concessions regarding Ukraine after the CIA chief's visit - WP
Kyiv • UNN
Ratcliffe failed to convince Putin to make concessions regarding Ukraine. After the visit, Russia intensified its strikes on civilian infrastructure.
CIA Director John Ratcliffe failed to persuade Russian dictator vladimir putin to make concessions regarding Ukraine during his recent visit to moscow. putin may instead be preparing for a further escalation of the war. The Washington Post reports this, citing sources, and UNN relays.
Details
"vladimir putin, seeking to take advantage of Ukraine's severely weakened air defense system, is intensifying a bombing campaign that he believes will force Kyiv to concede on some of its key territorial demands, possibly as early as this winter," the publication writes.
It is noted that in the 10 days since the rare and unexpected visit to moscow by CIA Director John Ratcliffe, Russian forces have intensified missile strikes and attacks by jet-powered drones, targeting civilian infrastructure, including energy and water-supply facilities, supermarkets, and food warehouses.
Against the backdrop of the worsening state of the Russian economy and growing public discontent, putin expressed confidence this week in the successful course of the war.
His words, the publication writes, appear to confirm assessments that Ratcliffe's visit not only failed to persuade the head of the kremlin to end the war but may also have strengthened his determination to avoid a ceasefire and continue pressuring Ukraine to cede territory to moscow.
In moscow, Ratcliffe warned his counterparts in the Russian security services that escalating the war would have the opposite effect. According to three people familiar with the course of his talks, he urged a return to negotiations, arguing that russia's position was weak and would continue to deteriorate.
However, after the meetings, Ratcliffe felt that he had delivered the intended message, "but was unable to change the situation." russia perceived the visit as an "attempt to persuade putin to stop, but putin interpreted it as weakness."
"The message was: things are not going very well for you. It is time to talk. Let's sort this out, because in six months or a year things will be even worse for you," the source said.
putin's response to the visit, the publication indicates, appears to have consisted of continuous, round-the-clock airstrikes on Ukraine, as well as his statements at a regional security conference in Kyrgyzstan, where he met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and promised support to Tehran in its war with the United States.
"The escalation of Russian strikes on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities following Ratcliffe's visit may be a certain signal to Washington that russia is continuing its offensive operation and that there is no need to change its position and become more flexible," the source said.
Russia's military advance in Ukraine has virtually stalled, while its budget is becoming increasingly strained: the deficit had grown to $74.4 billion by the end of July, or 2.8% of GDP, significantly exceeding the government's initial forecast of 1.6% for this year.
The advance of Russian troops toward the administrative borders of Donetsk region, a strategically important area of the fortress belt in eastern Ukraine, has been stalling for several months. But the recent rise in oil prices, caused by the resumption of hostilities between Iran and the United States, emboldened putin, the publication writes.
This allowed the Russian leadership to believe that it could still achieve gains regarding Ukraine, even though the chief economist of one of russia's largest state-owned banks publicly warned that russia cannot win a war of attrition against Ukraine as long as Kyiv is supported by the West, a Moscow businessman said.
"There is a view in the kremlin that a few more months of war are not a problem for russia and the Russian economy, but for Ukraine it is a huge problem," the Russian businessman said.

Iranian media report US strike on Iranian oil tanker near Kharg Island
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
09:39:48 UTC
18:39:48 KST

The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed that it targeted three oil tankers and three US-affiliated vessels in the Strait of Hormuz as the cycle of violence spirals after the US military struck three Iranian oil tankers earlier on Saturday, in response to Iran targetting the US navy on Friday.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards (IRGC) said that they had carried out attacks against three oil tankers and three US-linked vessels in the Strait of Hormuz on Saturday evening, following US strikes on Iranian tankers earlier in the day, as the cycle of violence in the key waterway keeps intensifying.
The IRGC said in a statement to the Iranian media that their naval forces "targeted three oil tankers on the unauthorised route of the Strait of Hormuz and three vessels affiliated with the child-killing America in other areas". They also warned other vessels against attempting to use routes that Tehran had not authorised.
A spokesperson for Iran's joint military command warned that strikes against US military ships would be more severe if the US continues to interfere with Iranian shipping, the Iranian state broadcaster reported.
Earlier on Saturday, the US military said that its forces destroyed three Iranian oil tankers after the IRGC fired ballistic missiles towards two navy warships that were patrolling the region, enforcing the US blockade of Iranian ports and thus choking Iran's oil exports which constitutes its economic lifeline.
Iran reportedly used for the first time anti-ship ballistic missiles launched from Isfahan and Kerman towards the US navy vessels in the Strait of Hormuz on Friday, in a significant escalation of Iranian military actions against the US in the latest flare-up of violence. The Iranian media did not provide details as to the targets nor any damage inflicted in the alleged attacks.
Former head of Israel’s military intelligence research department Danny Citrinowicz said in a post on X that "yesterday attack suggests that another threshold in Iranian decision-making has been crossed," as "it indicates that Tehran is becoming increasingly willing to accept risks it previously sought to avoid, including directly threatening some of the most important U.S. military assets in the region."
US Central Command (CENTCOM) said in a statement that a US aircraft carrier and a destroyer ship had "successfully evaded multiple unprovoked Iranian attacks" and that no American personnel were hurt.
"Following Iran’s failed attacks, CENTCOM permanently disabled the IRGC crude oil carriers M/T Downy off the coast of Kharg Island and M/T Stark 1 near Jask," the statement continued.
"American forces also completely destroyed the unladen crude oil carrier M/T Kylo (also known as the 'Noxen') in the Gulf of Oman, striking the vessel in multiple critical locations to render it inoperable after the crew was directed to abandon ship," it added.
Admiral Brad Cooper, the commander of CENTCOM, said the message to the IRGC was "clear": "If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost —taking out three of yours."
“We will not hesitate to defend American forces, and if necessary, destroy Iran’s limited and exposed oil fleet," he added.
The US statement called the tankers part of a shadow network helping to fund Iran's Revolutionary Guard and its armed proxies in the region.
Iran’s Foreign Ministry called the attacks a war crime, and said that the consequences for continued US aggression, including “economic warfare,” would rest with Washington and its allies.
The latest cycle of violence resumed last Sunday after US forces carried out strikes on Iranian rocket launchers in the Strait of Hormuz with CENTCOM saying it had taken "limited, precise action" against IRGC minelaying forces, which it said had posed an "imminent threat" in the waterway.
The IRGC confirmed strikes had hit Larak Island and vowed to retaliate, later launching its own attacks on US bases in Jordan, Kuwait and Bahrain.
CENTCOM forces carried out another wave of strikes on Tuesday, targeting what it said were IRGC air defence sites, mine laying capabilities, radar systems, maritime assets and facilities, and communications sites.
It said the move was in response to "recent attempted attacks by the IRGC against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz."
The US military has been helping to guide ships through the strait as Tehran asserts control and targets some vessels, but overall traffic remains low.

Rescuers pull Chinese national alive from Nepal tunnel after 10 days
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
09:39:48 UTC
18:39:48 KST

Rescuers in Nepal pulled a Chinese national alive on Saturday from a tunnel buried by debris, as emergency response teams dug with new vigour in the search for missing people 10 days after catastrophic flooding.
A joint rescue team comprising personnel from the Nepal Army and foreign experts rescued the man from 225 metres (738 feet) inside the tunnel of the Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project in Rasuwa district, a military statement said.
"His health is currently being assessed and further search and rescue operations are continuing," the army said.
The latest rescue brings to three the number of workers pulled alive from the Trishuli hydropower project.
Two Nepali workers were rescued from a tunnel at the Trishuli 3A hydropower plant on Friday.
About 900 workers remain missing from 12 hydropower projects across Nepal, with roughly 500 believed to be trapped in tunnels, according to authorities.
About 850 of those missing are foreigners, according to official figures from Nepal and China.
The disaster struck on August 26 when a glacier on Nepal’s Mount Langtang Lirung fractured at an altitude of about 5,200 metres (17,060 feet), killing at least 1,300 people.
The fracture triggered an ice-and-rock avalanche that developed into a massive debris flow and swept through valleys along the border.
Floodwaters and mudslides devastated Nepal’s Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and Kavre districts, as well as the Kathmandu Valley.

UN backs effort to depict Africa correctly on maps despite US opposition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
09:35:55 UTC
18:35:55 KST

Mercator, the world’s most commonly used map projection, was devised by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator in 1569 to help sailors navigate using compass bearings. | iStock
The United Nations on Friday largely endorsed a resolution to promote maps that reflect the true scale of continents after an African-led campaign to move away from the ubiquitous 16th-century Mercator projection.
The United States was the only country to vote against the initiative, denouncing it as part of a “much larger and more radical ideological project” and urging “countries to instill common sense to this body.” Estonia, Georgia, Lithuania, Moldova, Serbia and Ukraine abstained.
Mercator, the world’s most commonly used map projection, was devised by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator in 1569 to help sailors navigate using compass bearings.
Advertisement
But it distorts size, making landmasses appear larger the further they are from the Equator. As a result, Africa looks far smaller than it really is compared with countries in the Northern Hemisphere.
“A fair map does not change the geography of the world,” said Robert Dussey, Togo’s foreign minister and lead negotiator on behalf of the African group, ahead of the U.N. vote.
The non-binding resolution stated that “correcting cartographic distortions of continental sizes constitutes an act of cognitive justice and memorial reparation,” and calls on countries to promote the so-called Equal Earth projection, including at schools.
“This decision is about much more than cartography. It is about justice, dignity, equality and the way we represent our world,” Dussey rejoiced on X after its adoption.

Beskrestnov: SBU building attacked by one of 2 jet-powered Shaheds flying from Donetsk region
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05

Advisor to the President of Ukraine Serhiy "Flash" Beskrestnov reported that the building of the Security Service of Ukraine was attacked on Saturday by a Russian "Geran-4" jet-powered drone that was tracked flying from occupied areas of Donetsk region, thereby refuting false information circulating online alleging the attack was staged using a small drone.
"All systems recorded the flight path of this jet 'Shahed' from the Donetsk direction toward Kyiv at an altitude of over 7 kilometers. Thus, we understand who launched the UAV and from where. We have already examined the debris and established that it belongs to 'Geran-4', including most of the components. That is, we understand exactly what and in what configuration arrived here," Beskrestnov wrote on Facebook on Saturday.
He also reported that the occupiers launched two jet drones from the temporarily occupied territory that flew in pair. "During this special operation against the SBU, two jet UAVs were flying toward Kyiv as a pair. One made it," Beskrestnov informed.
A day earlier, when the strike occurred, he had also stated that the drone attack on the SBU building was a specifically planned enemy operation.
"My personal opinion: the 'Shahed' was controlled and guided online via a MESH radio repeater with Internet access, which a Russian agent switched on nearby (up to 5 km away) for a short period during the attack. Such a repeater is about half the size of a school backpack. There were no other 'Shaheds' in the air at that time. Therefore, chain-of-command control from the Russian Federation would be impossible," Beskrestnov wrote on Facebook on Friday.
As reported, on Friday afternoon, a Russian drone hit the central SBU building on Volodymyrska Street in Kyiv across from St. Sophia Cathedral. According to President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the drone "was directed straight at the office of the head of the SBU in this building." The enemy attack injured at least 15 people and damaged an architectural monument of national significance—the Consistory Building on the territory of the "Sophia of Kyiv" National Sanctuary.
Later, Zelenskyy reported the preparation of active retaliatory measures against Russian strikes and stated that Ukraine had already determined the geography for its response to the Russian attacks. "The timing will be chosen to deliver results," he said.

No registration number, no attendance: NMC warns medical colleges
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
09:31:05 UTC
18:31:05 KST

Medical colleges have one month to update faculty registration numbers on the attendance system. Failure to comply will result in blocked daily attendance for specified teaching staff. The National Medical Commission issued this warning after finding blank registration fields. Colleges must review and update all medical faculty and resident profiles accurately. Non-medical faculty will have 'NA' entered in the registration number field.
NEW DELHI: Medical colleges have one month to update the National Medical Register (NMR) or State Medical Register (SMR) numbers of their faculty and specified teaching staff on the Aadhaar Enabled Biometric Attendance System (AEBAS), failing which their daily attendance could be blocked and automatically rejected.The National Medical Commission (NMC) has warned that this may adversely impact the compliance status of the medical college during NMC assessments and inspections.The warning was issued on September 3 after the NMC found that nodal officers at several medical colleges had left the NMR or SMR registration-number field blank while registering faculty on the attendance portal.The commission has directed colleges to review and update the profiles of all medical faculty, Junior Residents, Senior Residents, tutors and demonstrators with correct and valid NMR or SMR numbers.For non-medical faculty and tutors or demonstrators holding Master of Science (MSc) and Doctor of Philosophy (PhD) qualifications, colleges have been instructed to enter “NA” in the registration-number field.The NMC has made it clear that leaving the registration-number field blank will not be permitted.
The directive effectively makes faculty registration details part of the attendance compliance process, rather than a routine profile correction.
The memorandum has been sent to deans, principals and directors of all medical colleges and institutions, besides state and Union Territory medical education departments, directorates of medical education and State Medical Councils.The move is under the provisions of the Undergraduate and Postgraduate Minimum Standard Requirements and Medical Assessment and Rating Board regulations, which provide for periodic, transparent and digitally verified assessment of teaching staff in medical institutions.
Anuja Jaiswal is a Senior Assistant Editor at The Times of India, with an impressive 18-year career in narrative journalism. She specializes in health and heritage reporting, expertly simplifying complex health information to make it engaging and understandable for readers. Her deep dives into heritage topics are well-researched, resulting in captivating narratives that resonate with her audience. Over the years, she has worked in Chandigarh, Chhattisgarh and West UP, gaining diverse on-ground experience that shapes her storytelling.

14 fall ill after dining at Eaton HK hotel restaurant
Preliminary investigations revealed that all five clusters are epidemiologically linked, Centre for Health Protection says
Hong Kong health authorities have detected seven additional suspected food poisoning cases linked to a hotel restaurant in Yau Ma Tei, raising the total number of affected diners to 14.
The Centre for Health Protection said on Saturday it had identified three additional food poisoning clusters involving The Astor restaurant at Eaton HK, after initially announcing two clusters on September 3.
“The centre’s preliminary investigations revealed that all five clusters are epidemiologically linked,” it said, adding that 14 people had been affected.
It said that officers from the centre and the Food and Environmental Hygiene Department jointly conducted an on-site investigation and required management to implement control measures.
“All affected people had patronised the buffet there before the operation,” it said.
The latest clusters involve one man and five women who consumed buffet meals at the restaurant between August 29 and 31. Between 16 and 40 hours later, all six developed symptoms including nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain and fever.

Argentina Reiterates Its Claims to the Falkland Islands and Announces New Naval Base
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
09:29:39 UTC
18:29:39 KST

The President of Argentina reiterated his country’s claims to the Falkland Islands and announced sanctions against companies operating on the islands without Argentina’s permission.
Javier Milei also announced the establishment of a naval base in Tierra del Fuego, which is located near the islands.
He also announced sanctions against companies planning to drill for oil off the coast of the Falkland Islands without permission from the Argentine government.
“We will use all diplomatic, economic, and legal tools to deter state and non-state actors who encroach on our sovereignty,” Milei stated in a televised address to the nation.
The basis for the measures he announced was the Sea Lion project, which is being promoted by companies from the United Kingdom and Israel.
The project involves oil extraction on the continental shelf approximately 220 kilometers north of the disputed archipelago.
British Defence Minister Wes Streeting criticized the Argentine president’s statements.
“The Falkland Islands belong to the United Kingdom because their residents chose to be British,” he noted, referring to the 2013 referendum in which a majority of the islands’ residents voted to retain their status as a British Overseas Territory.
Milei’s statement came after U.S. President Donald Trump cast doubt on the previous support for the United Kingdom in the dispute over the Falkland Islands.
The Falkland Islands, known in Argentina as the Malvinas, have been under British administration since 1833.
In 1982, hostilities broke out between the two countries over the archipelago, resulting in the deaths of about 900 people.
In 2013, the islands’ residents voted in a referendum to retain their British status. However, Argentina does not recognize the results of this referendum.

Russia shells Kametstal in Kamianske, killing 5 workers, plant shuts down – MP
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
12:28:28 EEST
18:28:28 KST

As a result of an overnight strike by Russian occupiers on the Kametstal plant of the Metinvest mining and metallurgical group, established on the facilities of the Dnipro Metallurgical Plant in the city of Kamianske, Dnipropetrovsk region, five workers were killed, and the enterprise has suspended its production process.
"Tonight they (Russian occupiers) struck Kamianske with five ballistic missiles. Kametstal was hit—an enterprise that continued to operate despite everything. Now it has stopped. The Russians tried once again to destroy what generations of Ukrainian metallurgists built. The death of five workers has already been confirmed. And after this, someone will still speak of a 'ceasefire'? Once again, such statements from the Kremlin turned out to be empty talk," Member of Parliament and member of the parliamentary subcommittee on industrial policy of the Economic Development Committee Musa Mahomedov wrote on his Facebook page.
According to him, Ukrainian metallurgy holds on not because of promises and words, but because of the people who report for work even under fire. "Buildings can be restored. Equipment can be replaced. Production can be restarted. People cannot be brought back. That is precisely what everyone talking today about 'peace' and 'ceasefire' should remember," the MP concluded.
According to local media reports, in the early hours of September 5, Russian occupational forces struck the Kametstal industrial enterprise in Kamianske.
Four dead and five injured were initially reported.
According to Mayor Andriy Bilousov, three of the injured are in the hospital under medical supervision, including a 30-year-old woman in intensive care. A day of mourning has been declared in Kamianske for the victims.
"Deepest condolences to the families and loved ones of the deceased; the families will be provided with the necessary assistance. Rescue units, medics, law enforcement officers, and relevant services were involved in liquidating the consequences of the enemy attack. Thank you to everyone who worked throughout the night and helped people," the sobitie.com.ua news outlet quoted the mayor as saying.
According to sources of the publication, operations at Kametstal are currently suspended, with two blast furnaces stopped. The fire has been extinguished, and relevant services are working at the site.
As previously reported by Head of the Dnipropetrovsk Regional Council Mykola Lukashuk, a day of mourning was declared in the city of Kamianske, Dnipropetrovsk region, on Saturday for those killed as a result of the overnight strike by Russian occupiers on the industrial enterprise in the city. "Four people were killed as a result of the overnight Russian attack on the industrial enterprise. Sincere condolences to the families of all those who died. Wishing a speedy recovery to the injured," Lukashuk wrote on Telegram.
According to him, Dnipropetrovsk Regional Council has provided for financial assistance to the families of civilians killed in Russian attacks. Under the relevant program, families can receive a one-time payment of UAH 300,000 per family.
Kametstal was established on the basis of PJSC Dniprovsky Coke Plant (DKHZ) and PJSC Dniprovsky Metallurgical Plant (DMK). It is part of the Metinvest Group.
Metinvest is a vertically integrated group of steel and mining companies. Its enterprises are located in Ukraine—in Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhia, and Dnipropetrovsk regions—as well as in European countries. The main shareholders of the holding are SCM Group (71.24%) and Smart-Holding (23.76%). LLC Metinvest Holding is the management company of the Metinvest Group.

We are sailing through rough waters but India and the EU have chosen partnership. We have concluded the mother of all deals. It is an expression of mutual respect. Our cooperation is directed towards international order. The FTA arrives at a critical moment. To make trading partnerships more predictable. If every community in Belgium is like the Indian community I would be a happy Prime Minister,” De Wever said.Goyal said the India EU FTA was in the making for 25 years. “It is a win-win agreement, it will open opportunities for farmers, start ups, women entrepreneurs, it has something for everyone. It’s been deftly negotiated protecting sensitive sectors on both sides. It offers huge potential for both sides," Goyal said.“66% India’s data center capacity is in Maharashtra. We want Belgium to be part of Maharashtra’s journey to a trillion dollar economy. We have bilateral trade of 13.8 billion USD. But it understates the potential. Maharashtra would like to contribute and be the principal engine of this growth story. I want to make a direct invitation. If Belgium companies are looking at India for investment after the FTA, look and come to Maharashtra. We have a manufacturing ecosystem. This should become a template for Belgium - Maharashtra partnerships,” Fadnavis said.Fadnavis said Maharashtra would like to be the first state to translate the FTA into action. “Belgium Maharashtra projects must be fast tracked. If Belgium companies identifies - project, we will dedicate a team and work with Belgium to make it happen. Come to Maharashtra and from Maharashtra serve India and the world.
Maharashtra is volunteering to convert strategic direction into action,” Fadnavis said.De Wever is on an official visit to India from 2-4 September. TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Some Line users risk losing access to their accounts, purchases, stickers, coins, and chat histories at the end of the year unless they add a phone number.
The rule applies to accounts linked only to Facebook that do not have a phone number set, with deletion scheduled after 11:59 p.m. on Dec. 31, per TVBS.
Users can check their status in the Line app by opening “Home,” tapping “Settings,” selecting “My Account,” and looking at the “Phone Number” field. A blank field means no number has been linked, and the setup can be completed entirely inside the app without using a webpage, per Line’s notice.
The company warned that phone numbers cannot be shared across Line accounts, while moving a number to another account can cause the original account to stop working.
Similar restrictions apply to email addresses and Apple and Google accounts. Reusing those credentials on a new Line account will remove their links from the original account and may render that account invalid, according to the notice.
Accounts should have an email address and password set, while at least one Apple or Google account should be connected. Both Apple and Google accounts can be added.
The phone-number requirement is intended to reduce dummy accounts and fraud risks and make the service safer. Users are also encouraged to help older relatives or friends who are less familiar with smartphone settings check their accounts.

As a result of the Taiwan-US Agreement on Reciprocal Trade signed in February, Taiwan will have to remove its import limits on cars from the US. With safety test standards differing from country to country, Taiwan has to set up a new post-market surveillance system including a safety test lab, per CNA.
The import quotas will be removed for cars conforming to the US Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards and to US emission regulations, the report said.

Hualien Physical Education High School eyes third dragon boat world title
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
09:19:52 UTC
18:19:52 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Hualien Physical Education High School captured its second gold medal at the 15th International Dragon Boat Federation Club Crew World Championships on Friday, winning the Premier Open 10-person small boat 200-meter final in 46.56 seconds at Liyu Lake in Hualien County.
The crew, which had topped the preliminary round in 46.54, held off Germany by 0.84 seconds in a rain-affected session that tested both technique and nerve on the choppy waters, Liberty Times reported. Team captain Lin Sheng-ju (林聖儒), a 2018 Asian Games dragon boat gold medalist, reportedly said the squad now hopes to challenge for a third title in the 2,000-meter race before the championships end Sunday.
The team’s first gold came on Wednesday in the Premier Open 10-person small boat 500 m. It finished in 2 minutes, 5.03 seconds to give the nation its first medal of the meet.
The Aug. 29–Sept. 6 event marks the first time the International Dragon Boat Federation’s (IDBF) flagship club world championship has been held in Taiwan, drawing teams from 21 countries to Hualien County.
Races feature 20-person standard boats and 10-person small boats over 200-m, 500-m and 2,000-m formats. There are open, women’s, mixed, and age-group divisions, plus inclusive categories such as Paralympic and cancer survivor crews.
Dragon boat racing is a team paddling sport in which crews of 10 to 20 athletes propel long, narrow boats decorated with dragon heads and tails. A drummer at the bow sets the pace with a drumbeat while a steersperson at the stern controls direction.
The sport traces its roots to Chinese rituals honoring the poet Qu Yuan, who is said to have drowned himself in Hunan Province’s Miluo River more than 2,000 years ago. According to legend, villagers raced out in boats to save him or retrieve his body, beating drums and splashing paddles to scare away fish.
This tradition evolved into the modern-day Dragon Boat Festival held on the fifth day of the fifth lunar month in Taiwan, which falls in May or June.
Modern competitive dragon boating emerged in the late 20th century as Hong Kong and other Asian cities standardized boat specifications and race formats, leading to the formation of the IDBF in 1991.

Sweden confirms 458 Britons deported or forcibly removed since Brexit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
09:16:01 UTC
18:16:01 KST

Sweden has confirmed 458 British citizens have been deported or forcibly removed by police since Brexit.
It is the first time the scale of the deportations of citizens who failed to secure residency in Sweden post-Brexit has been made public and comes amid mounting criticism of a cruel and hardline approach to Britons who had chosen to make the country their home before Brexit.
Some have been told to go after more than 25 years in the country and even vulnerable elderly people with dementia have been affected. One man was deported even though he had lived in the country since he was 10 years old.
Susanna Fonsell, a unit manager and legal expert at the Swedish Migration Agency, told Sverige Radio: “A rejected application does not necessarily result in deportation… and according to the agency statistics, the agency’s rejections of an application for resident status has been accomplished by a deportation decision in only approximately 400 cases,” she told Sweden Radio.
The Migrationsverket, the Swedish government agency responsible for migration, confirmed to the Guardian that 458 British citizens had been deported since Brexit. “According to the agency’s statistics, the Swedish Migration Agency’s rejection of an application for residence status has been accompanied by a deportation decision in only 458 cases,” a spokesperson said.
David Milstead, who heads up the 9,000-strong activist group Brits in Sweden, said it was important for Sweden to release full and transparent figures in relation to removals and deportations and their circumstances.
“We need to understand exactly what the 458 represents. Does it capture people who gave up and left when they realised their withdrawal agreement application was unlikely to succeed? Does it include people who were refused withdrawal agreement status, subsequently obtained a permit under national law and were only later ordered to leave?
“It certainly does not capture people who are currently managing to remain in Sweden on temporary permits, with little certainty about their long-term future.”
He said the figures illustrated a “broader problem” in that the data was issued piecemeal and sometimes in an opaque manner. “We still do not have basic published figures showing how many people submitted a missed-deadline application and the fraction of these which succeeded,” he said.
The last available data shows that there were 14,233 applications for post Brexit residency, which included family members joining British citizens after the deadline by 2024. Of those, just under 4,000 were rejected, a refusal rate three times higher than any other member state and considerably higher than the EU average of between 3% and 4%, according to Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) analysis.
Deportations are still happening. This week, the Swedish wife of a former business director from Cambridge told how her husband was detained in Stockholm on Tuesday ahead of a forced removal.
She said they had been fighting to overturn the decision by the migration authorities for five years and felt that they had been “hunted”.
Earlier this week, the Guardian revealed a 34-year-old British man, John Sellers, who had lived in Sweden since he was 10, had been deported, separating him from his wife, Caroline, in Gothenburg, who said people needed to know how Brexit had “crushed families”.
Another woman, 78-year-old British widow Joyce Thomas, has been told to remove herself from the country before next Wednesday. Friends are trying to get an injunction and have appealed to the European Commission for help.
If she fails to comply, not only will she face a forced deportation, but the court of appeal has told her she could face a “re-entry ban” and be “registered on a watchlist” preventing potential entry into a Schengen country, which includes Sweden “as long as the re-entry ban remains in effect”.
The Swedish Migration Agency told the Guardian it had “no indication that Sweden has in any way interpreted the withdrawal agreement in an extreme manner or differently from other member states. The Swedish Migration Agency has applied applicable law, and there has been an opportunity to appeal rejection decisions.”
Late applications for post-Brexit residency are allowed under the Brexit withdrawal agreement, both in the EU and the UK, but applicants have to show “reasonable grounds” for missing the deadline.
The FCDO has said that “in practice” late applicants in Sweden “are not likely to have their reasonable grounds accepted”.
Earlier this week, Sweden’s migration minister, Johan Forssell, said his government had followed the rules but that it was willing to look into the matter. “The relationship with the UK is very important to Sweden and the government will continue to safeguard the correct implementation of the withdrawal agreement. As part of this, the government is investigating whether further measures can be taken to facilitate the process in the future,” he said.
A spokesperson for the FCDO said: “We continue to raise this with the Swedish authorities and welcome their statement that they will look at this issue. We are ready to support them in doing so.”
Niels Paarup-Petersen, the migration spokesperson for Sweden’s opposition Centre party, said the government needed to go much further. He pledged to bring in new laws if his party won power at the next general election to allow British to reapply for post-Brexit residence, saying “a touch of humanity” was needed.

Oil and politics: What Trump’s ‘historic’ deal means for Venezuela
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
09:11:58 UTC
18:11:58 KST

Oil and politics: What Trump’s ‘historic’ deal means for Venezuela
Venezuelans are hoping for free and fair elections, but the US may prioritise oil production.
Since the last century, Venezuelan politics has been closely linked to the management of the country’s oil industry.
The debate for policymakers has centred on whether to liberalise or nationalise the sector, with the latter being the preferred option for the past 27 years.
Over time, a kind of “resource nationalism” has been instilled in the national psyche by the current governing party to consolidate its power and advance the interests of a regime that has used oil revenues to expand its political influence across the region, particularly in the Caribbean.
This all came to an abrupt end on January 3, 2026, when United States special forces abducted President Nicolas Maduro in a lightning military operation in Caracas and whisked him back to the US to stand trial on guns-and-drugs charges.
Since then, Maduro’s deputy and now interim President Delcy Rodriguez has aimed for privatisation of the oil industry in favour of US government interests.
Milestones reached during the past eight months include reforming the General Hydrocarbons Law, liberalising energy power plants and granting permissions, with prior US authorisation, to US and foreign oil companies – excluding any from China, Russia, Iran or North Korea – to participate in tapping Venezuela’s vast oil wealth in oil fields across the country.
The most significant development happened last week, when the two countries announced they had reached a deal granting US companies access to 65 billion barrels of crude oil reserves over the next 100 years.
Described by President Trump as the “biggest oil deal in world history”, this agreement not only marks a turning point in the governing party’s resource nationalism policy but also represents the culmination of the US government’s efforts to reinforce its dominance strategy and seize control of Venezuela’s oil and gas resources.
Furthermore, this deal is set to play a pivotal role in the Venezuelan political transition.
The US has developed a three-phase plan to promote stabilisation, recovery, and political reform since it removed Maduro from power. Now, all the parties involved must establish a roadmap to implement the deal and, at the same time, ensure that presidential elections are held in the country.
The signing of this oil deal is the starting gun for this complex process.
A win for the US – not so much for Venezuela
The precise terms of this oil deal have been the subject of discussion in specialised media outlets across the Western Hemisphere and beyond this week. Due to conflicting and sometimes contradictory accounts by US and Venezuelan authorities, the final conditions of the oil deal remain uncertain.
The Trump Administration has provided the most detailed information, confirming the transfer of 65 billion barrels of oil – 20 percent of Venezuela’s proven 303 billion barrels of oil – to US control for 100 years.
These reserves are distributed across 17 major oil fields, some of which had previously been granted to Chinese and Russian companies in concession. The fields will be operated by a private company called North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP), in association with the US Department of Defense’s Office of Strategic Capital (OSC). This entity will acquire a 35 percent stake in NABEP free of charge. Trump has referred to the latter to argue that this association will not charge American taxpayers or use their money.
Additionally, information from the US government suggests that the US has also secured the right to buy 20 percent of the current and future crude oil production from NABEP-controlled fields at production cost. That means production will not be subject to Venezuelan taxation, reducing the amount of revenue Venezuela will receive.
The OSC has the right of first refusal to buy the remaining 80 percent of production, or veto power if this is deemed necessary for reasons of national security. These clauses prioritise ensuring the US has access to Venezuelan oil reserves and meeting the requirements of the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR). These measures are undoubtedly intended to help the US achieve its national energy security goals.
The White House has also confirmed that NABEP is controlled by American citizens, which is a prerogative reserved by the US government to prevent foreign companies from managing it. In practice, this means that the US will control the operations, with NABEP merely acting as a vehicle for this control.
Another point relates to the royalties and taxes that NABEP must pay to the Venezuelan authorities. Top officials from both countries say the exploitation of the 17 oil fields will generate approximately $200bn dollars in tax payments following an expected $100bn investment. It is expected that this money will be managed by the current interim authorities to address the challenges of reconstruction after a long period of economic crisis.
However, there is uncertainty about the methodology used to determine this amount because the discretionary clauses granted to the US government make it impossible to calculate the exact amount of tax that will be paid.
Furthermore, the Venezuelan government has announced that the concession granted to NABEP will only be valid for 25 years – a figure far lower than the 100 years claimed by the US government. Notably, this type of contract has not featured in Venezuelan hydrocarbon legislation for half a century.
Too many obstacles?
Although the bilateral agreement could be a good way to attract investment to the Venezuelan oil sector, there remain multiple internal and external political, legal and economic obstacles to its successful implementation.
First, President Trump has so far failed to encourage major US oil companies, except Chevron, to enter the Venezuelan oil industry. This is because Venezuela lacks trustworthy and legitimate institutions, implying the absence of a stable legal framework for long-term production planning.
Setting aside the major oil companies such as Exxon Mobil, Chevron and ConocoPhillips, the only companies that appear as viable potential partners in the 17 oil fields seem to be small independent operators. This could lead to operational setbacks because the majors are the only ones with enough financial and technological clout to carry out long-term, large-scale investments in such ambitious projects.
The oil majors’ lack of confidence is also down to the absence of a legitimate government and the governing party’s continued dominance over the country’s main powers.
One of the biggest red flags surrounding the oil deal is the possibility that a government formed through free elections could in the future denounce or refuse to recognise its legitimacy, on the basis that these legal agreements are unconstitutional. Furthermore, the current governing party in Venezuela could potentially reject the terms of this deal if they feel they have sufficient strength to challenge US dominance again.
In addition to these concerns about the rule of law, it seems there is another relevant issue: The involvement of Alejandro Betancourt as president of NABEP’s operations.
Despite the Department of State’s attempts to clean up his past, Betancourt has an uncertain record due to multiple corruption cases brought against him in the past, including bribery, cost overruns and influence peddling in electricity projects overseen by the state-owned company PDVSA.
It is also important to note that a real, feasible increase in Venezuelan oil production will probably take several years, even in the best-case scenario. This contradicts the optimistic rhetoric used by senior Trump administration officials, who argue that this deal would increase local production almost immediately. Advancing at such a pace would require substantial investment, much of which is not currently guaranteed.
A ‘hemispheric’ strategy
Approval of the oil deal is part of a broader “hemispheric” strategy adopted by the US government, which wants to regain lost influence in the region. This was outlined in the Trump administration’s 2025 National Security Strategy and subsequent foreign policy documents, which designate the Western Hemisphere as a strategic zone of influence for the US. In this context, the US government views Venezuela as a strategic geopolitical pivot due to its energy resources – particularly its substantial proven oil reserves – and its proximity to its territory.
Based on this, the US government considers controlling the Venezuelan oil reserves to be a matter of national security that is closely linked to maintaining its SPR. This stance is particularly pertinent given that Washington is preventing countries it considers to be its enemies, such as China, Russia, Iran and North Korea, from participating in the Venezuelan oil industry.
It is also worth noting that the US government is not hesitating to use its existing national tools to secure its hegemony across the Americas. Indeed, the US is taking economic measures, as well as military action and exerting political influence, to discourage other countries from doing business with its declared enemies, including China, and even more so from allowing them to participate in critical infrastructure projects across the region.
Venezuela’s political transition
Since its removal of Maduro from power in January, the US government has begun a three-phase plan to promote stabilisation, economic recovery and political reform in Venezuela. The ultimate objective is to hold free and democratic elections, which would be the first step towards legitimising the country’s authorities and reintegrating it into the international arena.
Before this week’s oil deal was announced, various opposition leaders had been devising strategies to participate in the eventual presidential elections. These actors believed that the electoral process was the first step in recovering sovereignty and establishing a long-term partnership with the US based on oil business.
However, the plan of Trump’s administration has run in a different direction and at its own pace. For Washington, securing access to and control of the Venezuelan oil reservoirs was the top priority before promoting any democratic transition in the country.
Although top US officials, including Secretary of State Marco Rubio, have recently stated that the oil deal is limited to its own three-phase plan, the reality is that the US has made it clear that it will not allow any future government to change its terms and conditions.
Given the current situation, almost everyone involved in Venezuelan politics supports an oil deal that prioritises the participation of the US. However, opposition leaders such as Maria Corina Machado, currently the country’s most popular politician, are concerned about Delcy Rodriguez, an interim leader who lacks legitimacy, signing this deal.
Although Machado has not guaranteed that a future democratic government would refuse to recognise the deal’s terms, her position could spur the idea that Trump is motivated to keep Delcy Rodriguez in power rather than promote free elections to ensure the deal’s correct implementation.
These concerns have arisen in recent days after the US president publicly stated that Venezuela is not prepared for elections in the short term.
Ultimately, the effectiveness of the oil deal and its impact on the political transition in Venezuela will depend on the alignment of various internal and external political, legal, and economic factors.
For now, the US government holds the final say in determining the country’s future, to the detriment of its population, which has ultimately lost its right to self-determination.

UK Halts Large Military Exercises as Funding Shortfalls Hit British Armed Forces
The British Armed Forces have suspended military exercises involving 90 or more personnel due to budget constraints at the Ministry of Defense, according to a report by The Sun.
Units were instructed to stop collective training with immediate effect unless they are getting ready for deployment on active operations, leaving many troops with little to do.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Under the new directives, service members will continue to train in small squads to maintain basic skills, including vehicle operation, physical fitness, weapons handling, and drone usage.
However, company-level exercises, which usually involve 90 to 120 soldiers, as well as battle group training involving several hundred troops, have been significantly reduced.
The cutbacks affect major events, including a six-week exercise with tanks and attack helicopters scheduled to begin next week in Wales. Regular preparation will only continue for personnel preparing to deploy abroad or take up operational duty within the UK.
The Royal Navy and Royal Air Force have also been instructed to scale back training activities to save funds, though the impact on their operations is expected to be less severe.
According to The Sun, the cuts stem from a shortage of funds for current operating expenses this year. Although the Defense Investment Plan allocates an extra 2 billion pounds for training, those funds will not become available until 2027.
The Ministry of Defense acknowledged that the military must “determine priorities,” while noting that command staff exercises will continue so top leadership can practice managing large-scale operations.
The Chief of the Defense Staff, Rich Knighton, previously warned in late June 2026 that the UK Armed Forces were facing a financial deficit that could force military leaders to scale back training and operational activities.
“If you look back 20 years, the ratio between expenditure on current needs and capital expenditure was roughly 80/20. Today, it stands at roughly 60/40 — 60% for current activities and resources, and 40% for capital expenditure. Under current forecasts, by 2030 this ratio will be 50/50,” Knighton stated at the time.
One of the main reasons for this funding imbalance is the UK's large and costly rearmament programs.
These initiatives include building Dreadnought-class nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarines, developing a sixth-generation fighter jet under the GCAP program, constructing Type 26 frigates, and managing the troubled Ajax armored vehicle program.
Previously, the British Ministry of Defense shaped its new strategy around Ukraine's playbook of low-cost systems defeating high-value targets, with innovation cycles measured in weeks rather than years.
The plan redirected resources away from up to eight traditional warships, including Type 83 guided missile destroyers and Type 32 frigates, and instead committed approximately $6.7 billion to a broad drone transformation. Britain allocated funds to establish Europe's largest drone testing center alongside a dedicated task force, aiming to continuously scale up production and adapt to changing battlefield technologies.

Source: Lutsk City Council
Details: Nataliia was killed in action in Kharkiv Oblast on 1 September.
Nataliia was born in Donetsk, where she spent her childhood and youth. She studied at the Donetsk Institute of the Interregional Academy of Personnel Management. She later worked at the Tochmash plant, which manufactures drive equipment.
Following the beginning of Russia's war in Ukraine's east, Nataliia and her family were forced to relocate. The family initially settled in Mariupol and later lived in Bilytske and Dobropillia in Donetsk Oblast. They eventually found a new home in Yavoriv, Lviv Oblast.
In 2017, Natalia joined a border guard unit to defend Ukraine. After nine years of service, she was killed while carrying out a combat mission.
She is survived by her daughter, husband and mother.
"There was no better person for me. She was very decent and responsible, kind, sincere, caring and loving. She always worried about her family and tried to help and support them.
She was not just my wife – she was the person closest to me, my source of strength. It is hard to comprehend that she is no longer with us," Volodymyr, Natalia's husband, said.
Nataliia will be buried in Zakarpattia Oblast, where her mother lives.

Ukraine war: how escalating attacks are upending lives in Kyiv
Russia is now using more jet-powered drones, which are faster and harder for Ukraine to intercept than propeller-powered models
Commuters stranded; children rushed underground in the middle of the school day; festivals cancelled; walks punctuated by booming air defences. Near-constant drone attacks are the stark new reality in Kyiv, and daily life is likely to get harder.
Kyiv has survived many traumas since Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Despite the initial shock of war and the advent of attack drones and ballistic missiles, residents adapted and managed to impose a semblance of normality.
But as a fifth full winter of war approaches, that is becoming harder to maintain.
Over the summer, Moscow began sending swarms of high-speed, jet-propelled drones that are more destructive and harder to shoot down than older propeller-powered models.
For the last 10 days, air attacks have been around-the-clock rather than mainly at night, puncturing Ukrainians’ sense that their country’s own long-range drone campaign against Russia was swinging the war back in their favour.

A possible referral of Iran to the UN Security Council shifts responsibility to a higher authority that can enact further legally binding measures, including sanctions or asset freezes.

‘What would it take for US to hold Israel accountable?’: Two years since Aysenur Ezgi Eygi’s murder
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
09:05:39 UTC
18:05:39 KST

September 6 marks two years since Aysenur Ezgi Eygi, a 26-year-old Turkish-American activist, was shot in the head by an Israeli sniper while observing a peaceful protest against illegal settlement expansion in Beita in the occupied West Bank.
Since then, her family has buried her in Aydin, Türkiye, found ways to keep her memory alive, and spoken to dozens of lawmakers in an effort to hold those responsible to account.
They are still calling for the same thing: an independent investigation into her killing, the identification of the soldier who shot her, and accountability for what happened.
The Israeli military has acknowledged that one of its soldiers fired in the area where Eygi was standing. But its preliminary investigation concluded that she was "highly likely" hit "indirectly and unintentionally" while troops were responding to a "violent riot."
No soldier has been charged.
For Eygi's family, that explanation has never amounted to accountability. Two years later, her husband Hamid Ali says the frustration has only deepened.
“We still don't have any results of any investigation, either from the Israeli government or otherwise,” Ali tells TRT World.
“The US government has not been open to investigating, and hasn't communicated with us about any updates on her case or any willingness to investigate it or hold Israel accountable for killing one of its own citizens,” he explains.
Yet Ali says the past year has brought something else too: a sense that Eygi has not been forgotten.
“We've seen so much support from our community in Seattle and across the US, and it's really meaningful to see that, still, even after two years,” he says.
Washington has yet to investigate
Washington's position has remained largely unchanged across administrations.
Then-US President Joe Biden described Eygi's death as a "tragic error".
In December 2024, then-Secretary of State Antony Blinken told the family that Washington was waiting for Israel to complete its investigation.
That position hasn’t changed under the Trump administration, either.
Brad Parker of the Centre for Constitutional Rights, part of the family's legal team, says no US federal agency, including the Department of Justice or the FBI, has opened an investigation into Eygi's killing, despite their jurisdiction to investigate the killing of an American citizen abroad.
In the weeks after her death, more than 100 members of Congress signed letters calling for a US investigation. The family and its supporters have continued to press lawmakers for action, but Washington has yet to open the investigation they have sought.
With no federal investigation forthcoming, the family has also turned to lawmakers in Eygi's home state.
“We were pushing for a piece of legislation, a joint memorial, that outlined how Aysenur was killed and the need for accountability and investigation,” Ali says.
The measure would formally ask the federal government and President Trump to investigate Eygi’s killing, but the family says they have yet to receive a response or see any progress on that front.
“We've seen the genocide of children, men, and women in Gaza. We've seen brutal killings by settlers in the occupied West Bank, with the aid of the military. We've seen my wife shot in the head, unprovoked and unjustified,” Ali says.
“It's hard to understand what exactly it would take for this government to wake up and hold the Israeli government accountable, not only for killing innocent men, women, and children, but for killing its own citizens, without any pushback or change in the relationship,” he adds.
Türkiye pushes the case forward
While Washington has declined to open its own investigation, Türkiye has pursued the case through its own legal channels.
Ankara's chief prosecutor opened a criminal investigation within days of Eygi's killing, while then-Justice Minister Yilmaz Tunc said Türkiye had enough evidence, including video footage, to pursue international arrest warrants and an Interpol Red Notice for the Israeli personnel involved.
The case has since become part of Türkiye's broader legal efforts against Israeli officials.
Most recently, Ankara sought a Red Notice for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu as part of the domestic case before Istanbul's 11th Heavy Penal Court linked to the interception of the Global Sumud Flotilla.
Türkiye has also sought to bring Eygi's killing into the ICC's Gaza-related proceedings and joined South Africa's genocide case against Israel at the ICJ.
Those efforts have given the family another avenue for accountability, even though they have yet to result in criminal charges against the soldier who shot Eygi.
A case that reaches beyond Eygi
The family has also continued to push for action closer to home, in Washington State.
State lawmakers introduced companion joint memorials, Senate Joint Memorial 8014 and House Joint Memorial 4010, calling on the federal government to investigate her killing independently. The measures received hearings in the state's Law and Justice Committee earlier this year.
The family has worked with the For Aysenur campaign, CAIR-WA and the Rachel Corrie Foundation, drawing a connection between Eygi and Rachel Corrie, another activist from Washington killed by the Israeli military in Gaza in 2003.
Corrie's family spent years seeking accountability but did not see criminal charges brought against the Israeli personnel involved.
“On one hand, it's beautiful that this tragedy connected our two families. I consider the Corries close friends of ours. That's a beautiful thing,” Ali says.
“But at the same time, I wish we'd never had a reason to meet them this way. It's really sad that all of their advocacy over the last two decades hasn't changed anything.”
According to Ali, Aysenur felt the same way Rachel Corrie did.
“She was killed the same way Rachel was killed. And there's been no justice for either of them, still,” Ali says.
“As for my grief, the Corries actually helped us understand this early on. They told us it never gets easier, even after twenty years. You just get stronger and better at carrying the pain,” he adds.
Two years after Eygi was killed, Ali will mark the anniversary by travelling to Aydin’s Didim to visit her grave.
Ali says the family’s demand remains the same: justice.
“Justice means holding the soldier responsible for killing Aysenur, the person who pulled the trigger, the person who gave the order, the person who wrote the policy… all the way up the chain, to the high-ranking officials who support this kind of action or fail to take responsibility for it,” Ali says.
And for Ali, accountability for Eygi is only one part of what justice means.
“True justice includes accountability for every single Palestinian who's been killed the same way, or worse. There are thousands of stories in Palestine we'll never know, too many in the occupied West Bank and in Gaza for us to ever know them all.”
Ultimately, there can be no true justice until Palestine is liberated, he adds.

EU and Ukraine to hold first meeting of Drone Alliance next week

Unknown Publisher

EU and Ukraine to hold first meeting of Drone Alliance next week
The first meeting of the EU-Ukraine Drone Alliance, which aims to accelerate the deployment of drone technologies and counter-drone capabilities across the bloc, will take place in Brussels on 11 September.
Source: Euractiv, citing sources, as reported by European Pravda
Details: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen first proposed the idea of a Drone Alliance in last year's State of the Union address as part of a series of announcements aimed at countering drone incursions into the airspace of EU member states.
A Commission representative, speaking on condition of anonymity, said that EU Commissioner for Defence Andrius Kubilius would attend the meeting on 11 September.
Nineteen drone manufacturers from EU countries will join the meeting, including ORQA, Indra Group, Fincantieri, WB Electronics/WB Group, Destinus, Delair, RSI Europe, TERMA A/S and Quantum Systems on the EU side.
The Ukrainian companies taking part will include Skyfall Industries, Greentech Harvest, Tencore, Deviro, Vyriy Industry, the Research and Production Company ATHLON AVIA, TAF Industries, UFORCE and F-Drones.
According to sources, the meeting will focus primarily on assessing the current state of affairs in order to establish a timetable for action and discuss initial measures.
Simónas Šatūnas, Kubilius's chief of staff, said, "We're trying to learn from them a lot, how the ecosystem functions, how the government and drone industries function together."
Background:
- In July, the EU and Ukraine agreed on the Drone Deal, which aims to "provide a single, coordinated framework for cooperation between the EU and Ukraine to facilitate, coordinate and support" the full implementation of drone agreements that Kyiv has signed with several EU capitals.
- A few days ago, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Ukraine was finalising a Drone Deal agreement with Germany.
- Before that, such an agreement was signed with Norway.

amsterdam fashion week 2026 turns the city into a stage for design and performance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
09:01:58 UTC
18:01:58 KST

Amsterdam Fashion Week returned from September 1 to 5, 2026, spreading more than 40 shows, presentations, exhibitions, talks and workshops across the Dutch capital. Rather than concentrating the programme around a single venue, this year’s edition continued to treat Amsterdam itself as part of the fashion week, moving between museums, historic buildings, shops and unexpected everyday settings. The programme brought emerging designers together with established names while entering the second phase of AFW’s partnership with Copenhagen Fashion Week, which introduces its Sustainability Requirements framework into the selection process ahead of a full rollout in September 2027.
The week began by bringing fashion into dialogue with material and spatial design. Amsterdam Fashion Week’s opening dinner gathered 130 guests inside a monumental canal house on Kloveniersburgwal, where designer Sabine Marcelis collaborated with natural-stone company SolidNature on the setting. Marcelis designed bespoke stone candleholders that ran along communal tables, framed by translucent curtains and soft lighting, turning the dinner itself into a carefully composed installation. The event introduced an edition in which the boundaries between fashion, objects, interiors and experience remained deliberately porous.
ULKUHANBATUHAN | image by Olivia Witmond
FASHION, MEMORY AND EVERYDAY LIFE
That looseness also appeared in designers looking directly at Dutch identity. At the monumental Molen van West, Ruben Jurriën presented Maak Nederland weer Gezellig!, mixing embroidery, comic drawings, oversized denim, reinterpretations of the Dutch clog and the recurring figure of Toetie, a childhood plush toy turned superhero. The collection approached national symbols through affection and humour rather than nostalgia, while asking what ideas such as kindness, familiarity and gezelligheid might mean today. Elsewhere, The New Originals transformed Nxt Museum into something closer to a gathering than a runway for Home Is Where the Heart Is. Created with filmmaker Ebeneza Blanche, the presentation combined streetwear, live music, performance and film while connecting the Amsterdam platform’s community with stories of migration, family and belonging.
Other presentations used clothing to explore less tangible states of presence. Under his label Jinchoe, Youngjin Choe returned to the Rijksmuseum passage after winning Lichting in 2025, presenting Shadow Stepping as an investigation into destruction and reconstruction. Dense black outerwear, exaggerated layers, displaced panels and obstructed faces gradually shifted towards earthy colours and white, giving physical form to the idea of carrying darkness rather than erasing it. DEFIJTER&VANBRUGGEN, meanwhile, looked back to the nineteenth-century flâneur and flâneuse for De Belofte van Buiten. Exaggerated tailoring and sculptural silhouettes inhabited a set filled with furniture, street lamps and domestic objects, where models eventually sat, read and watched the audience, turning physical presence itself into part of the performance.
Ruben Jurriën | image by Resa Steenvoorden
WHEN THE SUPERMARKET BECOMES A RUNWAY
Perhaps the clearest example of AFW26’s interest in collapsing fashion into ordinary life came from Camiel Fortgens, who staged his SS27 show inside an Albert Heijn supermarket at Stadionplein after opening hours. Models pushed shopping trolleys and carried baskets through aisles of cheese, frozen food and soft drinks while employees continued stacking shelves. Against this deliberately mundane backdrop, Fortgens’ familiar vocabulary of cotton shirts, denim, bombers and layered outerwear revealed exposed seams, raw hems, reversed construction and apparently accidental combinations. The intervention was almost invisible: rather than transforming the supermarket into a fantasy, the clothes absorbed the gestures, repetitions and small imperfections of everyday use.
The runway became more overtly symbolic for ULKUHANBATUHAN, whose Mens, erger je niet transformed the familiar Dutch board game into a system of uneven rules. Designers Ülkühan Akgül and Batuhan Demir treated models as pieces moving across an imaginary board, using distorted proportions, sculptural hats, upcycled escalator brushes, wooden structures and garments covered with bells to address patience, conformity and unequal starting positions. Across AFW26, such experiments suggested that the most interesting runway might no longer look like a runway at all. From a supermarket aisle to a windmill, museum or domestic interior, Amsterdam Fashion Week used the city as a testing ground for how fashion can communicate through space, performance, material and collective experience, as much as through clothes themselves.

Camiel Fortgens | image by Olivia Witmond
The New Originals | image by Lois van der Wildt
Jinchoe | image by Resa Steenvoorden
SiolidNature and Sabine Marcelis opening dinner | image by Ruby Cruden

‘Sinn Féin traitors!’: how far-right rhetoric derailed party’s path to power in Ireland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
09:00:32 UTC
18:00:32 KST

For Siobhán Fenton, the dream of Sinn Féin winning power and leading a progressive leftwing government evaporated the day she was canvassing in Dublin and felt a cold, sharp sting on her neck.
She was in the passageway of a block of flats in the inner city, knocking on doors, and looked around for the source. Fenton, a media adviser to the party leader, Mary Lou McDonald, felt another sting on her shoulder, then another on her forearm.
They were coins, thrown from a balcony above, where a man’s voice was shouting. “Sinn Féin traitors!” he roared. “Mary Lou Mohammad! Ireland is full!”
It was May 2024, and instead of steaming towards victory in local and European elections – widely deemed a foregone conclusion, to be followed by a historic triumph in a general election – the party was experiencing a backlash fuelled by anti-immigrant sentiment in what was usually a bastion of working-class support.
The coins left Fenton with gashes and bruises that augured an electoral hammering.
“By the time the party realised how bad things had gotten it was almost too late,” she said. “The far right had infiltrated lots of Sinn Féin strongholds and we hadn’t picked up on it.”
In a rupture to the party’s reputation for secrecy and discipline, Fenton has written a rare insider’s account, titled Ourselves Alone: Sinn Féin Behind Closed Doors.
It lifts the lid on a debacle that ambushed the party on the path to power. Instead of winning a general election and turbo-charging the campaign for Irish unification by ratcheting up pressure for a referendum, the party stumbled and today remains in opposition.
It is a cautionary tale for progressive movements across Europe and elsewhere that struggle to reconcile tolerance for immigrants and refugees with clamours for crackdowns on new arrivals.
A surge in xenophobia among grassroots supporters had blind-sided and, for a time, paralysed party leaders, Fenton said in an interview. “There was a moment of genuine sheer panic and just not knowing what to do. We were struggling to adapt because it was a sense that things had started to spiral out of control.”
The book, published this week, depicts a largely well-intentioned but hapless party, and is also an account from a member of an organisation that many perceive as secretive and still in thrall to former IRA leaders on both sides of the Irish border, a perception Fenton disputes.
Fenton, 34, was an atypical “Shinner”, the informal name for party adherents. She came from a middle-class Belfast family that abhorred the violence of the Troubles and favoured constitutional nationalism, not flinty republicanism.
Fenton briefly worked for the Social Democratic and Labour party (SDLP) before studying English literature at Oxford, researching gender-based violence at Cambridge and becoming a London-based journalist for the Independent before returning to Northern Ireland in 2016, where she freelanced for the BBC and other outlets, including the Guardian, and wrote a book on the Good Friday agreement.
In early 2020, Sinn Féin offered Fenton a job in Dublin. The party was on a high. It had just won 24.5% of first preference votes in the Irish general election, overtaking Fianna Fáil and Fine Gael, two centrist parties that had alternated in power for a century.
As successor to Gerry Adams, McDonald, a Dubliner universally known as Mary Lou, offered a fresh alternative, especially to young voters who blamed the political establishment for a housing crisis.
Sinn Féin had run too few candidates to capitalise on the breakthrough, so Fianna Fáil and Fine Gael mustered enough seats to form a coalition, leaving Sinn Féin in opposition. Analysts expected it to win power after the next election.
After Sinn Féin became the biggest party in Northern Ireland in 2022, which paved the way for Michelle O’Neill to become first minister at Stormont, the onus was on the party’s southern branch to ensure McDonald became taoiseach at Leinster House. “Don’t fuck it up,” a Belfast colleague half-jokingly told Fenton.
For three years, Fenton, having relocated to Dublin, experienced the giddy nervousness of a party soaring in the polls while the ruling coalition slumped. The republican mantra – “tiocfaidh ár lá”, our day will come – seemed apt.
A section titled “the long fall” chronicles the unravelling amid missteps and a volatile public mood.
McDonald appeared to blame police for a riot that rocked Dublin in November 2023, and alarmed middle-class property owners by suggesting average Dublin house prices should fall to €300,000. More damagingly, the party failed to navigate growing xenophobia, the result of a housing shortage, a cost of living crisis, an influx of migrants and refugees, and far-right activism on social media and the streets.
“It was a blind spot,” said Fenton. Covid-19 restrictions and a focus on the parliamentary party withered grassroots networking, leaving leaders unaware of the extent to which conspiracy theories and hostility to Muslims had taken hold, she said.
The party should have tried to combat racist narratives by peeling people away from smartphones and having “really difficult conversations”, said Fenton. “Go door to door, talk about community concerns but be very, very clear that scapegoating immigrants and refugees is the wrong response.”
Instead of gains in the May 2024 local and European elections, the cascade of coins on to Fenton foretold haemorrhaging support, especially in working-class strongholds that branded McDonald a “traitor” for not seeking greater curbs on migration. Months later the party limped into a general election that kept Fianna Fáil and Fine Gael in power.
Fenton’s contract was not renewed and she returned to her native Belfast, where she now works as a writer and analyst. She is no longer a member of Sinn Féin.
Immigration remains a fraught issue for a party squeezed between those wanting a harder line and those who favour solidarity, said Fenton. Leaders may be tempted to sidestep the issue until the next election, then take a stance, she said. “It will be dependent on what the political environment looks like then.”
