The pressure on Burnham to appease the right is huge. But now is the time to step out of Reform’s shadow | Andy Beckett
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
09:00:32 UTC
18:00:32 KST

Despite the bright start to Andy Burnham’s premiership, and Reform UK’s sudden disarray, a shadow still hangs over British centre-left politics. Labour has a small poll lead, a cautious air of confidence and a leader who seems energised rather than overwhelmed by trying to solve the country’s problems. Meanwhile, Reform is having a terrible 2026: mired in deepening funding scandals, losing winnable byelections and, thanks to the drama and novelty of Burnham’s leadership coup and new government, no longer the freshest story around.
Yet Reform UK’s support has either held up or fallen only slightly in most polls since Burnham entered Downing Street. Even in the Makerfield byelection, where he beat it more decisively than expected, Reform’s vote share and total support actually rose. Nigel Farage may have spent the year uncharacteristically avoiding journalists, or in his prickly rather than jolly public mode, but the overwhelming majority of Reform supporters, almost a quarter of the electorate, remain faithful. “Power is within our grasp!” insisted Zia Yusuf, Reform’s home affairs spokesman, at its party conference in Birmingham on Friday, and they applauded with determined gusto.
Meanwhile, their preoccupations continue to shape politics and how the media processes it. Immigration, crime, the benefits system, “wokeness”, net zero policies: all are constantly presented as out of control and contributing to national decline. From our overcrowded prisons to our almost exhausted North Sea oil- and gasfields, what are widely considered to be the most politically realistic options for the government are generally what most Reform voters would like to happen. The likelihood that permanent crime crackdowns and further large-scale fossil-fuel drilling – which the government looks increasingly likely to approve – will be disastrous for a country with an ever more obvious climate crisis and unprecedentedly large prison population, by historical and European standards, does not disturb this deep-rooted rightwing consensus. The pressure on Burnham to go along with it as prime minister will be never-ending.
Yet the risks of governing under Reform’s shadow, while less discussed, are much larger. So far, Labour’s fragile poll recovery has mainly been built by taking support back from the Greens and Lib Dems, as the dip in their poll ratings since a Burnham premiership became likely has demonstrated. This change would almost certainly be undone if Burnham decided to follow a Reform-defined agenda. Keir Starmer’s abrupt announcement that he will leave parliament is the ultimate result of him making exactly that mistake in Downing Street – and has given the Greens’ leader, Zack Polanski, a chance to reverse the momentum shift from his party to Labour by standing as a byelection candidate.
Meanwhile, with Reform, Restore and the Tories all competing to be the most rightwing, and this country’s many reactionary media outlets doing the same, many right-leaning voters are even more convinced than usual that no Labour government is acceptable. So the appeasement of conservative Britain, designed by Morgan McSweeney and carried out by Starmer, not always with conviction, was never likely to win many converts for long. In a deeply divided country, the days of Labour premiers attracting and holding on to large numbers of rightwing voters, as Tony Blair, Harold Wilson and Clement Attlee once did, are gone, at least for now.
As a politician unusually keen by modern standards on cross-party collaboration and broad coalitions, Burnham could waste much of what may not be a long premiership trying to build bridges with the right. But there are some early signs he may pursue a more streetwise strategy. His debut contributions as prime minister in parliament this week mixed consensual catchphrases such as “problem-solving over point-scoring”, which made the Tory leader, Kemi Badenoch, sound rigidly confrontational in response, with sweeping attacks on areas where the right is vulnerable. Austerity, Brexit, privatisation and the centralisation of power in London have dwindling electoral support and even less credibility, however loudly the Tories and Reform defend some or all of them, because for decades these old-fashioned rightwing remedies have clearly failed to revive the country.
“Far from ‘taking back control’, the combination of those policies took control out of the hands of communities up and down Britain,” said Burnham, deftly turning a key promise of populism back against the rightwing populists. He knows that while Margaret Thatcher is still revered by Farage and Badenoch, the sometimes brutal economic changes that she and her Conservative successors drove through are not popular with all Tory and Reform voters. They may never switch to supporting Labour, but could support parts of Burnham’s programme, such as stronger public control over “the essentials of life” currently provided at excessive cost by toxic Thatcherite creations such as Thames Water.
The approval, tacit or otherwise, of usually hostile voters on a specific issue can provide useful political cover for a government – especially an unpopular one, which Burnham’s is likely to be, however he performs, given the number of parties arrayed against him in our fragmented political landscape. He may well need that cover if his government is going to restructure the economy even half as ambitiously as he promises. The shareholders, financiers, lawyers and corporate executives who have done extremely well out of privatisation are not going to give up their gains and privileges without a fight.
A temporary coalition of leftwing and rightwing voters may be the only way to overcome them. The economy is not democratic – much to the disappointment of generations of radical leftists – but in a democracy, powerful interests can be curbed or even defeated if they are challenged by a premier acting with broad public consent, as Attlee and Franklin D Roosevelt once did against some of the 20th century’s most entrenched economic elites.
Yet if Burnham is to govern with anything like those legendary reformers’ effectiveness, then in other policy areas his government is going to have to stand up to Reform supporters. New research about them by King’s College London and UK in a Changing Europe shows that, despite this summer being the UK’s hottest ever, almost two-thirds “want to scrap the 2050 net zero target”. Meanwhile, a new Ipsos poll shows that immigration remains the number one public issue, particularly for Reform and Tory voters, despite the fact that immigration is rapidly falling.
Sooner or later, Burnham is going to have to use his celebrated communications skills to tell Britons some home truths, whether rightwing voters want to hear them or not. Otherwise, Reform’s shadow will chill his government for good.
- 
  Andy Beckett is a Guardian columnist

The Swiss Catholics who don’t recognise the pope
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

The Swiss Catholics who don’t recognise the pope
Switzerland loves being different. Its four national languages, referendums and the militia army are among the best examples. But there is another, much more low-key one: a Catholic church that doesn’t recognise papal authority.
Sometimes encountered while leafing through a document or a set of statistics, its name often intrigues; its very existence even more so. The Christian Catholic Church of Switzerland is, however, very real, even though many Swiss people have never heard of it. Although officially recognised in several cantons, it remains almost invisible within the Swiss religious landscape.
With some 12,000 to 13,000 members, it accounts for between 0.1% and 0.2% of the population. Such a modest proportion that it disappears even from official statistics: the Federal Statistical Office classifies it under the generic category of “other Christian communities”, alongside the Orthodox and the numerous Evangelical churches.
A rarity on a global scale
Globally, Christian Catholics constitute a tiny minority. They belong to the family of so-called Old Catholic Churches, which emerged in the 19th century following disagreements with Rome and are now grouped together within the Union of Utrecht.
The movement is present in only a few countries, mainly the Netherlands, Germany, Switzerland and Austria. Yet, within this small religious community, Switzerland plays a far more significant role than its membership figures would suggest.
One might think of it as a little-known curiosity. Yet the Christian Catholic Church of Switzerland has around 30 parishes, more than half of which are located in the cantons of Bern, Aargau, Solothurn and Basel. It also has its own bishop and ranks among the world’s leading Old Catholic communities.
The paradox is therefore very real: while most Swiss are unaware of its very existence, this small Church possesses structures that many larger organisations might envy.
A split dating back to the 19th century
To understand its origins, we must look back to a Europe in the midst of transformation. In both Germany and Switzerland, the young modern states were seeking to assert their authority against Rome.
In 1870, the First Vatican Council proclaimed, among other things, the dogma of papal infallibility and strengthened the pope’s authority over the entire Catholic Church. For many Catholics, this development posed no problem. Others, however, saw it as an excessive centralisation of religious power.
In Switzerland, the controversy quickly took on a political dimension. Against the backdrop of the Kulturkampf, which pitted liberal authorities against the Roman Catholic Church, priests and the faithful rejected Rome’s new direction and decided to go their own way.
The split was finally consummated. In 1871, the Christian Catholic Church was founded. At the time, there was no indication that this movement would endure for decades. Yet, more than 150 years later, it has survived disputes that most Europeans have long since forgotten.
A Catholic church with liberal leanings
Anyone attending a Christian Catholic service for the first time is likely to be surprised by what does not surprise them. The liturgy does indeed bear a strong resemblance to that of a Roman Catholic Mass. The prayers, the sacraments and a large part of the rites are familiar. At first glance, there is little or nothing to distinguish the two Churches.
The differences become apparent above all when one looks behind the altar. The bishop, for example, is not appointed by Rome. He is elected by the National Synod, where laypeople play an important role alongside the clergy. Christian Catholics also trace their lineage to the tradition of the Church of the first millennium and therefore do not recognise certain dogmas adopted later by Rome, notably that of papal infallibility.
But it is, above all, some of their reforms that have attracted attention. From the very beginning, the Church adopted national languages for the liturgy and permitted priests to marry. Divorced people may enter into a new religious marriage. Since 1999, women have been admitted to the priesthood. Since 2022, same-sex couples have also been able to enter into a religious marriage.
Not exactly what one would expect to find in a Church founded in 1871. Though small in numbers, the Christian Catholic Church has often proved more daring than institutions a hundred times its size.
Between Rome and the Reformation
Ultimately, the Christian Catholic Church’s originality lies in its unique position. It retains the liturgy, sacraments and episcopal structure inherited from the Catholic tradition, while placing great emphasis on the participation of the faithful and on reforms generally associated with the Protestant world.
This middle ground is reflected even in the training of its clergy. Future Christian Catholic priests study at the University of Bern, within the Institute of Christian-Catholic Theology, which forms part of a faculty historically shaped by the Protestant tradition. This situation sums up the identity of this Church rather well.
This openness is also evident in its relations with other Christian denominations. As a member of the Utrecht Union of Old Catholic Churches, it is in “full ecclesial communion” with the Anglican Churches. In layman’s terms, this means that ministries and sacraments are mutually recognised, a closeness that few churches can claim.
More than 150 years after its founding, the Christian Catholic Church of Switzerland thus continues to occupy a unique place in the European religious landscape. Neither quite Roman nor truly Protestant, it has forged its own identity over time. In short, a Church too Catholic to be Protestant, but too independent to be Roman.

Marvel and Disney+ have issued a stacked watch list for fans ahead of the cinema release of Avengers: Doomsday on December 18.

Marvel released an official “Countdown to Doomsday” playlist with Disney+, featuring 15 official selections to help fans catch up on all the action before watching the new movie. Among the selections, fans will get refreshers on origin stories, team-ups, and key multiversal information gearing them up to the Doomsday storyline.

Disney+ releasing a homework list for its own film is a great bit of subscriber farming. It converts the hype ahead of the theatrical release into watching content on a streaming service that has to, in the meantime, justify its monthly cost.
Every title below streams on Disney+, which is available in many markets around the globe. Some titles are also available on other streamers, and most are available to rent or buy digitally through Amazon Prime Video or Apple TV.

NANCHANG, Sept. 5 (Xinhua) -- One person has been confirmed dead and 11 others are missing after a mudslide struck a village in Suichuan County, Ji'an City, east China's Jiangxi Province at around 4 a.m. on Saturday, local authorities said.
The disaster was triggered by days of torrential rains brought by Typhoon Saudel, according to the county's flood control and drought relief headquarters.
Three people have been rescued, two of whom are in stable condition while one has been confirmed dead. All-out search and rescue operations are underway, while efforts are also being made to relocate affected residents and prevent secondary disasters.
Following the disaster, the Jiangxi provincial committee for disaster prevention, mitigation and relief issued a Level-III provincial emergency response for disaster relief at noon on Saturday, as Typhoon Saudel had left around 161,500 residents affected in the province.
China's Ministry of Natural Resources raised its geological disaster response for Jiangxi from Level IV to III at 11 a.m. Saturday and dispatched a work team to the site to guide rescue efforts.
The China National Commission for Disaster Reduction and the Ministry of Emergency Management activated a Level-IV national emergency response for natural disaster relief, and sent a work team and an emergency survey team with equipment including slope radar to assist with rescue operations.
Local fire and rescue authorities have dispatched 41 vehicles and 224 personnel to the site, while communications and reconnaissance drones in nearby areas have been deployed for rescue.
China has a four-tier emergency response system, with Level I being the most severe. ■

China Focus: China moves to create phone-free classrooms, help minors navigate digital age
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
16:59:48 CST
17:59:48 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 5 (Xinhua) -- For Ye Hui, the past summer break has been a digital tug-of-war.
Every time she confiscated the tablet, her 10-year-old son found a way to crack the password. So when the new semester began, she finally felt relief -- not just because he was back in class, but because the law was now on her side.
"Teachers will be more persuasive, given that the ban on smart devices is no longer just a school policy," said Ye, who lives in southwest China's Chongqing municipality.
The ban Ye spoke of is stipulated in a local law on minor crime prevention, which took effect on Sept. 1. It prohibited Ye's son and his counterparts from bringing phones, tablets and other smart devices into school.
Official statistics showed that China has close to 200 million underage internet users, with over 97 percent of minors having online access.
Minors' attention being eroded by the algorithm is a problem faced by countries across the world in the digital age, said Wang Peng, a deputy research fellow at the Beijing Academy of Social Sciences.
Putting a mobile device school ban into law is necessary, as it provides legal support for schools to enforce the ban to keep students from such erosion, Wang said.
Chongqing is the latest to elevate a phone ban from a school policy to legislation, as the entire country is working to build a safe and healthy internet environment for children's wholesome growth.
A similar legal ban has already been put in place in Guangzhou in Guangdong Province, Zhengzhou in Henan Province and places across Fujian Province.
The aim is better prevention of internet addiction among underage students, according to Chongqing municipal legislature, noting the provision cited a 2021 guidance document on the protection of minors' rights and interests in school by the Ministry of Education.
In mulling over the local law on minor crime prevention, Chongqing's legislative body found that exposure to bad information as a result of smartphone usage caused some school-age children to develop unhealthy ideas and values, and even commit crimes.
Ye was one of the worrying parents struggling to keep their children away from smartphones' bad influence. Her son spent nearly eight hours every day on screen and even paid for virtual skins and props for online games during the past summer vacation. "He could always find a way to unlock the tablet."
Strict restrictions on smart device use could help nip internet addiction in the bud, Ye hoped.
Xiao Junyi, a student from the 29th Middle School in Chongqing, welcomed the phone ban in school, admitting phones had proven detrimental to students' level of concentration and undermined their learning.
"We would secretly take out the phone and surf online when class was on," Xiao said.
Teachers believe when the phone ban becomes a law provision, it will be more convincing to students and easier for them to enforce.
"It will save a lot of unnecessary lecturing," said Hu Ranrui'an, a deputy head teacher at the Science City Middle School Affiliated to Chongqing Normal University.
But in reality, some children, particularly middle school students who have no parent to take them from and to school, do need cell phones for emergency contact.
"It's not a one-size-fits-all ban," said Jiang Yongsong, a supervisor from the 29th Middle School. There is a provision in the law that allows parents to file a written application if students need phones in school, he said.
Countries around the world have also been introducing bans, with smartphones increasingly seen as a source of classroom distraction and a potential threat to students' well-being.
UNESCO's latest Global Education Monitoring Report showed that 114 education systems now have a national ban on mobile phones in schools, representing 58 percent of countries worldwide.
However, experts cautioned that restriction is not enough to address the problem, calling for joint efforts from society, school and family.
After physically isolating minors from the digital world, there will be room for efforts to foster their concentration and capabilities for in-depth and critical thinking, said Wang Peng.
Ye Hui has already mapped out the reclaimed hours from the screen -- board games on Mondays, jogging on Wednesdays and weekend hikes to replace the virtual battles. "It's about proving the real world can win the battle for his attention," she said. ■

Across China: Exhibition bridges gap between centuries-old Chinese encyclopedia, public
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
16:59:27 CST
17:59:27 KST

A girl views an image at an exhibition featuring the digital version of the Siku Quanshu, or The Complete Library of the Four Treasuries, in Lanzhou, northwest China's Gansu Province, Aug. 25, 2026. (Xinhua/Lang Bingbing)
LANZHOU, Sept. 5 (Xinhua) -- An art gallery in Lanzhou, capital of northwest China's Gansu Province, has turned a colossal ancient encyclopedia into something anyone can enjoy.
Instead of displaying dense classical Chinese that only scholars can master, it exhibits 122 images from this seldom-presented 18th-century compendium, such as a sketch of an ancient Indian unicorn, a star map nearly a millennium old, and the private scribbles of a stern, diligent emperor.
These images form part of a years-long project to digitize a copy of the Siku Quanshu, which translates as the Complete Library of the Four Treasuries, one of the most comprehensive collections of Chinese classical works in Chinese history.
Compiled during the Qing Dynasty (1644-1911), the book runs to nearly 800 million characters across thousands of volumes, covering everything from Confucian philosophy to farming techniques. Seven copies were originally produced, but only three and a half survive today, preserved in Beijing, Taipei and Lanzhou, respectively.
For decades, this massive treasured book was locked away. To better preserve its copy, Lanzhou built a dedicated library in an underground repository with constant temperature and humidity. In 2021, a project was launched to digitize it.
By the end of May 2022, the scanning work of the text was finished, and the project moved into data processing. A team of young editors then spent more than two years checking the data page by page, and along the way, they discovered something unexpected: the playful side of the massive and complex text.
"Most people think such a book would be too difficult to read," said Zhang Yang, deputy director of the digital publishing center at Duzhe Publishing & Media, the project's lead. "But as we went page by page, we found plenty of vivid images that could spark modern readers' curiosity."
What started as a routine check soon turned into a curatorial mission. The team selected 122 of the most striking images and organized them into twelve sections, covering tea culture, astronomy, architecture, medicine, costume, and even weapon-making. The editors gave the sections funny titles such as "Ancient Gardening Know-How" and "Ancient Stargazing Guide," bridging the gap between centuries-old social life and the modern day.
One section is called "World Mystery Box," featuring images from geographical works by Western missionaries during the Qing Dynasty. These images depict the Colosseum in Rome, the Colossus of Rhodes, and exotic and mythical creatures, such as lions and mermaids.
"We had long heard of the Siku Quanshu by name, but this is our first time seeing it up close," said Liang Tao, a visitor from Xi'an. "It's both fun and awe-inspiring."
That reaction echoes the goal of the exhibition. Song Xuejuan, who heads the digitization project, said the exhibition "transforms 'static preservation' into 'dynamic sharing', and turns an academic treasure into a public experience."
For a long time, there was a disconnect between traditional culture and younger generations. In recent years, however, new technologies, fresh perspectives, and innovative storytelling have helped connect ancient heritage with contemporary trends.
The Mogao Caves, a UNESCO World Heritage Site dating back to the 4th century, also in Gansu, are an example. In the 1980s, local researchers began exploring digital documentation. Today, they have completed high-precision digital capture of 323 caves. The images rendered on screen are now even clearer than what the naked eye can see on site, revealing details that once required climbing ladders to inspect.
Another example is the immersive interactive digital exhibition of oracle bone inscriptions, held in Tianjin in April. Using artificial intelligence and mixed reality technologies, it allowed visitors to experience the ancient ritual of oracle bone divination.
The Lanzhou gallery said it had previously received only a few hundred visitors per day on average. But since this new image exhibition launched, it has seen attendance surge to over 3,000 on peak days. Among the crowds were many children accompanied by parents.
For Song's team, they were no longer editors merely checking for data errors, but rather communicators sharing the treasures with the public.
"I used to think the Siku Quanshu was unreachable," said Song Jia'ni, a 34-year-old editor on the team. "But once you get into it, you will realize you don't have to begin with big history. One picture, or one detail, is enough to hook you." ■

Black-clad protesters in balaclavas block road at port of Dover in Kent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
08:57:37 UTC
17:57:37 KST

Dozens of people dressed in black and wearing balaclavas blocked the road at the port of Dover in Kent, forcing closures in both directions on Saturday morning.
Kent police said they were were in attendance and engaging with the protest, which the Port of Dover described as a “public order incident”. No arrests were made during the incident. Responsibility for the demonstration appears to have been claimed by an anti-immigration group with links to the far right.
The behaviour of the participants and the travel disruption they have caused has been condemned by the government. Traffic in and out of the port on the A20 was stopped, causing delays of up to 30 minutes and four miles of congestion, according to National Highways.
Videos shared online showed a large number of masked people in black marching on the road in a large group as lorries waited in traffic next to police cars.
By lunchtime, the protesters had dispersed and access roads to the port were “free flowing”, according to the Port of Dover. Ferry operators pledged to put those who had been delayed by the disruption on to the next available sailings.
The number of people involved was not immediately clear. One livestreamer estimated he was marching with hundreds of people but police did not give an official estimate.
Social media videos showed demonstrators linking arms in a blockade across the A20 and chanting “stop the boats”and “England till I die.”
A group called Patriot Platform, which styles itself as having “a fierce love for our homeland”, claimed responsibility for the blockade.
The far-right activist Tommy Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, reposted videos of the blockade, highlighting a live stream of the protest that directed viewers towards Patriot Platform.
In his post, Robinson encouraged more to join, saying: “Get there to support them.”
In another post, he wrote: “Simultaneously at different locations across Dover patriots have mobilised to close down the port. There are 3 plus locations that patriots have shut down so far with many more planned to be closed. People wanted action I’m guessing there are 100,000s of men willing to fill their shoes.”
The founder of Patriot Platform, Danny Thomas, also known as Danny Tommo, wrote on social media “live Dover somethings [sic] happening” and posted a live stream.
In a video posted on 2 September, he told his followers he was meeting with “a huge group [of] top, proper patriots” to prepare for a message he was planning to send to the government. 
 “Very, very soon, we are going to send a message that will make sure they understand that we will not go down without a fight. We will not allow our nation to be plagued in the way that it is.
“And when you see it and when you feel it, I guarantee the whole thing will change for the better. Because once the message is sent once, imagine the sheer numbers that will be sent on the second, the third, the fourth message.”
In further comments, he said: “From the hills of Scotland to the fields of Wales to the streets of Northern Ireland and to the towns and cities of England, we are building something that’s never been built before.
“And when you’re part of it and you see what’s about to go down, you will understand … we’re about to show you what can be done when men and women of this country, who have the blood that runs through them like their grandfathers, get off their asses and do something about it.”
On Saturday morning, the Port of Dover confirmed in a statement that the disruption was affecting “all routes” in and out, as well as around the town.
Nathan Ditchburn, who was on his way to work when he saw the group arrive at about 6.45am, told KentOnline: “I would say there are around 300 men, maybe more. Nobody will speak; they just handed me a piece of paper to look at. They have blocked off every entrance and exit of the Dover port area.”
One woman, who asked to remain anonymous, said: “I was at Dover port this morning, trying to get on a ferry to France. In the end we left and returned home – it wasn’t worth our while, we were only going to Lille for the day.
“But the headlines calling it a ‘protest’ suggest something very different to what took place – which looked like a highly organised event.
“Masked teenagers in black clothes were coordinated by walkie-talkie and I directly witnessed an older man, not in black, on an electric bike – coordinating in plain sight and being applauded by the masked teenagers as he gave them the thumbs up for their ‘good work’.
“The guy on the bike then went to the nearest police stop, [he was] obviously monitoring and reporting police activity.
“There were no banners and no slogans, just pure intimidation. It was a demonstration only in the sense that they wanted to demonstrate their power and to intimidate.”
Mike Tapp, the Labour MP for Dover and Deal, criticised what he described as “idiots coming to Dover to cause disruption”. In a post on Facebook, he said: “Parkrun cancelled and port access disrupted. I am fed up with idiots coming to Dover to cause disruption.
“I bet if you asked any one of those ‘protesters’ they wouldn’t know small boat crossings are down by 40% and we are working hard to fix the mess. Go home, enjoy your weekend/get a job.”
Chris Vinson, the leader of the Conservative group on Dover district council, said the protest appeared to be “illegal migration-related”, but said the demonstrators did not appear to have placards or banners.
“I’m not aware that there’s been any violence, although clearly, having the path of your vehicle blocked by men wearing black paramilitary gear and balaclavas is extremely intimidating, especially when it’s not clear why they’re there, and the police weren’t aware and so haven’t been able to warn people in advance and make sure that they are made to feel safe.”
A Home Office spokesperson said: “The right to peaceful protest is fundamental to our democracy, but we condemn the behaviour in Dover and the travel disruption it has caused.
“We appreciate the frustration of those who have been impacted today. Access to the port is now restored and traffic is flowing. Those travelling to the port are advised to allow for extra travel time and to follow guidance from providers.”
The shipping company DFDS and P&O Ferries said they would offer customers whose journeys were disrupted access to the next available departure.

South Africa rolls out baboon-proof bins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
08:55:47 UTC
17:55:47 KST

South Africa rolls out baboon-proof bins
The first 2,200 of 6,000 lockable baboon-proof bins are due to reach priority areas of South Africa’s Cape Peninsula from mid-September 2026, while a northern fence project awaits final environmental and administrative approvals.
The Cape Peninsula Baboon Management Joint Task Team (CPBMJTT), made up of SANParks, CapeNature and the City of Cape Town, said the rollout will initially focus on areas where baboon activity and conflict with residents have been reported most frequently.
The first areas to receive the new bins are Plateau Road, Castle Rock, Heron Park, Murdoch Valley South, De Oude Weg, Da Gama, Capri, Welcome Glen, Scarborough, Tokai East and Fir Grove. Simon’s Town is not included in the initial rollout because the Seaforth and Waterfall troops are earmarked for relocation to the planned Urban Wildlife Centre. Preparations are also under way for a northern boundary fence running from Zwaanswyk south to Constantia Nek.
According to the CPBMJTT, the process is expected to begin later in September once environmental checklists and administrative approvals have been completed. The task team said the fence is intended to prevent baboons from entering urban areas and farmland in the northern part of the peninsula, while securing habitat for an estimated 250 baboons.
A memorandum of understanding has been signed between seven wine-farm landowners bordering Table Mountain National Park in the Constantia Valley, the Cape Baboon Partnership and the City. The agreement sets out shared responsibilities for construction, maintenance and the long-term operation of the fence. The landowners and Cape Baboon Partnership will share the construction and upgrade costs, while the City has committed a once-off R10 million contribution.
The CPBMJTT said construction is expected to take about six months if all goes according to plan. Once the fence is in place, rangers will encourage the CT1 and CT2 troops towards the mountainside and will continue monitoring the troops and patrolling the fence.
The fence forms part of the approved Cape Peninsula Baboon Strategic Management Plan and is intended to create a clearer boundary between Table Mountain National Park and neighbouring agricultural and residential properties.
The Cape Baboon Partnership has appointed an experienced sanctuary manager, while stakeholders, environmental groups, community representatives and residents have visited the site over the past two months.
A Swansea University research project involving the Da Gama troop ended on August 21. The study tested non-invasive approaches using olfactory, auditory and visual cues to examine how baboons respond to simulated risks. The collars used during the research were designed to self-release and have now been collected. Data analysis is underway, with the findings expected to be made public once the study has been completed.

Department head at Prosecutor General's Office arranged "protection" for scam call centres – photo
The National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU) and Specialised Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO) have announced that they have uncovered a criminal organisation which investigators say was headed by the head of a department at the Prosecutor General's Office. Members of the organisation are suspected of regularly taking bribes from scam call centres and laundering the proceeds of crime.
Source: NABU; SAPO; UP sources in law enforcement agencies
Details: The investigation has established that an official at the Prosecutor General's Office set up the organisation in mid-2025 and recruited serving prosecutors and associates.
Sources have told Ukrainska Pravda that the official in question is Serhii Kropyva.
NABU says the members received illicit payments in exchange for not interfering with the operations of scam call centres whose victims included Ukrainians and people in other countries.
The money they received was laundered in various ways. Over UAH 20 million (about US$449,400) was spent on property, jewellery and other high-value assets.
According to NABU, the group's ringleader transferred ownership of additional assets with a market value of over UAH 12 million (US$269,600) – including property in an apartment complex near the Carpathian Mountains – to third parties.
The investigators say more than UAH 10 million (US$224,700) was placed in bank accounts belonging to close associates and disguised as business income.
Law enforcement agencies currently say they have exposed five members of the organisation.
The case has been provisionally classified as falling under articles of the Criminal Code that concern the establishment of and participation in a criminal organisation and the laundering of proceeds of crime. The investigation is identifying other possible members.
Background:
- Sources told Ukrainska Pravda that NABU and SAPO were conducting searches at premises belonging to Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko, his deputy Mariia Vdovychenko and Oleh Kiper, Head of Odesa Oblast Military Administration. The Prosecutor General's Office later denied that Kravchenko's premises had been searched.
- On the evening of 4 September, it was reported that NABU and SAPO were conducting investigative actions at the Prosecutor General's Office as part of a special operation to expose a criminal organisation.
- According to Ukrainska Pravda sources in business circles, NABU and SAPO have detained Serhii Kropyva, deputy head of the International Legal Cooperation Department of the Prosecutor General's Office.
- NABU and SAPO said they were conducting a special operation to expose a criminal organisation headed by an official from the Prosecutor General's Office and involved in protecting a network of scam call centres and money laundering.
- The Prosecutor General's Office said it will cooperate fully with the anti-corruption agencies in the case.
- The Prosecutor General's Office added that it will suspend the employee whose possible involvement in unlawful activities is being investigated.

Final sprint before Saxony-Anhalt vote: AfD campaigns at 'family festival' in Magdeburg

Ulrich Siegmund could lead the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt into government, marking the first time a far-right party has held state-level power in Germany's post-war era.
Supporters queue in lines stretching dozens of metres for a photo with him: AfD lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund. The 35-year-old is standing for the party in Sunday's state election in Saxony-Anhalt.
The state's Office for the Protection of the Constitution — a department of the Germany's interior ministry — has classified the Saxony-Anhalt AfD as a confirmed far-right extremist organisation. Siegmund, whose TikTok following has made him the party's poster boy in eastern Germany, has been received like a celebrity all over the state.
"I finally want to make policy for our own country again," Siegmund tells Euronews. He wants to overhaul migration policy, freeing up money he says is "currently being handed out around the world, for people who are here illegally, who commit crimes here." Policy, he says, should serve "our own interest, for our own country."
Within his first 100 days in office, Siegmund plans to introduce a "work obligation for asylum seekers." Fire service driving licences and the display of flags at schools are also near the top of his list. "Of course this isn't turning the really big wheel, but these are the first concrete steps where you can see the first progress across all areas of this society."
At the "family festival," as the AfD calls it, near Magdeburg's city centre, thousands cheer and celebrate their "Ulli." His face is emblazoned on countless T-shirts and placards. Chants of "We are the people" repeatedly cut through the crowd; some supporters also chant "We are the Wende." Between speeches, musicians take the stage and techno beats blare from the speakers.
Here at the "family festival", as the AfD calls it, near the Magdeburg city centre, thousands cheer and celebrate their "Ulli". His likeness is emblazoned on countless T-shirts and placards. Time and again chants of "We are the people" cut through the crowd. Some AfD supporters also chant "We are the Wende". In between, musicians take to the stage or techno beats blare from the speakers.
The party has rolled out its heavy artillery: well-known figures including Thuringian AfD politician Stephan Brandner and co-chair Tino Chrupalla fire up the crowd. Whenever speakers mention the CDU, SPD, or other parties, the crowd boos and whistles, some shouting "Shame."
AfD's supporters are hoping for a 180-degree turnaround in Saxony-Anhalt's state politics, led by Siegmund. "I support the AfD and I love Ulrich. Once you've done all sorts of things — rape, stabbings — then you can't live here, you have to go, and he makes sure of that. That's already good," Gerda tells Euronews.
The pensioner has travelled specially from Berlin, wanting to attend an AfD event in person, having already watched several on YouTube. "Gerda" isn't her real name; like many at the event, she doesn't want to give it, fearing possible consequences.
Even a heavy downpour doesn't stop fans from waiting for Siegmund's appearance. For them, everything is at stake: for the first time, the AfD could govern at state level — as part of a coalition, or possibly even alone.
It would mark the first time a far-right party holds power at state-level in Germany's post WWII era.
CDU politician: working with the AfD would spell the end of the Union
Current polls put the AfD at around 41%, according to Forschungsgruppe Wahlen on behalf of ZDF. The CDU trails far behind in second place with 23%, and the Left party is third with 11.5%. In the last election, in 2021, the AfD won 20.8%, while the CDU won by a clear margin with 37.1%.
This time the AfD hopes to win the election outright — but that might still not be enough to form a government. The party may fall short of the votes needed to govern alone, and it rejects any coalition with the CDU. The CDU, in turn, rejects a coalition with the AfD, having adopted a formal incompatibility resolution, or so-called "firewall" against it.
Dennis Radtke, head of the CDU's workers' wing (CDA), warns that his party would be finished if it formed a coalition with the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt. "The moment we start working with this party, bringing it into positions of responsibility, the CDU is finished," Radtke said on ZDF's "Maybrit Illner" programme.
Only the BSW can imagine tolerating an AfD-led government — that is, supporting an AfD single-party government with its votes without formally joining it. But the BSW is currently polling at four percent and could fail to clear the 5% threshold. The SPD and the Greens have also spent recent weeks hovering just below the threshold, though they have now climbed to 8.5% and 6% respectively.
Lead Left party candidate optimistic
Given current polling, Saxony-Anhalt may face a complicated coalition puzzle after the vote. A coalition between the AfD and CDU appears ruled out. A CDU–Left party alliance, as the basis for a majority government with the SPD and Greens, also looks unrealistic for now, since the CDU's incompatibility resolution applies to the Left party as well.
Just days ago, Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) said: "Both with the AfD and with the Left party there are such fundamental differences with the Union that cooperation is out of the question," he told the "Magdeburger Volksstimme" and the "Mitteldeutsche Zeitung."
The mood in the state parliament has changed significantly in recent years, Eva von Angern, the Left party's lead candidate, tells Euronews. A member of the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament since 2002, she says: "The climate is very hostile to women. Hate and incitement are what define a parliamentary sitting" — and this hostility has now spread into society and social media as well.
Despite the current forecasts, she says she is looking toward election day "optimistically." She is "firmly convinced" the AfD will not manage to form a single-party government in Saxony-Anhalt: "People have understood. They want to fight for diversity in Saxony-Anhalt."

The death toll from flash floods and mudslides along the Nepal-China border rose to 1,362 on Saturday, while 5,531 people remained missing 10 days after the disaster struck, according to official data.
 
Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said 1,331 people were killed, while 5,000 others, including 589 foreigners, remained missing.
 
Although an earlier report put the death toll at 1,344, the figure was later revised downward.
 
Chinese authorities said at least 31 people were killed, while 531 others remained missing in the southwestern Xizang Autonomous Region, also known as Tibet.
 
Of those missing, 850 are foreigners, according to official figures from Nepal and China.
 
The disaster struck on Aug. 26 when a glacier on Nepal's Mount Langtang Lirung fractured at an altitude of about 5,200 meters (17,060 feet).
 
The fracture triggered an ice-rock avalanche that developed into a massive debris flow and swept through valleys along the border.
 
Floodwaters and mudslides devastated Nepal's Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and Kavre districts, as well as the Kathmandu Valley.
 
The disaster also buried the Gyirong border crossing in Xizang.

Philippines' Duterte posts bail after president Marcos dispute, risking presidential bid

Philippine Vice President Sara Duterte posted bail on Saturday after a trial court ordered her arrest on three counts of grave threats linked to comments she made about President Ferdinand Marcos Jr, the first lady and a former House speaker.
The arrest order marks an escalation in Duterte’s legal troubles as she also faces an impeachment trial in the Senate, a process that, if it ends in conviction, could remove her from office and derail her 2028 presidential bid.
It is the latest development in a feud between the Philippines’ dominant political dynasties. Marcos and Duterte, both children of former presidents, formed an alliance in 2022 that allowed them to sweep to power before they fell out in 2024.
Dressed in black and surrounded by dozens of police officers, Duterte told reporters outside the court that she did not feel safe and accused authorities of harassment.
She said the case’s involvement of the president, the first lady and Marcos’ cousin heightened her fears.
“If I post bail, the harassment won’t stop. If I don’t post bail, I’ll be taken to the police. I have no trust in the police, I have no trust in the courts. I do not feel safe at all,” Duterte said.
She asked who would be held accountable “if I die tonight”, saying police would simply “wash their hands and call it an accident”.
The police accorded the vice president the respect she deserved, Interior Minister Jonvic Remulla said when asked to comment on Duterte’s remarks.
“It’s very unfortunate that all the pressure in her life is affecting her perception,” Remulla said in a phone message.
Marcos’ office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Duterte’s remarks about her safety. The office said on Friday that it would respect any decision or order issued by the court.
The court found probable cause to try Duterte on all three counts and set bail at $1,900 (120,000 pesos) per count.
The case stems from a November 2024 online press conference in which Duterte said she had spoken to an assassin and instructed him to kill Marcos, his wife, Liza Araneta Marcos, and his cousin, then-House Speaker Martin Romualdez, if she herself were killed. She has denied threatening them.
The alleged threats are also part of the impeachment complaint against her. Duterte also faces accusations of misusing public funds while serving as vice president and education secretary, allegations she rejects.

====================================================================================================

Mansour Abbas is betting on a Zionist to make Palestinian votes count
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
08:40:53 UTC
17:40:53 KST

Mansour Abbas is betting on a Zionist to make Palestinian votes count
Yoav Segalovich’s place on Raam’s slate is less about winning Jewish votes in the Israeli election than making Palestinian representation harder to exclude from coalition politics.
When Raam leader Mansour Abbas appeared alongside former Yesh Atid lawmaker Yoav Segalovich this week and announced that Segalovich would run second on the party’s electoral slate, much of the immediate attention went to the obvious novelty: An Israeli Jewish politician, openly Zionist and a former police major-general, running near the top of the list of a conservative Islamist Arab party. That combination is unusual, and it was meant to look unusual.
Jewish participation in political lists representing Palestinian citizens of Israel is not, in itself, unprecedented. Hadash was built around a Jewish-Arab political tradition and has for decades included Jewish candidates and lawmakers. Ofer Cassif sits in the Knesset today as one of its most outspoken Jewish members. What is distinctive about the Abbas-Segalovich arrangement is not that a Jew is running with an Arab list. It is the kind of Jewish political voice Abbas has chosen to place there: a Zionist former senior police commander whose political biography sits comfortably inside the Israeli mainstream, not outside it.
Segalovich is joining Raam’s slate, not Raam itself, and the difference is easy to miss if one stops at the photograph. According to the arrangement, he will join the electoral list and parliamentary faction but will not become a member of the party. Raam’s constitution and internal decision-making structure will not change. Segalovich is also expected to retain the freedom to vote independently on questions where the ideological distance is obvious, including religion and state, security and LGBTQ rights. Abbas is not converting Raam into a Zionist party and Segalovich is not becoming an Islamist. They are testing whether two political identities that remain quite far apart can inhabit the same electoral vehicle.
I am not convinced that the main purpose of the move is electoral, at least not in the simple sense of adding more votes. Segalovich may bring some. An August Channel 13 poll suggested that a slate including him could perform somewhat better than Raam has in other surveys, and he retains unusual credibility among Arab local leaders because of his work on organised crime while serving as deputy public security minister in coalition governments led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid.
In that period he became one of the few senior Jewish officials associated in Arab public memory not only with promises about crime, but with a governmental programme that actually tried to confront it. That helps Abbas now, when criminal violence remains one of the most immediate concerns of Palestinian citizens of Israel. The arithmetic still looks secondary. What Abbas is trying to change is the political value of the seats he expects to win.
Since breaking with the Joint List and entering the Bennett-Lapid coalition in 2021, Abbas has pursued a fairly consistent experiment. His argument, sometimes stated directly and sometimes only through practice, is that Palestinian citizens of Israel have accumulated representation without converting enough of it into governing power.
Arab parties could win ten, thirteen or fifteen seats and still be treated as politically untouchable when coalitions were formed. He tried to break that wall by making Raam available for coalition politics, including with parties whose positions on the Palestinian question were very far from his own. For a short period it worked, then it didn’t.
The government collapsed, Benjamin Netanyahu returned to power, October 7 arrived and the war that followed eroded the legitimacy Abbas had labouriously built for Arab participation in a governing coalition. Jewish opposition parties that desperately need Arab seats to reach a majority still hesitate to say openly that they would govern with Raam. Avigdor Liberman, who sat in the same government with Abbas in 2021, has already said Raam cannot be a coalition partner this time. Netanyahu has gone back to one of his most effective electoral weapons: warning Jewish voters that his opponents will depend on Arab parties to govern.
Segalovich’s place as number two on the list answers that problem more than it answers a shortage of ballots, because the obstacle facing Abbas was never only how many seats Raam might win, but whether those seats would be treated as usable once the counting was over. Jewish opposition parties may need Arab mandates and still refuse to say, in public, that they would govern with them; Netanyahu’s campaign has long fed on that hesitation and Liberman’s rejection of Raam as a partner shows how quickly the old taboo returned after October 7.
A Zionist former police commander standing immediately behind Abbas does not dissolve the ideological objections to the party, yet it makes the simpler charge – that Raam stands outside legitimate Israeli politics – harder to repeat without looking past the man placed in the second slot. He is not only a candidate. He is a certificate of political usability, a way of saying that Arab votes already cast should count towards government rather than remain representation without power. That may be worth more to Abbas after October 7 than the number of Jewish voters Segalovich can actually persuade to put a Raam ballot in the box.
Abbas has again resisted returning to a full Arab Joint List for the same reason. Hadash, Taal and Balad have rebuilt a reduced version of that alliance and left the door open to Raam, but the two projects are no longer travelling in the same direction. The Joint List is trying to maximise collective Arab representation and keep a recognisably Palestinian political address. Abbas is trying to maximise the ability of Arab representation to enter the machinery of government. The aims can overlap. They are not the same. The Joint List has already criticised him for choosing Segalovich rather than rejoining the Arab alliance, and reports before the announcement indicated it was willing to press Raam to return – without Segalovich.
Palestinian politics inside Israel has carried this tension for a long time, longer than one campaign cycle. Should an Arab party first represent the collective political identity of Palestinian citizens, even at the price of remaining outside government? Or should it accept ideological compromise, perhaps a great deal of it, in order to gain access to budgets, ministries and actual decision-making? Abbas has chosen the second route more clearly than any major Arab leader before him. Segalovich takes the experiment one step further. Until now, Abbas argued that an Arab party could cooperate with Zionist parties. He is now saying, in effect, that a Zionist politician can sit inside an Arab-led parliamentary list without either side pretending their ideological differences have disappeared.
Israeli politics has spent decades demanding that Arab politicians prove they are acceptable partners while rarely making the opposite demand of Jewish parties: that they demonstrate a willingness to share political space with Palestinian citizens as equals. Putting Segalovich second on Raam’s list turns that equation around, at least symbolically. The Jewish partner is no longer inviting the Arab into his coalition. He is entering an Arab-led list.
The price is harder to ignore. The more Raam defines its success through its acceptability to Zionist coalition partners, the greater the temptation to push the Palestinian national question further outside its political programme. Segalovich has been explicit that he remains Zionist and Jewish in his political worldview.
Raam has been equally explicit that it is not asking him to become something else. The honesty is better than a fake ideological unity, but it also lays the bargain out in the open. Abbas gains a partner who can help normalise Raam inside Israeli coalition politics. Segalovich joins a slate led by a party whose strategy increasingly emphasises civil integration, crime, budgets and practical governance while leaving the deepest questions of Palestinian national rights somewhere more distant.
The move will not look the same to every part of the electorate. To some Palestinian voters it may demonstrate maturity: politics is about delivering results, not guarding ideological purity from the opposition benches. To others it will look like another stage in transforming Palestinian political power into a tool whose value is measured by how little discomfort it causes the Zionist mainstream. Neither reading is empty. Asking whether Segalovich will bring Raam another seat or two is therefore a smaller question than the one Abbas is actually placing on the table.
He wants the argument after the election to be less about whether Jewish parties are allowed to rely on Arab votes and more about what they are prepared to offer for them. Segalovich is there to make that conversation easier for Jewish politicians. Whether the same move makes Abbas’s argument easier to defend among Palestinian citizens is a separate problem, and he knows it.
That is not simply coexistence. It is a political transaction, and perhaps a very calculated one. The test will not be how many Jewish voters follow Segalovich into Raam on election day. It will come afterwards, when Jewish opposition leaders still have to decide whether they can say publicly what they struggle to say now: that a government supported by Palestinian citizens and their political representatives is no less legitimate because of it.
If Abbas succeeds at that, Segalovich may bring Raam very few additional votes and still prove one of its most consequential candidates. The thing Abbas is really trying to increase is not Raam’s vote share. It is the political worth of an Arab vote after it has already been cast.

The Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) announced on Saturday, Sept. 5, that combat operations are ongoing following Russia’s refusal to agree to a proposed mutual ceasefire between Sept. 5 and Sept. 9.
The General Staff of the AFU told Ukrainska Pravda and Suspilne that a unilateral ceasefire is impossible because it would endanger military personnel, adding that defensive tasks are being executed in full according to plan.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Dmytro Filatov, commander of the 1st Separate Assault Regiment, stated that while the General Staff issued orders restricting strikes at an operational depth, no limitations were imposed on tactical-level combat.
The Russian Ministry of Defense confirmed its refusal to observe a temporary truce, publishing a report on Saturday detailing its overnight combined strikes on industrial facilities in the Dnipropetrovsk region and logistics and energy infrastructure in the Mykolaiv and Odesa regions.
Overnight strikes and proposed diplomatic pause
The Russian Defense Ministry’s claims correspond with reported strikes across southern and central Ukraine early Saturday.
A Russian ballistic missile struck an industrial enterprise in Kamianske in the Dnipropetrovsk region, killing four people and injuring five others. Regional authorities reported that three individuals were hospitalized, including a 30-year-old woman requiring intensive care.
In Mykolaiv, consecutive jet-powered “Shahed” drone strikes hit an Epicenter shopping center late Friday and early Saturday, injuring a 72-year-old man and a 17-year-old girl and triggering a large fire.
The Skeleton Putin Needs
The Saturday attacks follow a Friday strike that damaged a nine-story residential building in Boryspil, Kyiv region, where a fire broke out on the roof and in an upper-floor apartment.
The sustained aerial campaign comes despite Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s Friday announcement proposing a mutual halt to airstrikes.
The proposal was intended to accommodate the upcoming diplomatic mission of US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who are scheduled to visit Moscow and Kyiv this weekend.

Pentagon polygraphs dozens of US military staff over media leaks: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
08:37:34 UTC
17:37:34 KST

Pentagon polygraphs dozens of US military staff over media leaks
About 50 officers on the US Joint Staff have been interrogated over reports detailing depleted weapons stockpiles during Iran conflict, says The New York Times.
United States investigators have subjected about 50 members of the US military’s Joint Staff to lie detector tests following a series of unauthorised media leaks, according to a report by The New York Times (NYT).
The inquiry focused on whether civilian and military personnel leaked classified details to reporters, particularly concerning dwindling US ammunition reserves, the newspaper reported on Friday.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3‘To challenge deadly blockade’: New flotilla mission sets sail for Gaza
- list 2 of 3US imposes sanctions on Turkish bank, prompting legal threat
- list 3 of 3At least five killed in Sudan’s South Kordofan in attack by rebel group
The polygraph examinations took place last month after news outlets published several reports highlighting severe drops in key weapons supplies, including long-range missiles and Patriot air defence interceptors. US officials had pushed back on these reports, insisting their weapons stockpiles were more than sufficient.
In a statement to the NYT, Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell declined to address internal administrative or investigative actions directly, but emphasised that the department takes leaks of national security information “extremely seriously and investigates accordingly”.
“Securing classified information is critical to ensuring the security of the United States and of our troops deployed around the world,” Parnell added.
The Joint Staff, which consists of between 1,500 and 2,000 military and civilian staff, plays a key role in coordinating operational strategy, policy and war planning with combat commands globally.
Unprecedented move
Sources familiar with the inquiry told the NYT that the aggressive push was designed not only to identify the individuals behind the disclosures, but also to deter potential future leakers.
Legal and military experts say the scale of the investigation is unprecedented, as the top ranks of the US armed forces have never undergone widespread polygraph testing in modern history.
The move follows widespread reporting on how active military operations involving Iran have severely strained US weapon reserves, causing internal debates over the broader direction of the conflict.
US President Donald Trump has repeatedly pushed officials to crack down on unauthorised disclosures. In addition to calling for strict enforcement, Trump has publicly branded critical media coverage regarding munition shortages and the administration’s handling of the conflict in Iran as “treasonous”.
The persistent leaks have deepened an atmosphere of deep distrust inside the Pentagon, which current and former officials attribute to the management style of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
Operating alongside a tight circle of close aides, Hegseth has ousted or blocked the promotions of at least 80 generals, admirals and senior officials during his tenure, the report said.
The Pentagon has launched multiple leak probes in response to media coverage of Hegseth’s leadership, even as he faced criticism for sharing sensitive operational details in a Signal group chat.
The internal tensions escalated further last month when the Defence Department fired the top editor and publisher of Stars and Stripes, an independent, government-funded military news publication.
Staff members said the move was direct retaliation for stories detailing deteriorating conditions on board the aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln.
Despite the mounting friction, Trump has backed Hegseth, publicly praising his performance as “fantastic”.

Taiwan Army to spend NT$1.44 billion on converting cargo trucks to fire Hellfire missiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
08:30:39 UTC
17:30:39 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Army has budgeted NT$1.44 billion (US$45.2 million) to convert civilian-style delivery vehicles into disguised launch platforms for Hellfire missiles to counter amphibious assaults.
The procurement is included in the Army’s 2027 defense budget and will be carried out through the Ministry of National Defense’s Armaments Bureau Production and Manufacturing Center, per Liberty Times. The system is designed to blend into Taiwan’s road network and logistics centers in peacetime, then be deployed against enemy forces in a conflict.
The system integrates AGM-114 Hellfire anti-armor missiles, which are traditionally launched from attack helicopters such as the AH-64 Apache and AH-1 Cobra, into commercial-style cargo trucks. The Hellfire has an effective range of about 8 kilometers, while the ground-based system uses modified fire-control and targeting systems to support launches from hidden locations.
The Armaments Bureau's 209th Factory and the Army Aviation Maintenance Depot jointly developed the system, Liberty Times reported. The modifications address challenges associated with low-level ground launches, including obstructions from vegetation, buildings, and uneven terrain.
The system is primarily intended to counter amphibious assaults as part of an asymmetric defense strategy, according to Liberty Times. Its civilian appearance is intended to make it more difficult for surveillance satellites and drones to distinguish the vehicles from ordinary commercial traffic.
The Armaments Bureau has also indicated the system could potentially be adapted for battlefield air defense against low-flying helicopters and slower unmanned aircraft.

Majority of Poles believe Russian provocations against Poland are likely
Almost two-thirds of Poles (64.9%) believe that warnings about further Russian provocations against Poland are credible.
Source: the results of a SW Research poll commissioned by Onet, as reported by European Pravda
Details: When asked, "Do you consider warnings about possible new Russian provocations against Poland credible?", 64.9% of respondents answered in the affirmative. Some 29.4% answered "definitely yes", while 37.2% said "probably yes".
A total of 18.8% of respondents expressed the opposite view. The option "definitely no" was chosen by 7.6%, while 11.6% answered "probably no". Another 14.3% chose "hard to say".
The SW Research poll commissioned by Onet was conducted from 31 August to 1 September 2026 using computer-assisted web interviewing (CAWI). As part of the study, 800 interviews were conducted among a nationwide sample of adults. A quota sample was used to ensure representativeness by gender, age and the population size of the respondents' cities.
Background:
- This week, Polish Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said that his country is strengthening the protection of its airspace due to recent provocations by Russia.
- From 10 September to 9 December 2026, eastern Poland will be included in the EP R134 temporary restricted airspace zone.
- On 30 July, a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile manufactured in the second quarter of 2026 at a plant in the Moscow Oblast fell in Lublin Voivodeship.
- Earlier, media reported that Poland, Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia are cooperating on protecting against potential Russian attacks on infrastructure in these countries, which could be carried out under a "false flag", as allied intelligence agencies have repeatedly warned.

Indonesia's Mt. Anak Krakatau erupts, spews rocks, volcanic ash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
08:27:03 UTC
17:27:03 KST

Saadet Gokce
05 September 2026•Update: 05 September 2026
Indonesia's Mt. Anak Krakatau erupted overnight into Saturday, spewing rocks and volcanic ash into the air, the country’s Geological Agency said.
“As of today, September 5, 2026, at 4:40 a.m. Western Indonesian Time, the eruption is still ongoing, and rumbling can still be heard from the Krakatau Pasauran PGA Post,” the agency said in a statement.
The volcano's eruptions have continued since July 2, when its alert status was raised to Level III, local media outlet Tempo reported.
“The height of the eruption column was not observed, but the bright red color of the eruption plume was clearly visible,” the report said.
MAGMA Indonesia, a digital platform that provides real-time information about geological hazards across the country, said seismic activity linked to the eruption was recorded from Friday morning, with the seismograph registering a maximum amplitude of 33 millimeters and a duration of 14 seconds.
Three more eruptions occurred Friday morning, followed by a lull before another series late Friday.
Six eruptions were recorded through 12.01 am local time Saturday (1701GMT Friday).
The Geological Agency said the eruption resembled a “lava fountain” that produces lava flows, adding that continuous eruptions lasting several hours are common.
The agency said it received reports of booming sounds and vibrations in parts of West Java, Banten and Lampung that occurred at the same time as Anak Krakatau's activity and are suspected to be related.
It said the volcano's growth since the Dec. 22, 2018, eruption remains relatively small, adding that there is no potential for a collapse large enough to trigger a tsunami.
Indonesia lies along the Pacific “Ring of Fire,” a seismically active zone of fault lines and volcanoes where earthquakes are frequent.

Localized ceasefire takes effect at Zaporozhye Nuclear Power Plant — IAEA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
08:26:46 UTC
17:26:46 KST

BERLIN, September 5. /TASS/. A localized ceasefire has taken effect at the Zaporozhye Nuclear Power Plant (ZNPP) to enable power line repairs, International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) Director General Rafael Grossi said in a statement.
"Another IAEA-brokered localized ceasefire has taken effect to enable power line repairs necessary for the restoration of off-site power to the Zaporozhye NPP after a long outage," the statement reads.
"Due to military activity on the northern side of the Dnieper River, the plant lost the connection to its sole remaining power line - the 330 kilovolt Ferosplavnaya-1 - on August 20. Since then, the ZNPP has depended on emergency diesel generators to cool its six reactors and spent fuel pools. The plant is now running low on diesel fuel reserves and faces a possible station blackout within days unless off-site power is restored or more fuel reserves can be transported to the site, located in an active war zone," the document added.
Under the temporary ceasefire around the damaged power line, Ukrainian technicians will begin power line repairs later today following demining of the area, Grossi said, adding that both sides had been engaging constructively with the IAEA for the sake of nuclear safety and security. An IAEA team will monitor the repairs during the ceasefire.
ZNPP Spokesperson Yevgenia Yashina told TASS earlier that the situation at the plant remained tense as the facility had completely lost power and was relying on generators, while its power units required stable electricity supplies for safety and cooling.

Iranian tanker hit by US attack near Iran’s Kharg Island, Tasnim says

- Kharg Island is a key oil export hub for Iran, which exports 90 per cent of its crude there; US naval blockade since April has disrupted these flows.
- US attacks on Kharg Island increase pressure on Iran's oil industry and economy amid ongoing tensions, after Iran blocked the Strait of Hormuz, a vital oil passage.
AI generated
DUBAI - An Iranian tanker was hit by US forces on Sept 5 near Iran’s key oil export hub, Kharg Island, in the Gulf, the semi-official Iranian news agency Tasnim reported.
According to a Tasnim correspondent from Kharg, the tanker was hit by four US missiles in the area of Kharg Island’s anchorage.
Tasnim quoted local sources as saying there were no casualties and the tanker’s crew was being evacuated.
There was no immediate official announcement by Iranian authorities and US Central Command did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
US President Donald Trump said on Aug 31 in a one-line social media post accompanied by an AI-generated video that Kharg Island was being “blown to smithereens”. Iranian authorities have vowed a strong response if Kharg is attacked.
Iran is the third-largest producer in the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and exported 90 per cent of its crude via Kharg Island before the war, but flows have been disrupted since a US blockade of Iranian oil exports began in mid-April.
Trump said on June 11 that he wanted to take over Kharg Island, but then said a threatened US military operation there was off the table for now, days before Tehran and Washington signed an interim agreement aimed at ending the war on June 17.
A US attack on Kharg would heap further pressure on Iran’s oil industry and its wider economy, which is already reeling from the US naval blockade.
The US imposed its blockade on Iranian ports after Iran effectively shut the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway that carried one-fifth of the world’s oil supply before the war. REUTERS

Factbox: Latest relief and rescue progress at mudslide-hit border port in China's Xizang
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
13:20:49 CST
14:20:49 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 6 (Xinhua) -- A fast-moving chain mudslide, triggered by a high-altitude glacier collapse in Nepal, struck Gyirong Port on the China-Nepal border in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region on Aug. 26, causing heavy casualties and leaving many missing.
Chinese rescuers immediately launched all-out search and rescue operations. Here is what we know about the deadly mudslide and the latest progress in China:
-- Thirty-one people had been confirmed dead and 531 others remained missing as of 6 p.m. Friday.
-- After the land route to Gyirong Port was basically restored on Wednesday morning, large machinery has been used to clear obstacles and create working areas, followed closely by specialized firefighters conducting targeted searches and life-detection equipment verifying suspicious locations.
-- More rescue forces entered the core affected zone of Gyirong Port on Saturday. China Railway Group Limited has provided steel gabions for road reinforcement at the site.
-- The barrier lake above the core area of Gyirong Port has been drained, the river channel has returned to normal flow, and the associated hazard has been largely eliminated.
-- With support from China's National Health Commission and authorities in other regions, more than 210 psychological professionals arrived in Gyirong in three batches. Some counselors with foreign-language skills provided psychological support for families of foreign nationals reported missing in the disaster.
Specialists also assessed the psychological well-being of frontline rescuers, providing group counseling and individual support.
-- Local authorities have organized Tibetan medicine doctors to provide medical treatment and psychological counseling services to resettled residents. ■

SEOUL, Sept. 6 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's cumulative exports this year had reached 709.4 billion U.S. dollars as of Saturday, surpassing the country's record annual total of 709.3 billion U.S. dollars set last year, according to the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources and the Korea Customs Service.
If the current robust export momentum continues, South Korea is expected to reach 1 trillion U.S. dollars in annual exports around early December, according to a report by the head of the Korea Customs Service, which was cited by the South Korean president on social media on Saturday.
Despite challenging external conditions, including hostilities in the Middle East, the country's exports have continued to grow, led by semiconductors, the report said. ■

Putin shows ‘saint-like patience’ – former US judge (VIDEO)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
08:23:09 UTC
17:23:09 KST

Putin shows ‘saint-like patience’ – former US judge (VIDEO)
Russia has the right to strike NATO plants making weapons for Ukraine, but President Vladimir Putin is showing great restraint to avoid a direct clash with the bloc, former American judge Andrew Napolitano has said.
Kiev has been launching hundreds of fixed-wing drones deep into Russian territory on a daily basis in recent months, many of which are manufactured in European countries. Earlier this year, the Defense Ministry in Moscow published a list of enterprises producing the UAVs, some of which are based in the UK, Germany, Italy, Czechia, and other NATO-member states. London and Paris are currently also discussing plans to make long-range SCALP/Storm Shadow missiles in Ukraine.
In an interview with RT on Friday, Napolitano, who hosts the popular ‘Judging Freedom’ interview channel on YouTube, said that “President Putin has demonstrated an almost saint-like capacity for patience and forbearance” by not ordering Russian forces to target those facilities.
“Under international law, he would have every right to strike at the munitions plants and the military, not the civilians… of the countries that are producing the weapons that are striking deep into Russia,” he said.
“I’m sure he understands that. My guess is that he’s considered it, but he’s been consistently patient. Sometimes even to the dismay of his strongest supporters,” the former New Jersey Superior Court judge added.
Putin is focused on the Ukraine conflict and “does not want a war against NATO,” he argued.
The Russian president previously labeled claims of Moscow having aggressive designs against the bloc as “nonsense,” saying that they are only made by Western politicians to distract the public from problems at home and justify growing military spending.
However, Moscow warned the UK in late August that its military facilities and equipment in Ukraine and beyond could become legitimate targets for Russia if Kiev continues to use British-supplied weapons for strikes on Russian territory.
Russian officials also said that if Latvia, Estonia, and Lithuania knowingly helped to facilitate Ukrainian drone attacks against northwestern Russia, Moscow could consider them complicit in those actions and would have the right to self-defense under the UN Charter.
Napolitano said that the Ukraine conflict is “headed into an acceleration” and that he expects “a last-ditched effort by some of the NATO countries to try and prevent the inevitable, which is the achievement by the Russian military of its objectives.”
“The Ukrainians are aware that they’re on their last legs, so to speak, in the war. They know that their days are numbered,” he stressed.
